value.Title: AKU faculty appointed to CPSP Committees for health development
value.NewsSummary: The College of Physician and Surgeons Pakistan (CPSP), appoints faculty from AKU’s Department of Pathology and Microbiology, to constitute a number of committees for Pathology specialties.
value.NewsContent:
The College of Physician and Surgeons Pakistan (CPSP), as a WHO Collaborating Centre for Training in Research and Educational Development of Health Personnel, has recently appointed faculty from AKU’s Department of Pathology and Microbiology, to constitute a number of committees for various Pathology specialties. Faculty appointments are as follows:

  • Prof. Naila Kayani as Dean, Faculty of Histopathology

  • Prof. Afia Zafar as Convener, Committee of Microbiology

  • Prof. Shahid Pervez as Member, Committee of Histopathology

  • Dr Imran Siddiqui  as Member, Committee of Chemical Pathology

  • Dr Rumina Hassan as Member, Committee of Microbiology

  • Dr Erum Khan as Member, Committee of Microbiology

The CPSP, as one of the WHO Collaborating Centres dealing with human resources for health development, aims to contribute to the improvement of health systems performance through research, training and support in the area of ‘health human resources’, which has been identified by WHO and others as one of the most critical areas of intervention. Currently there are over 700 WHO collaborating centres in over 80 member states working with WHO on areas such as nursing, occupational health, communicable diseases, nutrition, mental health, chronic diseases and health technologies.

value.Title: Dr Sarfaroz Niyozov to join as director of IED, Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: ​Dr Sarfaroz Niyozov will be joining the Aga Khan University as Director, Institute for Educational Development, Pakistan in August 2015.
value.NewsContent:
​Dr Sarfaroz Niyozov will be joining the Aga Khan University as Director, Institute for Educational Development, Pakistan in August 2015.

Niyozov is not new to AKU and AKDN. He studied MEd Teacher Education with the first class of IED,P in 1995; received the Aga Khan Foundation International Scholarship Award for PhD in education at the University of Toronto in 1997; and worked with AKU on several educational endeavors, including the establishment of the University of Central Asia in 2000.

Prior to joining AKU, Dr Niyozov served as Associate Professor, Curriculum, Teaching and Learning at the Ontario Institute for Studies in Education, University of Toronto where he was a faculty member for a decade.

His research interests focus on teaching; researching; teacher development and education reform in developing, Muslim and post-communist contexts; global education; and international and comparative curriculum studies.

His doctoral dissertation “Understanding Teaching in the Post-soviet Rural and Mountainous Tajikistan” received two honors, including 2002 Best Dissertation Award by American Education Research Association and 2002 Best Dissertation Award by Comparative International Education Society.

Recently, Dr Niyozov served as a co-director of the Center for Comparative, International and Education Society, and as an editor of the Journal of Curriculum Inquiry at the University of Toronto. He has written extensively about education in post-Soviet countries and the experiences of teachers working with Muslim students in multicultural classrooms.                

In addition, he founded and led the Central Asian Studies Unit at the Institute of Ismaili Studies, London.

​Dr Niyozov was born in Tajikistan, and completed his Honors Degree in Arabic from Tajik State University in 1983. Subsequently, he worked and studied in Yemen, Syria, and Tunisia. Upon completing his graduate studies, he taught at both Dushanbe and Khorog Universities in Tajikistan.​​​

value.Title: AKU Faculty wins prestigious Global Sepsis Award 2015
value.NewsSummary: Dr Madiha Hashmi is honoured for championing improved outcomes from sepsis, promoting World Sepsis Day and the goals of the World Sepsis Declaration in Pakistan.
value.NewsContent:
The jury for the Global Sepsis Awards (GSA) recognized the exemplary efforts of Dr Madiha Hashmi, Assistant Professor, Department of Anaesthesiology, AKU, and President, Pakistan Society of Critical Care Medicine, in championing improved
 outcomes from sepsis, promoting World Sepsis Day and the goals of the World Sepsis Declaration in Pakistan with the 2015 Global Sepsis Award in the category for individual nominees.

The GSA and World Sepsis Day issued the 'Global Sepsis Awards' to honour excellent sepsis awareness and education initiatives and to recognize major achievements of governments, organizations and individuals, consistent with the aims of World Sepsis Declaration and the World Sepsis Day movement. The award jury-comprising internationally recognized experts in patient safety and sepsis management-evaluated all award submissions and identified award recipients.

Dr Hashmi will be presented with the award in a ceremony at the World Federation of Societies of Intensive and Critical Care Medicine meeting in Seoul, later this year.

value.Title: AKU conducts a ‘Heart and Circulation’ CME course
value.NewsSummary: The programme aimed to maintain and raise the standards of anaesthetic care at the highest possible level through continuing medical education in anaesthesiology.
value.NewsContent:
The Aga Khan University (AKU)’s Department of Anaesthesiology in collaboration with the Department of Continuing Professional Education (at AKU), Committee for European Education in Anaesthesiology (CEEA, which is affiliated with European Society of Anaesthesiologists), and World Federation of Societies of Anaesthesiologists (WFSA), successfully organized the CEEA Continuing Medical Education course titled ‘Heart and Circulation’ from March 20-22, 2015.

The programme aimed to maintain and raise the standards of anaesthetic care at the highest possible level through continuing medical education in anaesthesiology. The course included interactive lectures, case based discussions, hands-on workshops on Ultrasound-guided Vascular Access, Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation and Echocardiography. The course was attended by consultants and anaesthesia trainees from AKU and other teaching hospitals of Karachi, Hyderabad, and Nawabshah.

value.Title: AKU Medical College, Pakistan launches strategic planning exercise
value.NewsSummary: Working groups will deliberate and make recommendations to strengthen academic culture and performance.
value.NewsContent:
In order to meet and capitalize on emerging challenges and opportunities, remain contextually relevant and consolidate on existing strengths to allow for its continued excellence, the Medical College, Pakistan initiated a major strategic planning and strengthening exercise to deliberate and make recommendations with reference to the mission, vision and mandate of the Medical College, Pakistan and the Aga Khan University (AKU). 

“A university’s role ultimately is to educate, to produce new knowledge, to help understand the issues that society is facing and to then impart that knowledge in a way that improves the quality of life for an individual and society. At AKU, we do that through our research, knowledge, education and service”, said Mr Firoz Rasul, President and Interim Provost, AKU, in his introductory remarks at the official launch of the exercise, on Thursday at the AKU Auditorium.
The Interim Provost also emphasised the need to reflect on several trends that are redefining the global education and health landscape, including:
The changing role of the ‘educator’ in teaching and education, owing to the use of and advancements in technology, varying education systems and the evolving nature of students: educators are no longer seen just as teachers or 'imparters of knowledge' but as coaches, facilitators and mentors, which significantly affects how learners in formal and informal learning spaces are engaged.
The significance of multi-disciplinarity and its value and impact on student learning
Rapid advancements in technology and their impact on the way medicine and nursing are practiced and taught
The gradual shift from health-care being provided solely in hospitals, due to increasing costs, lack of access, technology advancements and changing lifestyles
The recent explosion of Massive Open Online Courses by leading global universities and the general population’s reluctance to complete the courses after starting them despite their access to all relevant learning resources
The ability to attain a balance between what is relevant and appropriate to the local context yet competitive in global markets
To ensure meaningful and focused discussions, Working Groups have been constituted to deliberate on the progress, developments, innovations, issues and challenges in key areas including: Undergraduate programmes, Graduate programmes, Postgraduate programmes, Continuing Professional Education/Continuing Medical Education programmes, Research and Faculty matters (including faculty campus life, faculty development, succession planning, leadership development, academic support structures and academic/service balance, amongst many others).

The groups will conduct a self-analysis in each area over a six-week period and will present their findings and recommendations at two half-day workshops: one on teaching/learning and associated activities; and the other on research, scholarship and faculty matters, planned for April/May 2016. The recommendations of the groups will become part of a wider Medical College, Pakistan strategic plan as it enters into its next phase of development.

value.Title: Non-communicable diseases pose an increasing threat to health in Pakistan​​
value.NewsSummary: Published in The Lancet, the study was conducted by an international consortium of researchers working on the Global Burden of Disease project and led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation at the University of Washington. Co-authors incl
value.NewsContent:
​​People across Pakistan are living longer but spending more time in ill health as rates of nonfatal diseases and injuries – including major depressive disorder, iron-deficiency anemia, and low back pain – decline more slowly than death rates, according to a new analysis of 301 acute and chronic diseases and injuries in 188 countries.

Published in The Lancet, the study ‘Global, regional, and national incidence, prevalence, and years lived with disability for 301 acute and chronic diseases and injuries in 188 countries, 1990-2013: a systematic analysis for the Global Burden of Disease Study 2013’ was conducted by an international consortium of researchers working on the Global Burden of Disease project and led by the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) at the University of Washington.

“The health of Pakistanis is increasingly threatened by non-communicable diseases such as depression, chronic back pain, and migraines,” said Professor Zulfiqar Bhutta, Founding Director of the Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health at the Aga Khan University and Co-Director at the Center for Global Child Health at The Hospital for Sick Children, and one of the study’s co-authors.

“At the same time, diseases like iron-deficiency anemia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and diabetes are also costing people in Pakistan many years of healthy life. It is critical that we understand which diseases and injuries are causing disability so that we can effectively allocate resources for national planning,” he added.

‘Years lived with disability’ quantifies the impact of health problems that impair mobility, hearing or vision, or cause pain in some way. In 2013, migraines, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and diabetes were among the 10 leading causes of YLDs in Pakistan. Other leading causes included hearing loss, anxiety disorders, and neck pain. For both sexes combined, the leading causes of years lived with disability have remained largely the same during this period, but they take an increased toll on health due to population growth and aging.  

For women in Pakistan, other musculoskeletal disorders – which include shoulder injuries and fractures from osteoporosis – have replaced diarrheal diseases as a leading cause of years lived with disability. Between 1990 and 2013, YLDs from other musculoskeletal disorders and diabetes increased by 163 and 170 per cent respectively. Iron-deficiency anaemia had the smallest per cent increase among top causes of YLDs at 11 per cent.  

Diabetes YLDs also increased for men in Pakistan between 1990 and 2013, climbing 100 per cent. YLDs from depression increased by 94 per cent, and iron-deficiency anemia YLDs decreased by 9 per cent. 

Between 1990 and 2013, YLDs increased globally from 537.6 million in 1990 to 764.8 million in 2013 for both sexes. Men and women around the world share the same leading causes of YLDs, with the exception of schizophrenia as a leading cause for men and other musculoskeletal disorders for women. Musculoskeletal disorders, mental and substance use disorders, neurological disorders, and chronic respiratory conditions were the main drivers of YLDs in 2013. The disease burdens of both low back pain and depression have increased more than 50 per cent since 1990.  

Researchers found that as people aged they experienced a greater number of ailments resulting from nonfatal diseases and injuries. Many people also suffered from multiple conditions at the same time. The number of people who suffered from 10 or more ailments increased by 52 per cent. And it is not just the elderly who are affected. Although the impact of YLDs increases with age, of the 2.3 billion people who suffered from more than five ailments, 81 per cent of them were younger than 65 years old.

A relatively small number of diseases have a massive impact, researchers found. Just two acute diseases – affecting people for less than three months – caused more than 20 billion new cases of disease globally in 2013: upper respiratory infections (18.8 billion) and diarrheal diseases (2.7 billion). And just eight causes of chronic diseases – affecting people for three months or longer – impacted more than 10 per cent of the world’s population. These included tension-type headaches and iron-deficiency anemia.  

In 2013, war and conflict was a leading cause of YLDs in several countries as well, including El Salvador, Guatemala, Lebanon, Peru, and Syria. In three countries – Cambodia, Nicaragua, and Rwanda – war was the top cause of years lived with disability. Other notable causes of YLDs in different regions included falls (Central Europe), asthma (a top-10 cause in many Latin American countries), and opioid dependence (a top-five cause in several Middle Eastern countries). Nonfatal conditions are not yet becoming the dominant source of disease burden in sub-Saharan Africa as they are in other parts of the world, but their impact has grown since 1990.

“What ails you isn’t necessarily what kills you,” said IHME Director Dr Christopher Murray. “As nonfatal illnesses and related ailments affect more people of all ages, countries must look closely at health policy and spending to target these conditions.” 

Leading causes of YLDs in Pakistan for both sexes, 2013

​​1. ​Major depressive disorder
​2. ​Iron-deficiency anemia
3.​​ ​​Low back pain​​
​4. ​​Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
​5. ​Diabetes mellitus
​6. ​Age-related and other hearing loss
​7. ​Anxiety disorders
​8. ​Neck pain
​9. ​Diarrheal diseases
 
Leading causes of YLDs in Pakistan for men, 2013

​​1.​ Low back pain
2​. ​Iron-deficiency anemia
​3. ​Major depressive disorder
4​. ​Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
5​. ​Migraine​​
6​. ​Age-related and other hearing loss
7​. ​Diabetes mellitus
​8. ​Anxiety disorders
9.​ ​Neck pain
10.​ ​Diarrheal diseases
 
Leading causes of YLDS in Pakistan for women, 2013

1​. Major depressive disorder​
​2. ​Iron-deficiency anemia
​3. ​Migraine
​4. ​Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
​5. ​Low back pain
​6. ​Anxiety disorders
​7. ​Diabetes mellitus
​8. ​Neck pain
​9. ​Other musculoskeletal disorders
​10. ​Age-related and other hearing loss​​

value.Title: AKU’s FCPS candidate receives Burki Gold Medal 2014
value.NewsSummary: Dr Zainab Abbas, receives the prestigious honour at the 49th convocation of the College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan, making her the fourth family medicine candidate to achieve this distinction, in the award’s 46-year history.
value.NewsContent:
Dr Zainab Abbas, the Aga Khan University’s candidate for the College of Physicians and Surgeons’ fellowship in family medicine has received the 2014 Burki Gold Medal at the 49th convocation of the College of Physicians and Surgeons Pakistan on Saturday.

Dr Abbas scored the highest marks in all specialities in the year 2014. In the award’s 46-year history, she is only the fourth family medicine candidate to achieve this distinction.
Born and raised in Karachi, Dr Zainab Abbas did her MBBS from Dow Medical College in 2007. After finishing her house job, she entered AKU’s family medicine residency programme in 2009, graduated in 2013, and appeared for her speciality FCPS examination in 2014.

“The Aga Khan University has a major role in establishing family medicine as a speciality not only in Pakistan but also in South Asia. I am extremely grateful to my alma mater and my teachers for giving me an opportunity to be a well-rounded physician. I dedicate this gold medal to the Department of Family Medicine,” she said.

“We are proud of Zainab for achieving distinction in a speciality that is changing health care around the world with its holistic approach towards preventive, curative and rehabilitative care,” commented Dr Waris Qidwai, Professor and Chair, Department of Family Medicine, AKU.“Because family medicine physicians provide primary care and work in the community, they have a better understanding of issues faced by patients and families. Their presence on the front line allows early detection of diseases that can be better managed with fewer resources and better outcome,” he added.

Dr Abbas is currently practising family medicine at a teaching clinic in Calgary, Canada.
Sponsored by CPSP’s founding president Lieutenant General W. A. Burki, the medal is awarded to candidates with the highest marks in FCPS-II with the proviso that marks are over 70 per cent and all CPSP examinations are passed in the first attempt.

value.Title: AKU joins the International Network for Quality Assurance Agencies in Higher Education
value.NewsSummary: The International Network for Quality Assurance Agencies in Higher Education has accepted the Aga Khan University as an associate member.
value.NewsContent:
The International Network for Quality Assurance Agencies in Higher Education has accepted the Aga Khan University as an associate member. The membership has been granted in recognition of the University’s excellent work in the area of quality assurance in higher education.

​“This is a testament to AKU’s commitment to the highest academic standards to ensure students have the best of learning experiences at par with any respected university in the world,” said Dr Tashmin Khamis, Director, AKU’s Networks of Quality Assurance and Improvement, and Teaching and Learning.

AKU’s firm commitment to cultivating a culture of quality in education has been acknowledged by the Inter-University Council of East Africa and the Higher Education Commission. Both have recognized the role AKU’s QAI_net has been playing in improving the academic quality of programmes according to international best practices. 

“By becoming a member of INQAAHE, AKU has access to enormous reassurance, support and assistance in our daily quality assurance work, including a Good Practice database and guidelines, peer mentoring on QA and sharing of lessons through the INQAAHE Bulletin and journal Quality in Higher Education,” stated Dr Khamis.

INQAAHE is a global association of over 200 organizations active in the theory and practice of quality assurance in higher education. The majority of its members are quality assurance regulatory agencies, including those in countries where AKU has campuses.

value.NewsContent:
The UK may be under a grey cloud until March, but this week saw Londoner's attention turn to the sunny skies of Morocco, East Africa and Egypt as ISMC hosted a sell-out evening as part of the 2015 
Nour Festival of Arts.  

Over 70 people gathered at Kensington's Leighton House to hear three renowned experts speak on Islamic parks and gardens as vehicles of social change. 

The evening's Chair, Philip Wood, introduced fascinating presentations from Jurjen van der Tas: Deputy Director of the Historic Cities Program of the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, Tom Stuart-Smith: 

Internationally-renowned landscape gardener and RHS Chelsea Gold medallist and Mark Bryant: Development Officer for the Centre for the Study of Islam, University of Cardiff.  

The ensuing discussion was wide-ranging and included thoughts on how to usefully include traditional Islamic water features in London gardens, to ideas on how to maintain the beauty and tranquility of Al-Azhar Park in Cairo.

value.Title: ​ISMC offers a hand up to Kabul’s MA hopefuls
value.NewsSubTitle: ​Pilot course for students in Kabul
value.NewsSummary: ​​ISMC pilot course offers a hand up to young Afghani students
value.NewsContent:
​​In Kabul, Afghanistan, 16 young university graduates are hard at work on a six-week prep course for the International English Language Test System, or IELTS, a standardised English test for students hoping to study in an English-speaking country. The men and women taking the Kabul IELTS prep course have a singular goal in mind: a test score of 6.5, the benchmark for applications to ISMC’s MA in Muslim Cultures. 

​Eshaq Muqbel, an MA-hopeful from Badakhshan province, is counting on the course to get him to the ISMC – and from there, to a career in academia and development in Afghanistan.

“I want to be a lecturer at a highly accredited Afghan university and do voluntary work for the betterment of society, perhaps working with the AKDN agencies in the related field,” he said. But first, Eshaq needs to continue his education – and this course, funded in part by the ISMC, is designed to help him and his colleagues make the leap from national stand-outs to international success stories.

“We are thinking of preparing leaders for the future,” said Fakhrullah Safari, a programme organiser and a member of the Aga Khan National Council of Afghanistan.

“Education in Afghanistan isn’t up to this level, but the ISMC is, and Afghanistan needs these kinds of people.”
Safari said the course was designed to spur interest in the study of Muslim culture, and also to meet an ​increasingly common need in the Afghan economy: for better-educated adults.

“In previous years, we had job opportunities in Afghanistan for anyone with a 12th-grade education or a Bachelor’s degree. But now companies want a Master’s degree. The people in this class want to pursue their education, and in the future, they want leading positions in our society.” ​The pilot course builds a crucial bridge for students who need to up-skill before writing the IELTS, but can’t afford the $350-$400 cost of private prep courses. It begins and ends with a practice test,  so students can track their progress, and includes regular IELTS mock tests. At the end of the six-week gauntlet, students take a Password test that assesses their knowledge of English grammar and vocabulary, as well as listening and speaking skill, and gives them a good indication of their IELTS level. For students like Eshaq, this sort of in-classroom learning is a crucial part of test preparation. 

“The skills and techniques we learned about the IELTS  are really valuable and helpful,” he said. “The practice and daily activities push the students to read more and help us be better prepared for the test.”

ISMC’s support has been crucial in getting this prep course off the ground: ISMC funding covers the cost of a classroom and an experienced instructor, as well as tea and biscuits for students – a valuable bit of cultural prep for 16 young people dreaming of London. Student Khudai Behrdi, intent on a career in education with a focus on youth and  Islamic issues, said his English skills had noticeably improved. “What was unique for me in class was the hard work of our instructor. I feel great changes in myself as a result of attending the course.”

For student Khadija Rahyab, the course has made an enormous difference to her English skills – but whether that will be difference enough remains to be seen. “The most valuable parts were the teacher, the materials, and the course outline. But it was too short and we need more time, because as English is not our native language still there are some common mistakes we make that might decrease our points,” she said. Despite any shortcomings, Safari is convinced that if Eshaq, Khadija and their colleagues hit the IELTS benchmark and make their way to the ISMC, the power of a course like this will be clear. “This is a unique degree. For their future, for the careers they are dreaming about, this ISMC degree will be life-changing,” he said. Safari and his colleagues are well aware of the risk that this prep course could in some way facilitate the ‘brain drain’ whereby the country’s most able students leave for better opportunities elsewhere, but they cite a broader trend where young people leave, become better educated, gather experience – and often a second citizenship – and then return to their home country. But for the young people from Bamiyan, Badakhshan, Sangin and beyond, all buckling down to study in a Kabul classroom, the only horizon that matters now is the one at the end of this month.​

value.Title: Reproductive, Maternal, Newborn and Child Health: Priorities for action!
value.NewsSubTitle: Recent seminars and workshops
value.NewsSummary: ​A series of workshops and seminars was held recently in Karachi.
value.NewsContent:
Pakistan faces huge health challenges due to the existing burden of poor reproductive, maternal and child health and malnutrition as well as the emergence of non-communicable diseases. 

To discuss these challenges, Aga Khan University’s Centre of Excellence in Women and Child Health held a series of workshops and seminars on the AKU Stadium Road Campus in Karachi on February 19-22, 2015. 

Pre-seminar workshops were organized on topics like women’s empowerment for reproductive health, emergency obstetrical care, and emergency newborn care, amongst others. 

The last in the series of events on Regional Mother Newborn and Child Health provided a unique platform to the faculty, students, nurses and researchers to come and present their studies via talks and poster presentations. 

The series attracted a great deal of interest (with over 160 abstracts received and recorded in the Abstract Book) and was well attended by people from AKU as well as outside (approximately 250 people), including leaders of Pakistan Paediatric Association, Society of Obsterics and Gynaecology - Pakistan, Pakistan Medical Association, Federal Director General Health Services, Provincial Health Managers of MNCH, LHW and EPI programmes, health practitioners (doctors, nurses and paramedics staff), staff and students of AKU.​

value.Title: ​Dr Malik Ajani publishes his first book: ‘Citizenship, the Self and the Other’
value.NewsSummary: ​​ISMC graduate Malik Ajani (Class of 2006) published his first book: “Citizenship, the Self and the Other"
value.NewsContent: ​After completing a PhD at Royal Holloway in 2014, ISMC graduate Malik Ajani (Class of 2006) published his first book: “Citizenship, the Self and the Other – Critical Discussions on Citizenship and How to Approach Religious and Cultural Difference”. In his book, Malik uses discussions with citizenship educators in England to share insights regarding the challenges and opportunities of creating a pluralistic society in today’s globalised world and to develop an understanding of how religious and cultural difference can be approached. The book focuses on multi-faith and multi-ethnic societies, gathering ideas and research from a wide field of international scholarship, such as political science, philosophy, education, and cultural studies. Dr David Taylor, Director of ISMC said: ‘Malik’s work is an important intervention in one of the key debates of our time.’

value.NewsSubTitle: ​Mayotte 2015: excavation led by Dr Stephane Pradines unearthed a treasure trove of discoveries
value.NewsSummary: An excavation led by ISMC Associate Professor, Dr Stephane Pradines has unearthed a treasure trove of discoveries.​
value.NewsContent:
​An excavation led by ISMC’s Dr Stephane Pradines has unearthed a treasure trove of discoveries. The dig on the tiny island of Mayotte, part of the Comoros archipelagos in the Western Indian Ocean, is held every year with the aim of understanding settlement patterns and discovering more about the people who lived and traded in this part of the world.

This year, the team found large quantities of rock crystal fragments, chips and flakes of different sizes. Objects made from rock crystal are highly prized by collectors and art-lovers and are displayed worldwide in museums including the Victoria and Albert Museum in London, the Louvre in Paris and the Metropolitan Museum in New York. Indeed rock crystal is incorporated into the treasures of Christian kingdoms such as Saint Mark's Basilica in Venice and the Basilica Cathedral of Saint-Denis near Paris. 

The Mayotte site is world-renowned for its rich history and this discovery has far reaching implications for accurately pinpointing trade routes and settlement patterns. Dr Pradines explains: “Objects can’t lie! We discovered a range of artefacts, for example ceramics, which mean that we can be much more certain that there was active trade between this area and the East. Previously we needed to rely on written accounts – and they are not as reliable. This latest discovery helps us to be much more certain about the exact international trade routes at the time than we could be when relying on manuscripts alone. What struck me most, is the complexity of international trade in the Indian Ocean in the early Middle Ages – an early example of what would now be called globalisation.” 

This dig also uncovered two Muslim burial sites from the mid-12th century, showing that the central area of the site was dedicated to ritual activities, probably with a cemetery and a mosque, showing that the local population converted to Islam during or before the 12th century.  
So what is the next chapter for the team? Dr Pradines is optimistic that the site has many more stories to tell. He says; “I would love to find some architectural remains of houses or religious settlements. That will definitely be the next big discovery.” 

The excavation, led by Dr Stephane Pradines, was coordinated by the French Department of Cultural Affairs (Réunion) and supported by the ISMC-AKU and Conseil Général (Mayotte). Read more and listen to an interview​ with Dr Pradines.​

value.Title: ​Farewell to Prof Pauline Rea-Dickins
value.NewsSummary: ​​On June 11, at an event at the New Africa Hotel in Dar es Salaam, about 130 faculty, staff, students and friends of AKU, and IED, EA celebrated Professor Pauline Rea-Dickin’s 5-year tenure as director of the Institute and bid her farewell.
value.NewsContent:
​On June 11, at an event at the New Africa Hotel in Dar es Salaam, about 130 faculty, staff, students and friends of AKU, and IED, EA celebrated Professor Pauline Rea-Dickin’s 5-year tenure as director of the Institute and bid her farewell. The occasion was also used to welcome the incoming director, Professor Joe Lugalla. The University was represented by Vice Provost Kweku Bentil who delivered the welcome address and read a personal message from Provost Greg Moran to Pauline and all colleagues at IED, EA.

Along with Dr Bentil, other speakers included Assistant Professor Dr Nicholas Wachira, MEd student Natasha Kassam, IT Manager Arbogast Fabian, incoming Director Joe Lugalla, Head of Research, Professor Anjum Halai, and Pauline who delivered a short but emotional farewell speech.  

Pauline was presented with a plaque from her colleagues at AKU and she and her partner, James Dickins, were given a gift of a set of Tanzanian-made bed linens. The highlight of the evening was a 10-minute slide show, “Down Memory Lane with Pauline,” featuring a collection of photos of Pauline at various times at IED. The slide show and the entire programme were developed by a planning commi​ttee consisting of IED, EA faculty, staff, and student representatives, with oversight and support from the Office of the Provost.​​

value.Title: ​Parks and Gardens - Bringing Social Change Where it Matters
value.NewsSubTitle: ​ISMC Hosts Panel Discussion at This Year's Nour Festivale
value.NewsSummary: ​ISMC Hosts a Panel Event as Part of 2015 Nour Festival
value.NewsContent:
​Islamic parks and gardens have long been treasured as havens of tranquillity in a busy world, but today, the Aga Khan Development Network is developing  green spaces that do much more – they are the catalysts for , acting as agents of change for the communities around them. 

On 3 November, three renowned experts in Islamic gardens came together to debate how Islamic parks can act as catalysts for social and economic change. The event was organised by the Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations as part of the Nour Festival of Arts, an annual event that brings together authors, artists, academics, 
historians and social commentators to shine light on the best of contemporary Middle Eastern and North African art and culture. “Parks that reflect Islamic values in their design and operation offer an environment that is conducive not only to unwinding, re-energising and reflection, but also to social bonding, family togetherness  and social cohesion,” said Jurjen van der Tas, Deputy Director of the Historic Cities Program of the Aga Khan Trust for Culture.

Mr van der Tas, whose speciality is transforming vast public spaces, spoke as part of shared a panel with the Royal Horticultural Society’s Chelsea Gold medallist Tom Stuart-Smith, a gardens and planting expert, and the University of Cardiff’s Mark Bryant, an expert on biodiversity conservation and ecological sustainability from an Islamic perspective. Islamic parks, with their cooling water features, tiled walkways and shaded nooks for quiet conversation, have long been a treasured spot for rest and contemplation across the Middle East and 
North Africa. Londoners may be spoiled for choice when it comes to walking and rambling, but these gardens offer a different sort of appeal – and vital social and economic benefits.The full effect of a vast green space, bespoke plantings, sustainable design and urban renewal can be witnessed in a megalopolis like Cairo, where the Al-Azhar Park offers vital breathing space  to nearly two million visitors each year. This project transformed not just the a sprawling, 200-year-old garbage dump that became into a lush, manicured garden, but revitalised 
the entire community around it.

Expertise and investment from the Aga Khan Trust for Culture​ has facilitated lasting economic and social development both led by and directly benefiting local the people and local businesses around the park. Al-Azhar Park now employs more than 200 staff and generated nearly US$1 million in income last year.
The ethical underpinning of Al-Azhar Park shows the AKDN ethos in action – a space designed to include all people, that demonstrates stewardship of the earth’s resources and offers a sense of peace and harmony to all who enter. It is also about building enterprise and agency in the local community.

​​Arms and armoury enthusiasts formed an appreciative audience for ISMC's guest speaker Dr Manouchehr Khorasani on Friday 6 November.  The lecture was chaired by ISMC Associate Professor, Dr Stephane Pradines and saw Dr Khorasani share insights from his new book; Persian Fire and Steel, Historical Firearms of Iran.  A world-renowned expert on Iranian arms and armoury, Dr Khorasani has written five books and co-authored four books, as well as publishing 147 articles in different journals across the world, winning the Book Prize of the Islamic Republic of Iran in 2009 and 2012.

value.NewsSummary: ​​The AKU Network of Teaching and Learning (TL_net) has embarked on a new initiative in collaboration with members from other universities in Kenya.
value.NewsContent:

value.Title: ​Philip Wood awarded prestigious British Academy grant
value.NewsSubTitle: ​British Academy Rising Star Engagement Awards 2016
value.NewsSummary: ​​ISMC receives BARSEA award
value.NewsContent:
​ISMC is delighted to announce that Philip Wood has been awarded a British Academy Rising Star Engagement Award. The award will be used to support a two-day workshop later this year to train academics in how to communicate their research via digital media.

ISMC’s Director, David Taylor, said; “Congratulations to Philip on a major mark of recognition by the UK’s most senior body in the humanities and social sciences. Our colleague, Sarah Savant received the same award a year ago. For a small institution like ours to receive two of these highly competitive awards is a remarkable achievement.”

The British Academy’s Rising Star Engagement Awards (BARSEA) enables established early career scholars to actively engage in the work of the Academy and to enhance their own skills and career development through the organisation of events, training, and mentoring activities for a wide range of other early career researchers.

Philip Wood summed up what the award will mean; “The support from the British Academy will enable ISMC to early to mid-career academics an opportunity to improve their knowledge and understanding of digital media - an increasingly important avenue for all of us to ensure our work is publicised.”

value.Title: Global Launch of Turnitin Implementation at AKU
value.NewsSummary: ​AKU has embarked on using Turnitin to accomplish its vision to enhance the quality of academic activities.
value.NewsContent:
​​Turnitin is an antiplagiarism software that evaluates work against multiple sources to identify unoriginal content including tracking of work online. AKU has embarked on using Turnitin to accomplish its vision to enhance the quality of academic activities. 

Turnitin global license was acquired so that the software could be used as an educational tool in writing the ‘right way.' 

Initially Turnitin was made available to students and then to faculty members, including entity resource persons. A partnership was constituted between the Network of Quality Assurance & Improvement, Registrar’s Office and the Information and Technology division to implement Turnitin in a holistic manner. 

At AKU, 110 faculty and 398 students in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, UK, and Pakistan have been trained. Currently, training sessions are being conducted in Pakistan. Helpdesks for Turnitin have been created in each of AKU's country campuses.​

For more information, contact Faisal Notta, Assistant Director, QAI_net.

value.Title: Moving Towards a New Learning Agenda: AKU Teaching Champions
value.NewsSummary: ​The Network of Teaching and Learning launched its first bi-monthly learning session for AKU’s Teaching Champions on March 12, 2015.
value.NewsContent:
​​​The Network of Teaching and Learning launched its first bi-monthly learning session for AKU’s Teaching Champions on March 12, 2015. These learning sessions are intended to develop a community of practice and enquiry, thereby contributing to the scholarship of teaching and learning at AKU.

​​The learning session, which was titled “Engaged Learning: Are We All on the Same Page?” was attended by 29 faculty members from across AKU’s schools and institutes: SONAM, East Africa and Pakistan; IED, East Africa; DED; and Medical College.

​​Effective teaching and engaged learning are often used in the same breath and, therefore, the session set out to explore the following questions: What exactly is engaged learning? Why is it important? What are its manifestations in our classrooms? How do we ensure that it occurs in our classrooms? What is the student’s role in this process? What is AKU’s vision of and strategy for engaged learning? The session was abuzz with discussion throughout. 

​​At the end of the session, one participant, Raheel Lakhani, Educational Technologist, commented: “I really enjoyed your session… I really like the model you shared and it makes so much sense for both curriculum design and pedagogy, and fostering autonomy and lifelong learning which service industry demands. Your session was very engaging.”

The AKU Teaching and Learning Framework​​ provides a shared understanding of teaching excellence.

For more information, contact Jane Rarieya, Assistant Director, TL_net.​

​​​

value.Title: ​​Time to Think Flexibly About Learning
value.NewsSummary: ​The Network of Teaching and Learning hosted the first of its seminar series on March 25, 2015. The seminar, “Thinking Flexibly About Flexible Learning,” was attended by 117 people from across AKU.​
value.NewsContent:
The Network of Teaching and Learning hosted the first of its seminar series on March 25, 2015. The seminar, “Thinking Flexibly About Flexible Learning,” was led by Professor Susan Crichton, Director of Faculty of Education at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan.

The seminar was attended by 117 participants from across AKU campuses, including Kabul.

Professor Crichton reminded the audience that information is NOT in short supply since the internet has been around for over 20 years and therefore, teaching and learning in higher education needs to explore pedagogical approaches that leverage the tools of our time. value.Title: ​Professor Abdou Filali-Ansary honoured by AKU
value.NewsSubTitle: ​Professor Abdou Filali-Ansary confered title of Professor Emeritus
value.NewsSummary: ​​Professor Abdou Filali-Ansary confered title of Professor Emeritus​​
value.NewsContent: ​ISMC is pleased to announce the conferment of the title of Professor Emeritus on Professor Abdou Filali-Ansary. Professor Filali-Ansary is a distinguished philosopher and writer who was instrumental in the establishment of the Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations, and who led it throughout its formative years, serving as the Institute’s founding Director and more recently, lead in the Institute’s project on ‘Governance for the Public Good in Muslim Contexts’. This project has focused on understanding how traditions of good governance in the Muslim world can be the basis for governance in the contemporary world. Dr David Taylor, ISMC’s Director said; “We are enormously grateful for the great contribution Professor Filali-Ansary has made to ISMC. Our faculty and staff work hard to ensure that our work today stays true to those founding principles of intellectual exchange and inquiry. We are reminded now, more than ever, of the importance of that mandate.” To find out more about Professor Filali-Ansary click here ​to read the full citation, honouring Professor Filali-Ansary’s work and contribution to AKU.

The forum includes a conference which will provide a unique opportunity for quality assurance practitioners, top administrators of higher education institutions, executive members of national accreditation bodies, higher education researchers and policy makers to share ideas on quality assurance issues, systems, practices, challenges and promoting for prom​​oting quality in higher education prospects in East Africa. ​

value.Title: ​ AKU hosts the 5th East African Higher Education Quality Assurance Network (EAQAN) Regional Forum in Kenya​
value.NewsSummary: ​Over 120 participants from universities in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda attended the forum.
value.NewsContent:
EAQAN, a network of quality assurance practitioners in East Africa held its fifth Regional Forum in Limuru, Kenya on May 4-8, 2015. Over 120 participants from universities in Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda attended the forum. This consisted of quality assurance practitioners, vice chancellors and deputy vice chancellors, executive members of national accreditation bodies and the Inter-Univ​ersity Council for East Africa (IUCEA). 

The objectives of the forum were to:
- Build capacity of QA officers through expert led training workshops on QA issues in higher education 
- Disseminate best practices on QA from the region through sharing of research and scholarship by QA officers 
- Network and garner support for HE quality from senior university management

The forum was officially opened by the Kenyan Cabinet Secretary for Education, Science and Technology Prof Jacob Kaimenyi. 

Dr. Tashmin Khamis, Director of AKU Networks for Quality Assurance and Improvement and Teaching & Learning, is the current president and hosted the conference in collaboration with Commission for University Education Kenya, which was supported by the IUCEA, DAAD (The German Academic Exchange Service) and HRK (The German Rector’s Conference). AKU, as part of the secretariat, was commended for its leadership in enhancing quality of higher education in the East African region including on enhancing teaching quality.  

Under the theme “Enhancing Quality in Higher Education to Strengthen the Student Learning Experience” the forum provided a unique and an important opportunity for AKU faculty to showcase the work that we are doing in quality, teaching and learning. 

​AKU contributed to the conference through faculty presentations on sharing best practices and running a workshop on engaged teaching by Dr Jane Rarieya, Assistant Director, TL_net.​​​

value.Title: ​AKU registers with International Quality Assurance Agencies in Higher Education
value.NewsSummary: ​The membership approval was given in recognition of the excellent work of AKU in the area of quality assurance under the leadership of Dr Tashmin Khamis.
value.NewsContent:
​The International Network for Quality Assurance Agencies in Higher Education (INQAAHE) has approved AKU as an associate member. INQAAHE is a global association of over 200 organizations active in the theory and practice of quality assurance in higher education. The majority of its members are quality assurance regulatory agencies, including those in countries where AKU has campuses, and this membership will facilitate our relationships with those agencies.​

The approval was given in recognition of the excellent work of AKU in the area of quality assurance under the leadership of Dr Tashmin Khamis. In her capacity as director of the AKU Networks of Quality, Teaching and Learning, she attended the 2015 INQAAHE Conference in Chicago in early April and engaged actively in discussions there. Dr Khamis, who is also president of the East African Higher Education Quality Assurance Network (EAQAN), was supported to attend the conference by INQAAHE and the Inter-University Council for East Africa to represent EAQAN and to present on the internal quality assurance work at AKU.

Read more about INQAAHE here or contact Dr Tashmin Khamis.​

value.Title: ​AKU Provost opens the Network of Teaching & Learning’s Scholarship of Teaching & Learning Inaugural Conference 2015
value.NewsSummary: ​AKU TL_net opens Scholarship of Teaching & Learning Inaugural Conference.
value.NewsContent:
​On August 20, the AKU Network of Teaching and Learning (TL_net) held its first Scholarship of Teaching & Learning Inaugural Conference titled, Engaged Teaching for Engaged Learning.  Over 150 faculty in Karachi, Dar es Salaam, London and Nairobi took part both in person and virtually.

In his opening remarks the Provost reflected on his personal experience as a new young faculty member and the challenges he faced in the classroom - challenges that led him to understand the importance of teaching support of faculty.  This is the second time the Provost as been instrumental in setting up a unit for teaching and learning.  He pointed out the importance of having a place where faculty, especially ones new to the university, can get support services easily. 

The Provost congratulated the Director of the Networks of Quality, Teaching and Learning and the Network staff as well as AKU’s faculty for their commitment to improvement in teaching and learning. The Provost said:

'In AKU’s desire to be a student-centred “university of and for the developing world,” TL_net is critical to the improvement of AKU’s teaching and, thus, the success of our students in three very specific areas: (a) teaching and learning support; (b) promoting the scholarship of teaching and learning; and (c) evaluation, accountability and outreach on teaching and learning.'

Over the next two days, more than 60 faculty members will present posters and papers and will participate in workshops along with the other participants. Guest speakers, Prof Janet Welch from the University of Alberta and Prof Arshad Ahmad from McMaster University’s Institute for Innovation and Excellence in Teaching & Learning (MIIETL), will give keynote addresses on various topics in the area of teaching and learning.

value.Title: Scholarship of Teaching and Learning Conference 2015: Engaged Teaching for Engaged Learning​
value.NewsSummary: ​SoTL Conference in Karachi took place on August 20-21, 2015
value.NewsContent:
The Network of Teaching and Learning (TL_net) held its inaugural Scholarship of Teaching and Learning Conference on August 20 and 21st 2015, the largest AKU faculty development session involving all AKU entities in Pakistan and East Africa. The Conference, titled “Engaged Teaching for Engaged Learning”, brought together 130 AKU faculty members, in person and online, from Pakistan, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, and the United Kingdom. In addition, 20 participants joined from AKDN institutions, including Aga Khan Foundation (AKF), Aga Khan Education Services (AKES), and the Institute of Ismaili Studies (IIS). There were thirty papers and nineteen digital poster presentations focused on innovative pedagogies, teaching with technology, and assessment for learning. 

Participants noted that the faculty development workshops were the most useful in terms of rethinking their teaching practice. Workshops were conducted on the following areas: 

  • The Ultimate Teaching Technology: Students as Scholarship of Teaching and Learning Partners - Arshad Ahmad, McMaster University
  • Changing the Culture of the Classroom - Janet Welch, University of Alberta
  • Improving Assessment to Promote Learning - Jeff Tan, ISMC London
  • Effective Teaching for Effective Learning - Zahraa Bhimji & Zaitoon Shivji, AKUH Karachi
  • The Role of Contemporary Educators: Engaged Teaching for Engaged Learning in Virtual Learning Environments - Jacqueline Dias, SONAM Pakistan
  • Facilitating Real Learning in Our Classrooms - Jane Rarieya & Tashmin Khamis, TL_net
  • Faculty also greatly appreciated the keynote sessions by Professor Arshad Ahmed and Professor Janet Welch which focused on using the science and evidence behind effective teaching as well as the use of technology to promote better student engagement
Feedback from the Conference was exceptionally positive. Below are a few testimonials from participants:

“First of all, congratulations on planning and conducting a wonderful conference. It was good to see (at least for me first time in a conference – I have only observed this in ERC meetings) health and educational professionals working together. Thank you so much. Secondly, the workshop facilitated by both of you was wonderful. Thank you for engaging us in planning and implementing (instead of just telling us theory).” — Dr. Sadia Bhutta, Faculty IED, Pakistan

“I wanted to say all the sessions I attended were very stimulating. It was great to see how much rich discussion there was in many of the sessions.” — Sheila Manji, Aga Khan Foundation Geneva

This Conference has undoubtedly benchmarked Scholarship of Teaching and Learning at AKU. The Network of Teaching and Learning commits to support our faculty, and will be holding the next SoTL​ Conference in August 2017.

value.Title: A Chance to be Mentored Virtually by Academics Without Borders
value.NewsSubTitle: ​Academics Without Borders: virtual mentorship programme
value.NewsSummary: ​​Ag​a Khan University’s (AKU) President Mr Firoz Rasul formally launched the Virtual Faculty Mentorship Programme, an initiative of AKU’s Network of Teaching and Learning on October 26, 2015.​
value.NewsContent:
President Firoz Rasul formally launched a virtual Faculty Mentorship Programme that pairs mentors from Academics Without Borders with AKU faculty mentees drawn from medicine, nursing and education. AWB members from Canada and the US, and AKU faculty members from Kenya, Tanzania and Pakistan – 25 participants in all – joined the event online.

An initiative of AKU’s Network of Teaching and Learning, the programme brings together mentor and mentee virtually for at least two years. AWB Mentors bring a rich experience in teaching, research and faculty development to this relationship.
 
“The mentor-mentee partnership is meant to prompt actionable research that will ultimately improve teaching practice, ” Dr Tashmin Khamis, Director, TL_net, explained, “with the overall aim of enhancing scholarship of teaching and learning at AKU.”
 
Mentors will support faculty members by collaboratively engaging in projects to enhance teaching and learning: providing assistance in publishing their work by co-writing, reviewing draft publications or identifying avenues of publication; and offering advice on relevant resources/links to further develop their scholarship in teaching and learning.

Steve Davis, Executive Director and Founder of AWB, lauded the successful partnership with AKU to date, and reiterated AWB’s commitment to assisting AKU faculty members in the years ahead.

Expressing his appreciation and excitement at the launch of this initiative, President Rasul said: “Mentoring, coaching, and developing faculty, as all of you know, is a very important part of a university’s role in building capacity for teaching and research. Without access to the type of experience that you all offer and bring, we would not be able to do the things we do.”

value.Title: Balkan or Anatolian: The Perpetual Predicament of Classifying Turkish Cities
value.NewsSubTitle: ISMC's Dr Aptin Khanbaghi Shared his Expertise
value.NewsSummary: ISMC's Aptin Khanbaghi, Senior Researcher and Project Team Leader for Muslim Civilisations Abstracts offered his perspective on the topical issue of
value.NewsContent:
Turkey's unique geographical position has sparked numerous debates attempting to categorise Turkish and Ottoman urban architecture as Western or Eastern. 

Dr Khanbaghi discussed how the rich diversity of the Muslim world is strikingly expressed through its myriad of cities.   As a consequence, a number of these analyses have diffused a subjective understanding of Turkish and Ottoman culture. ISMC's Muslim Civilisations Abstracts project has gathered the perspectives and interpretations of a series of Turkish researchers whose objectives have been to display the realities of Turkish cities and the most pressing issues of Turkish urban centres. The examination of these books reveals the distinctness of Turkish cities and at the same time highlights their similarities with global urban hubs and Third World mega cities. Dr Khanbhagi's presentationcentred on examining the Turkish city as perceived in Europe and the changing Turkish city as projected by local Turkish authors.​

value.Title: ​How Do We Know That We Are Providing A Programme of Good Quality? A Modern (R)evolution.
value.NewsSummary: ​​QAI_net holds Provost Speaker Series
value.NewsContent:
​The AKU Network of Quality Assurance and Improvement (QAI_net) hosted the Provost Series on November 24, 2016. Titled How Do We Know That We Are Providing a Programme of Good Quality? A Modern (R)evolution, the session was facilitated by Dr Sam Scully. Dr Sam Scully is an Academics Without Borders (AWB) volunteer working with QAI_net. Dr Scully is also the Founding Chair of the Ontario Universities Council on Quality Assurance and Past Vice President Academic and Provost of Dalhousie University, Halifax, Nova Scotia, and University of Victoria, British Columbia.

The event was attended by 48 faculty and staff in 4 sites across AKU entities in Pakistan, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. The speaker gave the background on programme quality and the need for a richer understanding of the value and benefits of modern practice in quality assurance. The speaker also articulated the importance of student voice in reviews and the shift to focus more on learning outcomes. The speaker also spent time discussing on what makes a self-study effective. He pointed out the importance of some self-Study components such as leadership, evaluation criteria, collective commitment to improvement, total honesty, rigour, reflection, self-critical analysis and a realistic improvement plan. 

The QAI-net will continue to support entities to continuously focus on improving programmes offered by the university.

value.Title: ​Ms. Louisa Lambregts Joins the Network of Teaching and Learning as Digital Learning Specialist
value.NewsSummary: ​Digital Learning Specialist Joins TL_net
value.NewsContent:
Ms. Louisa Lambregts has joined the Networks of Teaching and Learning and Blended and Digital Learning as a Digital Learning Specialist for 6 months. Louisa joined us on January 12th 2016. Louisa’s appointment has been made possible through the Aga Khan Foundation Canada (AKFC) CADEX Programme which provides AKDN field agencies the opportunity to engage Canadian development professionals in support of agency institutional priorities.

Louisa will be working with the Network of Teaching and Learning to support faculty and students across all AKU entities to enhance effective teaching and learning with technology. Her primary responsibility will be to develop a digital teaching and learning strategy for the university as well as its implementation plan. She will also design and implement professional development activities (including consultation clinics) for faculty on the effective use of technology in teaching, including the use of a learning management system.Louisa has over 12 years’ experience in higher education as an educational technologist and trainer, teacher, multimedia developer, and instructional designer. She is currently an Educational Technologist with Algonquin College’s Learning and Teaching Services Department in Ottawa. Louisa has supported faculty to integrate educational technologies with a focus on efficient workflows and pedagogical effectiveness. She has also delivered training sessions on integrating various educational technologies into courses and the classroom setting.

value.Title: ​​Dr Tashmin Khamis Meets with the New Executive Secretary of Inter-University Council of East Africa​
value.NewsSummary: ​​Dr Tashmin Khamis Meets with the New Executive Secretary of Inter-University Council of East Africa​
value.NewsContent:
Dr Tashmin Khamis, the Director of the Network of Quality Assurance and Improvement (QAI_net) and Network Teaching and Learning (TL-net) paid a courtesy call on the new Executive Secretary of Inter-University Council of East Africa (IUCEA), Professor Alexandre Lyambabaje.  Prof Lyambabaje has assumed office to lead the Inter-University Council for East Africa (IUCEA) for the next five years following the end of tenure of Prof. Mayunga Nkunya who led the institution since 2010. IUCEA is a legally mandated body that was created by the East African Community (EAC) to:

  • Facilitate networking among universities in East Africa, and with universities outside the region;

  • Provide a forum for discussion on a wide range of academic and other matters relating to higher education in East Africa; and​​

  • Facilitate maintenance of internationally comparable education standards in East Africa so as to promote the region's competitiveness in higher education.

Dr Tashmin Khamis is currently the President of the East African Higher Education Quality Assurance Network (EAQAN), a responsibility she has diligently executed for the last two years as her term comes to an end in May 2016. EAQAN is the technical arm of IUCEA on quality issues where AKU has been well represented by the President and faculty during EAQAN Conferences. AKU is also an associate member of IUCEA.

Dr Tashmin briefed Prof Lyambabaje on EAQAN’s milestones for the last 2 years including the development of a new strategic plan and the need for continued support from the IUCEA in order to implement the new strategic plan and ensure sustainability of EAQAN. Prof. Lyambabaje and the Deputy Executive Secretary Prof. Pontien Ndabaneze noted the significant contribution made by EAQAN in supporting higher education institutions to promote internal quality assurance and raise their standards, and IUCEA thanked AKU in taking the lead. 

AKU will continue to partner with regional bodies to create greater influence about AKU and its programmes.

value.Title: Study: Cultural perceptions around gender roles remain an obstacle in early childhood education
value.NewsSummary: Project will compile over 800 publications from Sub-Saharan Africa and by African scholars.
value.NewsContent:
On 9th February 2015 the Tuwaendeleze Watoto Wetu (TWW, www.tww.or.tz) research team at IED-EA held its final dialogue brief. AKU-IED worked in very close partnership with the Tanzania Early Childhood Development Network, and with government Ministries, particularly with the Ministry of Community Development, Gender and Children during the project. Professor Alan Pence from the University of Victoria, Canada joined the team as Co-PI with IED’s Professor Pauline Rea-Dickins.

This event brought together Early Childhood Care Education and Development (EC) specialists and stakeholders from across Tanzania, mainland and Zanzibar, and scholars from the East African region to engage with the findings from the TWW project and chart possible ways forward to promote the development of EC services in Tanzania and the East African region at large.  Nearly 45 specialist EC practitioners across a range of constituencies – NGOs, Community-based organisations, higher and further education institutions and education training centres - attended the event. Two colleagues from IED-Pakistan were also able to participate - Dr Almina Pardhan and Cassandra Fernandes – enabling closer ties between the two IEDs to be nurtured in this important area of education.

As this is the first study of its kind to attempt to map EC education capacity across Tanzania, key objectives of this event were to provide an avenue for the dissemination of the TWW project findings, to seek feedback on these findings, to gain additional insights from the different sectors at the dialogue, as well as to stimulate debate among EC stakeholders. 

The findings covered sensitive issues related to gender and leadership, standards and assessment, the lack of professionalization of EC teachers and carers, and issues of language.

Gendered Identities

Several participants discussed cultural perceptions around gender roles. For example, the opportunities available to men and women were different because of cultural perceptions about what men and women do. Men were seen to be in leadership positions because “men will always think they are strong and powerful” (HEI, Kilimajaro), while women take care of the home. Some participants suggested that others believe that the nature and attitude of women is more conducive to working with small children than in dealing with managerial tasks. 

“It is more cultural than anything else … it has something to do with our culture we believe women take care of children better than men it is an issue of gender … we believe this vocation of nursery school can be taken care of better by women than men” (HEI, Mwanza)

Standards & Assessment

On mainland Tanzania, universities, government and private TTC’s all used government curricula. However, different books and teaching materials are used. One participant noted other existing gaps in the provision of ECE programs in the country to be a lack of uniformity around the standards used to assess their programmes. 

Inclusion & Equity

We have found examples of ‘best practice’ that are focused on marginalized, vulnerable groups and children to special needs. However, focusing on a specific group leaves out large numbers of children who do not fall into these more urgent ‘priority’ categories. Thus, by default, significant numbers of children lose out on scaffolded development opportunities available for others. This in turn raises issues not only of quality for all but also access for all.

A major output of the project has been the development of a Compendium of over 800 publications that includes for the first time a considerable number of publications from Sub-Saharan Africa and by African scholars. This work, led by our Canadian research team members, Professor Alan Pence and Emily Ashton at the University of Victoria, provides a unique and seminal resource for the region. 

Benedict Missani, Acting Director of Ministry of Community Development, Gender and Children “The whole thing is a very nice experience. For the first time the University sector is working closely with government and providing us with recommendations in areas important to early childhood.”

The TWW Dialogue participants were encouraged to stay in touch with the research team at IED and in particular to contribute resources to be included on the webpages for TWW that have just been set up and to support the research team in keeping the Compendium current.​

value.Title: AKU applauded for its significant commitment to educate future leaders
value.NewsSummary: 84 graduates were conferred degrees at Aga Khan University’s convocation ceremony in Dar es Salaam
value.NewsContent:
​​​The Tanzania Commission for Universities’ Executive Secretary Professor Yunus Mgaya applauded the Aga Khan University’s significant commitment to an ambitious expansion plan in Tanzania and East Africa to educate the future leaders the region needs to launch a new era of development.​ 

He was speaking as the chief guest at the University’s convocation ceremony in Dar es Salaam.  

“As AKU is confident in Tanzania’s future, I am confident in the University and its future in Tanzania. We at the TCU are indeed very proud of the Aga Khan University being among the few institutions that are offering more specialized and demand driven programmes in this country,” said Professor Mgaya.

​The education offered at AKU is of the highest quality comparable to any world class university said the TCU Executive Secretary, and that graduands should be proud that they have been prepared to provide crucial leadership – to boost standards in specific areas of practice, ​​to enhance the performance of their institutions and to contribute to the improvement of the entire health and education system in the country. 

This year, AKU awarded degrees to 84 graduands from the Institute for Educational Development, the School of Nursing and Midwifery and the Postgraduate Medical Education programme.

Sixty-one graduated with a Master of Education degree, 22 with a Post-RN Bachelor of Science in Nursing, and one with Master of Family Medicine, marking 552 AKU alumni in Tanzania to date.

Margareth Yagaza, of the School of Nursing and Midwifery, gave the valedictory speech.

“We thank the University Chancellor, His Highness the Aga Khan, and the Board of Trustees for their vision and direction to mold this precious academic institution which has contributed and continuously contributes to transform this world into a better place,” said Margareth appreciating the support they received from faculty and staff during their year of study.

On the occasion, AKU President Firoz Rasul talked about the University’s plan to develop as a comprehensive university educating the future leaders of East Africa in a wide range of fields. The plan includes the establishment of the University’s principal East African campus in Arusha, the construction of a new campus for the Institute for Educational Development in Dar es Salaam, building a new Aga Khan University Hospital in Kampala, and the creation of new medical and nursing education programmes as well as the expansion of existing programmes. 

He thanked donors and supporters for their generosity and commitment to AKU’s mission of educating leaders for East Africa and the developing world. Among many, he mentioned the Canadian government which is providing over $31 million to improve pre-primary and primary education in Lindi and Mtwara towards the strengthening of education systems in East Africa and the Tanzania Commission for Universities, for its guidance, support and encouragement in the development and approval of new programmes in Tanzania. 

Lindi and Mtwara towards the strengthening of education systems in East Africa and the Tanzania Commission for Universities, for its guidance, support and encouragement in the development and approval of new programmes in Tanzania. 

“All of the support we have received speaks loudly about the impact of the University and the trust it has earned. An example is the recent appointment by President Magufuli of one of our faculty, Professor Joyce Ndalichako, as the Minister of Education, Science, Technology and Vocational Training,” said President Rasul.

He also lauded the role of civil society organisations in East Africa. “When civil society is strong, communities and countries thrive. Rather than being discouraged, it should be embraced as an essential contributor to the public good. Rather than being seen as a threat to government, it should be seen as the guarantor of good governance. Rather than fearing that it threatens order and stability, we should see its diversity and peaceful disagreements as a sign of national strength and maturity.”

He told the graduates that they are now ready to serve their countries as leaders and innovators in nursing, medicine and education.

“I have every confidence in you because the Aga Khan University has prepared you for leadership, you have learned to practice at the highest international standards, to think creatively and independently, to work effectively with individuals from many different backgrounds,” emphasized President Rasul.

The convocation ceremony was attended by the graduating students, their parents, faculty and staff members.
