value.Title: Low folate in mothers at conception may cause brain damage to babies
value.NewsSummary: "Mothers deficient in folate at the time of conception might give birth to babies with neural tube defect," Dr Rahat Qureshi, Associate Professor Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Aga Khan University stated this addressing the last event of the series of s
value.NewsContent:
​"Mothers deficient in folate at the time of conception might give birth to babies with neural tube defect," Dr Rahat Qureshi, Associate Professor Obstetrics and Gynaecology, Aga Khan University stated this addressing the last event of the series of seminars on Women's Nutrition and Health held at AKU Stadium Road Campus.

Organised by the Pakistan Nutrition and Dietetic Society in collaboration with AKU, the seminars were held under the Continuing Nutrition Education Seminar Series 2006 in the month of March, focusing on providing current scientific information regarding nutrition on topics particularly relevant to women's health.

Dr Qureshi described the devastating effects of folate deficiency in the mother on the foetus. This occurs in the first 27 days of pregnancy. She pointed out that unfortunately by the time the woman realises that she is pregnant, the damage may already be done to the foetus. "Therefore it is important to ensure that women of child bearing age are educated regarding the good food sources of folic acid (B vitamin) such as green leafy vegetables and fruits and encouraged to include them in their diets," she said.

Dr Qureshi elaborated upon the high mortality and morbidity associated with pregnancy in Pakistan and emphasised the role of good nutrition in ensuring the proper development of the foetus.

Sumaira Nasim, Senior Lecturer Baqai University and a senior member of the Pakistan Nutrition and Dietetic Society, pointed out that it was not enough to worry about the woman's nutrition only during pregnancy. She talked about the intergenerational effects of malnutrition on pregnancy outcomes saying that women who are malnourished as children grow up to be malnourished females and improving diet during pregnancy is not enough to undo the harm of deprivation throughout life. Thus the nutrition of the girl child must receive proper attention if we wish to decrease maternal morbidity and morality, she said.

She pointed out that low birth weight remains an ongoing problem in Pakistan with 30-40 % of the babies born being below 2.5 kg at birth. It is now being recognised in the scientific community that babies that have low birth weight are also at increased risk of chronic disease such as diabetes, hypertension and heart disease.

Dr Ghazala Rafique, Senior Instructor from the Department of Community Health Sciences, AKU presented a case study on Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) which is a temporary condition that occurs for the first time during the second and third trimesters of pregnancy. Usually, there are no symptoms of Gestational Diabetes and it is diagnosed through blood tests at 24 to 28 weeks of pregnancy. Dr Rafique said that risk factors for developing this condition include a previous diagnosis of GDM, age over 35 years, obesity, a history of polycystic ovary syndrome and being a member of a population considered to be at high risk for diabetes that includes women of South Asian descent.

Discussing the dietary management of GDM, Ms Saima Rasheed, Nutritionist from Park Lane Hospital, informed the audience that diets containing 40-45% of total energy intake from carbohydrates have shown to reduce postprandial blood sugars. She said that the carbohydrate intake throughout the day should be distributed into three small-to-moderate sized meals and 2-4 snacks. She stressed upon the role of exercise which helps to lower both fasting and postprandial sugar levels and should be used as an adjunct to dietary management.

As a part of its social responsibility and commitment to the advancement of health research and education, AKU regularly holds seminars, symposiums and events to raise awareness about health and education related issues which are of national importance and interest.

value.Title: AKUH's 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programme preventable renal stone disease among major causes of death in Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: "Renal stone disease continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and chronic kidney disease in Pakistan even though it is preventable," This was disclosed by prominent urologist Dr. Syed Raziuddin Biyabani at a public health awareness programme
value.NewsContent:
​"Renal stone disease continues to be a significant cause of morbidity and chronic kidney disease in Pakistan even though it is preventable," This was disclosed by prominent urologist Dr. Syed Raziuddin Biyabani at a public health awareness programme by Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) held at Indus Hotel, Hyderabad on Friday.

Dr Biyabani who is the Associate Professor and acting Head, Section of Urology, Department of Surgery at AKUH, Karachi was speaking at the 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' Programme of AKUH.

Addressing the audience, Dr Biyabani said that according to AKUH, the incidence of the disease varies from 2.4 per 100,000 population in the north to 200 cases per 100,000 cases in the south of the country. He added that the stones form in the presence of dehydration, hot climate, infection in the urinary tract and with excess calcium and oxalate and protein in the diet. Those patients with a family history of stone disease and those with certain rare metabolic diseases are also at risk of forming stones, he added.

Discussing the symptoms, he said that the patients with stone disease may suffer from pain, fever, blood in urine or at times with altered renal function.

Investigations are directed at looking for urinary tract infection, determine renal function and imaging studies, including ultrasound, x-rays or CT scan are required to look at the size, site and degree of obstruction of the stone. These also help to find out how best to treat the stone.

Currently, open surgery is only rarely required to treat the stones. Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy is used to break the stones into small pieces which come out through the urinary passage. Endoscopy is used to treat stones in the ureter and urinary bladder. Larger stones in the kidney can be removed with Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), which involves approaching the stones through a small hole in the skin. This can be combined with lithotripsy to completely remove all stones.

"Once the kidney stones form, 50% patients have chances of recurrence in 5-10 years," Dr Biyabani informed the people. He said that stone recurrence can be prevented by treating and preventing urinary infection, increasing fluid intake, decreasing protein intake and moderation in diet. Alkalinization of urine with diet and in some cases medication can help prevent stone formation. Excess calcium and salt in the diet should be avoided while moderate amount of milk intake is allowed, he concluded.

Dr Nuzhat Faruqui, Instructor and Consultant Urologist spoke about the common urological problems in females. She pointed out that urinary problems in females are under reported and under treated because of the lack of availability of trained female urologists in the field, and also because of the reluctance of female patients to consult a male urologist. She also pointed out a widespread belief among women who think urinary problems are a necessary part of aging.

Dr Faruqui said that urinary incontinence is involuntary loss of urine that is severe enough to cause a social or hygienic problem. It is more common in elderly females. "The overall prevalence in Asia has been reported to be about 14.6% in females and 6.8% in males,' she told the audience.

Most of the urinary problems in females are not due to aging alone. With proper evaluation, most patients can be cured, treated or adequately managed with improvement in the quality of life, she stressed.

As part of its outreach programme and societal commitment to creating awareness of early diagnosis and timely treatment, AKUH has organised over 200 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programmes in Karachi, Hyderabad and the UAE, benefiting more than 40,000 people. Similarly, Aga Khan University Hospital's Patient Welfare Programme offers financial assistance to those patients who are unable to afford the medical cost of treatment. In 2004, 74 per cent of all patients treated at AKUH were from low- to middle-income groups. Since the inception of this welfare programme in 1986, over Rs. 1.4 billion has been disbursed to more than 250,000 needy patients.

value.Title: AKUH's 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' Programme
value.NewsSubTitle: Well-cooked food is safe from bird flu virus
value.NewsSummary: "Bird influenza is not transmitted through well-cooked food as the H5N1 virus is sensitive to heat," Professor Riaz Qureshi, Chairman, Department of Family Medicine, Aga Khan University (AKU) informed the audience at a public health awareness program
value.NewsContent: ​"Bird influenza is not transmitted through well-cooked food as the H5N1 virus is sensitive to heat," Professor Riaz Qureshi, Chairman, Department of Family Medicine, Aga Khan University (AKU) informed the audience at a public health awareness programme. He was addressing AKU's Signs, Symptoms and Care Programme held in the AKU auditorium on March 25, 2006. Professor Qureshi disclosed that it is safe to eat chicken and domestic birds as long as certain precautions are taken in countries currently experiencing outbreaks. He elaborated that the normal temperatures used for cooking (70oC in all parts of the food) will kill the virus. He requested the consumers to ensure that all parts of the poultry are fully cooked with no "pink" parts left and eggs should also be properly cooked with no "runny" yolks. Professor Qureshi also informed that if the infection spreads to humans, it can prove to be serious but certain drugs for example Tamiflu, are available for treatment. People coming in contact with a patient will also require preventive medication, he added.He also described the most important warning signals that would indicate that a serious epidemic (pandemic) is about to start. These included detection of a number of cases with severe symptoms and signs of influenza, closely related in time and place, as this would suggest human to human transmission is taking place, said Professor Qureshi.Dr Mirza Ikram Ali Baig, Senior Instructor, Department of Family Medicine, Aga Khan University, provided a brief overview of Avian Influenza (Bird Flu). He said that bird flu is a viral disease caused by an Avian Influenza virus (H5N1) which is different from the seasonal influenza virus affecting humans. The virus H5N1 is mainly carried by wild birds and can be transmitted to domestic birds like chickens, ducks and turkeys while pigs have also been seen to be infected, he pointed out. The virus produces overwhelming disease in domestic birds which usually die when infected. Birds transmit the virus through their saliva, nasal secretions and faeces. The current outbreaks of highly pathogenic avian influenza, which began in Southeast Asia in mid-2003, are the largest and most severe on record. Never before in the history of this disease have so many countries been simultaneously affected, resulting in the loss of many birds. Poultry outbreaks caused by the H5N1 virus were initially reported in eight Asian nations: the Republic of Korea, Vietnam, Japan, Thailand, Cambodia, Lao People's Democratic Republic, Indonesia, and China.Dr Baig stressed that the Avian Influenza virus is not easily transmitted from infected birds to healthy humans. However, people in close contact with the infected poultry are at risk of catching the virus. Elaborating on the possibility of infection spreading to humans, he said that direct contact with infected poultry or surfaces and objects contaminated by their faeces, is presently considered the main route of human infection. To date, most human cases have occurred in rural or periurban areas where many households keep small poultry flocks, which often roam freely, sometimes entering homes or sharing outdoor areas where children play. Exposure is considered most likely during slaughter, defeathering, butchering, and preparation of poultry for cooking. The health care workers in direct contact with suspected or confirmed H5N1 infection are also at risk of getting the infection.So far, the confirmed human cases in the current outbreak have occurred in Cambodia, Indonesia, Iraq, Thailand, and Vietnam.As part of its outreach programme and societal commitment to creating awareness of early diagnosis and timely treatment, AKUH has organised over 200 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programmes in Karachi, Hyderabad and the UAE, benefiting more than 40,000 people. Similarly, Aga Khan University Hospital's Patient Welfare Programme offers financial assistance to those patients who are unable to afford the medical cost of treatment. In 2005, 74 per cent of all patients treated at AKUH were from low- to middle-income groups. Since the inception of this welfare programme in 1986, over Rs. 1.4 billion has been disbursed to more than 250,000 needy patients.​

value.Title: One-third of the world's population infected with TB
value.NewsSummary: World tuberculosis Day is being observed this year with the knowledge that every third person in the world is infected with TB. This year, the Day will focus on the efforts of frontline TB care providers and their crucial role in stopping TB.
value.NewsContent:
​World tuberculosis Day is being observed this year with the knowledge that every third person in the world is infected with TB. This year, the Day will focus on the efforts of frontline TB care providers and their crucial role in stopping TB. The section of Pulmonary and Critical Care Medicine, Department of Medicine, Aga Khan University held a seminar on Tuesday which covered different aspects of the fight against TB especially in the context that 33 % of TB cases in the world occur in the South-East Asia Region.

Experts at the seminar pointed out that incomplete or poorly supervised treatment regimens cause the bacilli to develop resistance to drugs and people infected later carry the same resistant strain. They said that incomplete or poor treatment was worse than no treatment at all.

Dr Ahmed Suleman Haque, Dr Rumina Hassan, Dr Mohammad Wassay, Dr Muhammad Irfan, Dr Ali bin Sarwar Zuberi, Dr Nisar Ahmed Rao of Aga Khan University addressed the seminar while Professor Nadeem Rizvi, head of Department of Chest Diseases, JPMC Karachi delivered the keynote address.

It is estimated that 1.75 million deaths resulted from TB in 2003 while one new person is infected with TB bacilli every second in the world. World TB Day aims to mobilise support for fighting the spread of TB prominently on global agenda and ensure its elimination by 2050.

Held annually on 24 March, the Day commemorates the date in 1882 when Dr Robert Koch presented his discovery of the TB bacillus to a group of doctors in Berlin. The United Nations Millennium Development Goals include cutting down TB prevalence and death rates to half of the present rate by 2015.​

value.Title: Fourth Kenya University exhibition
value.NewsSummary: The fourth Kenya University exhibition was held at the Kenyatta International Conference Centre from 15 to 18 March 2006.
value.NewsContent: ​The fourth Kenya University exhibition was held at the Kenyatta International Conference Centre from 15 to 18 March 2006. The four-day exhibition was opened on Wednesday by Assistant Minister Education, Mrs. Beth Mugo. It brought together 15 public and private universities, one constituent college, the Commission of Higher Education (CHE), the Joint Admissions Board (JAB) and the Higher Education Loans Board (HELB). It was the first time that the JAB was participating at such an event. The institutions advised parents and students on their academic programmes. Vice-chancellors and other heads also held seminars at the same venue on various issues affecting the institutions. The turnout this year was high, and the queries from the public more specific about the programmes being offered by the universities. There was a lot of interest expressed in AKU’s programmes, particularly the nursing programmes. The general opinion was that AKU had reached the stage to venture into undergraduate programmes in nursing and medicine, providing alternative to the only two public universities currently offering those programmes. The universities are University of Nairobi and Moi University. There was also interest particularly with AKU Karachi’s undergraduate programme in medicine, with the issue of tuition fee and living expenses raised. Application forms and admission related information were given to prospective students, who are finalizing their high school studies this year.​

value.Title: Kidney disease affects every fifth person in Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: Every fifth person over the age of 40 years in Pakistan may be affected by chronic kidney disease, Dr Tazeen Jafar, Head, Section of Nephrology pointed this out at a seminar to mark the first World Kidney Day on March 9, 2006 at the Aga Khan Univeris
value.NewsContent:
​Every fifth person over the age of 40 years in Pakistan may be affected by chronic kidney disease, Dr Tazeen Jafar, Head, Section of Nephrology pointed this out at a seminar to mark the first World Kidney Day on March 9, 2006 at the Aga Khan Univeristy (AKU) Auditorium.

The seminar was organised by AKU on the inaugural theme of 'Early detection and prevention of chronic kidney disease' as similar events took place all over the world. The well attended seminar was intended to inform primary care physicians, general practitioners and family practice doctors about kidney diseases and their treatment.

The event was significant in the wake of worldwide statistics indicating that deaths claimed by infectious diseases will decline by 3% over the next decade while those by chronic diseases - that already account for 72% of the total global burden of disease in people over 30 - will increase by 17% over the next decade. The first World Kidney Day on March 9, 2006 was an effort jointly launched by the International Society of Nephrology (ISN) and the International Federation of Kidney Foundations (IFKF), to raise awareness about chronic kidney diseases. 
Dr Tazeen Jafar also discussed screening strategies and programmes that are best suited for a country like Pakistan in her speech at the seminar. Dr Jaffar Naqvi, Chief Executive of the Kidney Foundation of Pakistan, shared his views about the situation of patients with kidney failure on dialysis in Pakistan, and recounted his experience of the End Stage Renal Failure Registry. He stressed the need for government sponsored haemodialysis projects

Other speakers included Dr Waqar Kashif, Assistant Professor and Consultant Nephrologist at AKU, Dr Arshad Ahmed, Consultant Nephrologist, Dr Iqtidar Ahmed Khan, Professor and Consultant Paediatric Nephrologist, and Dr Raziuddin Bayabani, Assistant Professor and Consultant Urologist at AKU.

A panel discussion followed, in which prominent nephrologists of Karachi including Dr Fazal Akhtar (SIUT), Dr Aasim Ahmed (Kidney Center), Dr Muhammed Azharuddin (AKU), Dr Rauf Mazhar (AKU), Dr. Mansoor Shah (AKU), and the speakers of the seminar participated.

Earlier, Dr David Taylor, Acting Provost AKU, cited the seminar as being part of AKU's mission of taking the lead in organising global public health disease prevention programmes. He expressed hope that this seminar will help create awareness about the screening of people in "high-risk groups" for kidney disease and broadcast the importance of this message to government health officials, general physicians, allied health professionals, individuals and families.

AKU regularly holds such seminars, symposia and events as a part of its social responsibility and commitment to the advancement of health research and education, in order to raise awareness about health and education related issues which are of national importance and interest.

value.Title: Organises Cleanliness Day in Sultanabad
value.NewsSummary: In continuation of its commitment towards community development, Aga Khan University's (AKU) Department of Community Health Sciences (CHS) organised a Cleanliness Day in Sultanabad, a squatter settlement of Karachi, on Monday, March 6, 2006. The even
value.NewsContent:
​In continuation of its commitment towards community development, Aga Khan University's (AKU) Department of Community Health Sciences (CHS) organised a Cleanliness Day in Sultanabad, a squatter settlement of Karachi, on Monday, March 6, 2006. The event was organised in order to mobilise the community to address the ongoing trash problems that face urban slum areas, and to sensitise the community stakeholders about the importance of garbage disposal, cleanliness and environmental hygiene.

The Community Health Management Association (CHMA) collaborated with AKU in the organisation of the event which involved community members, children from local schools, the Union Council Nazim and the Counsellors, CHS Residents and Masters Students and CHS faculty and staff.

Dr Gregory Pappas, Director of CHS, who was present at the occasion to support the community members in this initiative, remarked: "It is important to involve the community in garbage disposal activity, and to disseminate education that would help resolve the problem of environmental hygiene by promoting a sustainable community participation process. I hope this event will galvanise the community to hold monthly Cleanliness Days."

Mr Mairajuddin, Nazim, and Mr Shah Nawaz Jadoon, Naib Nazim, UC 2, along with the counsellors appreciated the efforts by AKU and the community on Cleanliness Day in Sultanabad. They encouraged the community to continue this practice and promised that all the facilities and logistics would be provided in the upcoming programmes of cleanliness in the area.

Mr Sultan, President of CHMA Sultanabad, said, "CHMS has been working with AKU for the last 10 years for the betterment of the health and socio-economic status of Sultanabad. We will continue to focus on cleanliness and provide every support to AKU, the community and the Nazim to improve the garbage disposal system of the area."

Dr. Khalil Qureshi from CHS presented a demonstration on how to pick up garbage and school children made speeches on the importance of cleanliness. The members then divided into four groups and each group chose an alley to clean. Tetley Tea sponsored the programme.

The programme is expected to increase awareness among the local people about the hazards of improper waste disposal to public health and enhance their knowledge on environmental health issues.

value.Title: Educational research association launched by AKU-IED
value.NewsSummary: The international conference on ‘Quality in Education: Teaching and Leadership in Challenging Times’ organised by Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) concluded successfully at the Institute’s Karimabad campus in Karach
value.NewsContent:
​The international conference on ‘Quality in Education: Teaching and Leadership in Challenging Times’ organised by Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) concluded successfully at the Institute’s Karimabad campus in Karachi. Three days of deliberations and discussions by national and international researchers, academics and educationists led to several outcomes including the identification of areas and issues for research and dissemination at future conferences.

A significant outcome of the conference was the launch of Pakistan Educational Research Association (PERA) on the final day of the conference. The launching ceremony was attended by a large group of educationists, academics and researchers from private and government institutions, including Dr Hafiz Iqbal, Director, Institute of Education and Research, University of Punjab; and Prof Noor-ul-Haq, Director, Provincial Institute of Teacher Education (PITE), Balochistan.

Speaking at the launching ceremony of PERA, AKU-IED Director Dr Muhammad Memon described it as a ‘community of researchers’. Noting that promotion of research and scholarship was part of AKU‘s strategic vision, he said: “It is in fulfilment of this vision that the University is committed to support the creation of PERA which would be a national resource in educational research for Pakistan.”

The Head of Research and Policy Studies at AKU-IED, Dr Anjum Halai, provided an overview of and rationale for PERA. She said that PERA aimed to sustain and promote a vibrant educational research culture in Pakistan; enhance the impact of research on policy and practice; provide a forum for educationists and educational researchers to share research findings and best practices; disseminate research findings and encourage scholarly inquiry; and provide opportunities for members to build and enhance their research capacity. Although AKU-IED would support PERA in the initial phase, it would ultimately become an independent body with membership representing public and private sectors, she added.

The conference also resulted in a set of papers that will be compiled as conference proceedings. This would be a significant resource as it would document a large number of papers on the topic of quality education with specific reference to issues pertaining to Pakistan and the developing world.

AKU’s academic, research and service activities – encompassing ten teaching sites in seven countries of South Asia, Eastern Africa and Europe – are targeted at helping the developing world, and especially the Muslim Ummah, to progress in areas of education and health.

value.Title: AKU Bird Flu committee: Public service message
value.NewsSummary: Bird flu has recently been identified in Pakistan . In an effort to alert and educate the public, Aga Khan University (AKU) has prepared this public service message.
value.NewsContent:
​Bird flu has recently been identified in Pakistan .  In an effort to alert and educate the public, Aga Khan University (AKU) has prepared this public service message. AKU is working with the Government of Pakistan to address the threat of bird flu.  This message is based on the best science available on bird flu draw from the WHO and the Centers for Disease Control.    ​​​​

Avian influenza A (H5N1) viruses usually affect wild birds but now are infecting and causing serious disease among poultry, such as chickens. Human infections with H5N1 viruses are rare, but have occurred during 2003 - 2006 in Cambodia , China , Indonesia , Iraq , Thailand , Turkey and Vietnam , with many cases resulting in death.

Most cases of H5N1 infection in humans are thought to have occurred from direct contact with infected poultry in affected countries. Therefore, when possible, care should be taken to avoid contact with live, well-appearing, sick, or dead poultry and with any surfaces that may have been contaminated by poultry or their faeces or secretions. Transmission of H5N1 viruses to two persons through consumption of uncooked duck blood may also have occurred in Vietnam in 2005. Uncooked poultry or poultry products, including blood, should not be consumed.  Cooking poultry products kills the virus.

Countries that have experienced confirmed outbreaks of H5N1 infection among poultry and other birds in 2005-2006 include Pakistan, Austria, Azerbaijan, Bulgaria, Cambodia, China (including Hong Kong SAR), Croatia, Egypt, Germany, Greece, India, Indonesia, Iran, Italy, Kazakhstan, Mongolia, Nigeria, Romania, Russia, Slovenia, Thailand, Turkey, Ukraine, and Vietnam.. Poultry outbreaks were also reported in Japan , Laos , and Malaysia during 2004.

Below are some common questions asked about bird flu and answers provide by the Centers for Disease Control of the US government. The information here also is true for Pakistan .   

What is avian influenza (bird flu)?

Bird flu is an infection caused by avian (bird) influenza (flu) viruses.  These flu viruses occur naturally among birds. Wild birds worldwide carry the viruses in their intestines, but usually do not get sick from them. However, bird flu is very contagious among birds and can make some domesticated birds, including chickens, ducks, and turkeys, very sick and kill them.

Infection with avian influenza viruses in domestic poultry causes two main forms of disease that are distinguished by low and high extremes of virulence. The "low pathogenic" form may go undetected and usually causes only mild symptoms (such as ruffled feathers and a drop in egg production). However, the "highly pathogenic" form spreads more rapidly through flocks of poultry. This form may cause disease that affects multiple internal organs and has a mortality rate that can reach 90-100%, often within 48 hours.

How does avian influenza spread among birds?

Infected birds shed influenza virus in their saliva, nasal secretions, and faeces. Susceptible birds become infected when they have contact with contaminated excretions or with surfaces that are contaminated with excretions or secretions. Domesticated birds may become infected with avian influenza virus through direct contact with infected waterfowl or other infected poultry or through contact with surfaces (such as dirt or cages) or materials (such as water or feed) that have been contaminated with the virus.

Do bird flu viruses infect humans?

Bird flu viruses do not usually infect humans, but more than 100 confirmed cases of human infection with bird flu viruses have occurred since 1997.

How do people become infected with avian influenza viruses?

Most cases of avian influenza infection in humans have resulted from direct or close contact with infected poultry (e.g., domesticated chicken, ducks, and turkeys) or surfaces contaminated with secretions and excretions from infected birds. The spread of avian influenza viruses from an ill person to another person has been reported very rarely, and transmission has not been observed to continue beyond one person. During an outbreak of avian influenza among poultry, there is a possible risk to people who have direct or close contact with infected birds or with surfaces that have been contaminated with secretions and excretions from infected birds.

What are the symptoms of avian influenza in humans?

Symptoms of avian influenza in humans have ranged from typical human influenza-like symptoms (fever, cough, sore throat, and muscle aches) to eye infections, pneumonia, severe respiratory diseases (such as acute respiratory distress syndrome), and other severe and life-threatening complications. The symptoms of avian influenza may depend on which specific virus subtype and strain caused the infection.

How is avian influenza detected in humans?

A laboratory test is needed to confirm avian influenza in humans. This test is only available in a few specialty hospitals in the country at the current time. 

What are the implications of avian influenza to human health?

Two main risks for human health from avian influenza are 1) the risk of direct infection when the virus passes from the infected bird to humans, sometimes resulting in severe disease; and 2) the risk that the virus - if given enough opportunities - will change into a form that is highly infectious for humans and spreads easily from person to person.

How is avian influenza in humans treated?

Studies done in laboratories suggest that the prescription medicines approved for human influenza viruses should work in treating avian influenza infection in humans. However, influenza viruses can become resistant to these drugs, so these medications may not always work. Additional studies are needed to determine the effectiveness of these medicines.

Does the current seasonal influenza vaccine protect me from avian influenza?

No. Influenza vaccine for the 2005-06 season does not provide protection against avian influenza.

Should I wear a surgical mask to prevent exposure to avian influenza?

Currently, wearing a mask is not recommended for routine use (e.g., in public) for preventing influenza exposure. In the United States , disposable surgical and procedure masks have been widely used in health-care settings to prevent exposure to respiratory infections, but the masks have not been used commonly in community settings, such as schools, businesses, and public gatherings.

Is there a risk for becoming infected with avian influenza by eating poultry?

There is no evidence that properly cooked poultry or eggs can be a source of infection for avian influenza viruses

What precautions can be taken to reduce the risk for infection from wild birds in the Pakistan ?

As a general rule, the public should observe wildlife, including wild birds, from a distance. This protects you from possible exposure to pathogens and minimizes disturbance to the animal. Avoid touching wildlife. If there is contact with wildlife do not rub eyes, eat, drink, or smoke before washing hands with soap and water. Do not pick up diseased or dead wildlife.

What precautions can people working with poultry to reduce the risk for infection when hunting birds in the Pakistan ?

Poultry farmers and those who butcher poultry should take protective measure like wearing gloves, gowns, and boots.  Washing body and clothing after contact with poultry is essential.  More comprehensive measures are recommended by occupational health and safety officials because poultry workers are at higher risk than the general population of contacting bird flu.

What precautions can hunters take to reduce the risk for infection when hunting birds in Pakistan ?

Hunters should follow routine precautions when handling game, including wild birds. Recommendation for hunters include:

  • Do not handle or eat sick game.
  • Wear rubber or disposable latex gloves while handling and cleaning game, wash hands with soap and water (or with alcohol-based hand products if the hands are not visibly soiled), and thoroughly clean knives, equipment and surfaces that come in contact with game.
  • Do not eat, drink, or smoke while handling animals.
  • Cook all game thoroughly.

Avian Influenza A (H5N1)

What is the avian influenza A (H5N1) virus that has been reported in Asia and Europe?

Influenza A (H5N1) virus - also called "H5N1 virus" - is an influenza A virus subtype that occurs mainly in birds, is highly contagious among birds, and can be deadly to them.

Outbreaks of avian influenza H5N1 occurred among poultry in eight countries in Asia ( Cambodia , China , Indonesia , Japan , Laos , South Korea , Thailand , and Vietnam ) during late 2003 and early 2004. At that time, more than 100 million birds in the affected countries either died from the disease or were killed in order to try to control the outbreaks. By March 2004, the outbreak was reported to be under control.

Since late June 2004, however, new outbreaks of influenza H5N1 among poultry have been reported by several countries in Asia ( Cambodia , China [ Tibet ], Indonesia , Kazakhstan , Malaysia , Mongolia , Russia [Siberia], Thailand , and Vietnam ). It is believed that these outbreaks are ongoing. Influenza H5N1 infection also has been reported among poultry in Turkey and Romania and among wild migratory birds in Croatia .

Human cases of influenza A (H5N1) infection have been reported in Cambodia , China , Indonesia , Thailand , Turkey , and Vietnam .

What are the risks to humans from the current H5N1 outbreak in Asia and Europe?

H5N1 virus does not usually infect people, but more than 140 human cases have been reported. Most of these cases have occurred from direct or close contact with infected poultry or contaminated surfaces; however, a few cases of human-to-human spread of H5N1 virus have occurred.

So far, spread of H5N1 virus from person to person has been rare and has not continued beyond one person. Nonetheless, because all influenza viruses have the ability to change, scientists are concerned that H5N1 virus one day could be able to infect humans and spread easily from one person to another. Because these viruses do not commonly infect humans, there is little or no immune protection against them in the human population.

If H5N1 virus were to gain the capacity to spread easily from person to person, an influenza pandemic (worldwide outbreak of disease) could begin. No one can predict when a pandemic might occur. However, experts from around the world are watching the H5N1 situation in Asia and Europe very closely and are preparing for the possibility that the virus may begin to spread more easily from person to person.

How does H5N1 virus differ from seasonal influenza viruses that infect humans?

Of the few avian influenza viruses that have crossed the species barrier to infect humans, H5N1 virus has caused the largest number of reported cases of severe disease and death in humans. In the current situation in Asia, more than half of the people infected with the virus have died. Most cases have occurred in previously healthy children and young adults. However, it is possible that the only cases currently being reported are those in the most severely ill people and that the full range of illness caused by the H5N1 virus has not yet been defined.

Unlike seasonal influenza, in which infection usually causes only mild respiratory symptoms in most people, H5N1 infection may follow an unusually aggressive clinical course, with rapid deterioration and high fatality. Primary viral pneumonia and multi-organ failure have been common among people who have become ill with H5N1 influenza.

How is infection with H5N1 virus in humans treated?

Most H5N1 viruses that have caused human illness and death appear to be resistant to amantadine and rimantadine, two antiviral medications commonly used for treatment of patients with influenza. Two other antiviral medications, oseltamivir and zanamavir, would probably work to treat influenza caused by H5N1 virus, but additional studies are needed to demonstrate their current and ongoing effectiveness.

Is there a vaccine to protect humans from H5N1 virus?

There currently is no commercially available vaccine to protect humans against the H5N1 virus that is being detected in Asia and Europe. However, vaccine development efforts are taking place. Research studies to test a vaccine that will protect humans against H5N1 virus began in April 2005, and a series of clinical trials is under way.

Can a person become infected with avian influenza A (H5N1) virus by cleaning a bird feeder?

At the present time, the risk of becoming infected with H5N1 virus from bird feeders is low. Generally, perching birds (Passeriformes) are the predominate type of birds at feeders. While there are documented cases of H5N1 causing death in some Passeriformes (e.g., house sparrow, Eurasian tree-sparrow, house finch), in both free-ranging and experimental settings, most of the wild birds that are traditionally associated with avian influenza viruses are waterfowl and shore birds.

Influenza Pandemic Preparedness

What changes are needed for H5N1 or another avian influenza virus to cause a pandemic?

Three conditions must be met for a pandemic to start: 1) a new influenza virus subtype must emerge; 2) it must infect humans and causes serious illness; and 3) it must spread easily and sustainedly (continue without interruption) among humans. The H5N1 virus in Asia and Europe meets the first two conditions: it is a new virus for humans (H5N1 viruses have never circulated widely among people), and it has infected more than 100 humans, killing over half of them.

However, the third condition, the establishment of efficient and sustained human-to-human transmission of the virus, has not occurred. For this to take place, the H5N1 virus would need to improve its transmissibility among humans. This could occur either by "reassortment" or adaptive mutation.

Reassortment occurs when genetic material is exchanged between human and avian viruses during co-infection (infection with both viruses at the same time) of a human or pig. The result could be a fully transmissible pandemic virus-that is, a virus that can spread easily and directly to humans. A more gradual process is adaptive mutation, where the capability of a virus to bind to human cells increases during infections of humans.

Source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

value.Title: International Education Conference-Hamida Khuhro praises AKU-IED for promoting quality education
value.NewsSummary: The opening ceremony of the international conference on 'Quality in Education: Teaching and Leadership in Challenging Times' was held at Aga Khan University (AKU) on Tuesday, Feb 21, 2006. Dr Hamida Khuhro, Minister for Education and Literacy, Govern
value.NewsContent:
​The opening ceremony of the international conference on 'Quality in Education: Teaching and Leadership in Challenging Times' was held at Aga Khan University (AKU) on Tuesday, Feb 21, 2006. Dr Hamida Khuhro, Minister for Education and Literacy, Government of Sindh, was the chief guest at the ceremony.

The three-day conference was organised by Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED). Educationists from Pakistan, India, East Africa, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, Malaysia, Poland, UK, US and Canada are participating in the conference.

Lauding AKU-IED's work, Dr Khuhro said that since its inception, the Institute has been engaged in developing and delivering quality programmes in teacher education, educational leadership, early childhood education and development, environment education, inclusive education, gender education, citizenship education and health education. She further added that the series of policy dialogues conducted by AKU-IED during the past three years on key issues in education with government and other agencies had been remarkable. "These dialogues have enabled policy makers in identifying problems, designing and analysing research and making policy recommendations."

In her keynote address, the Director of the Institute for Development Studies and Practices, Quetta, Dr Quratulain Bakhtiari, said that leadership was built by integrating with people, not by isolating educational institutions from the people. "The formal education system does not consider the experiences outside the schools as an educational development process. In fact, schools negate all that goes on in the communities and in the lives of the ordinary people or in the isolated communities, thus limiting all the opportunities of developing leadership opportunities through an educational process."

Earlier in his welcome address, AKU President Shamsh Kassim-Lakha introduced the chief guest and welcomed the delegates of the conference. Pointing out the fact that in many low-income countries, teachers do not meet even the minimum required standards for their profession, President Kassim-Lakha recounted the factors that encouraged AKU to concentrate on education of teachers, school heads as well as policymakers. "The impact of the Institute and its Professional Development Centres (PDC) have been far reaching. Graduates of AKU-IED return to their schools of origin well-equipped to enhance not only their own pedagogical skills but more so those of their colleagues as well as address challenges in school systems," he added.

In his opening remarks, AKU-IED Director, Dr Muhammad Memon welcomed the guests and said that quality in education could not be realised without improving the quality of teachers, curriculum, assessment, teaching-learning process and enabling environment. "The role of teachers and other educational personnel in providing quality education needs to be recognised and their working conditions and status also need to be improved."

Elaborating on AKU-IED's research work, he said AKU-IED was actively engaged in conducting research in education with special emphasis on school improvement and teacher education. "To date, 62 research studies by the faculty and 243 MEd dissertations have been completed. Several consultancy reports have also been prepared."

Dr David Taylor, Acting Provost AKU, also highlighted the role of AKU-IED in improving the quality of education in developing countries. He also emphasised the relationship between the quality of education and research.

The Chair of the International Conference Committee and Head of Research and Policy Studies, AKU-IED, Dr Anjum Halai, in her concluding remarks, said such conferences were a significant voice in the debate for quality in education. "Significant, because it is rare if not unusual for academic gatherings to be arranged in this part of the world; gatherings, which are focused on issues pertaining to quality education with specific reference to the developing world."​

value.Title: International Academics & Educators to attend AKU-IED’s Education Conference on quality in education
value.NewsSummary: The Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) is holding a three-day international conference on “Quality in Education: Teaching and Leadership in Challenging Times” from February 21-23, 2006. Dr Hamida Khuhro, Minister for
value.NewsContent:
​The Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) is holding a three-day international conference on “Quality in Education: Teaching and Leadership in Challenging Times” from February 21-23, 2006. Dr Hamida Khuhro, Minister for Education and Literacy, Government of Sindh, will be the Chief Guest at the opening ceremony to be held at the AKU Auditorium in Karachi.

The conference aims to disseminate educational research and learning from the experiences of practitioners, debate issues of quality in education, and identify the key factors in the provision of quality education. The papers and ensuing discussion will focus on three conference themes: Quality in teacher education; Leadership for quality teaching; Globalisation and teaching and learning.

Academics, researchers and educators from Canada, East Africa, India, Malaysia, Pakistan, Poland, Sri Lanka, Tajikistan, and UK are participating in the conference. The keynote speakers at the conference include Dr Quratulain Bakhtiari, Director, Institute for Development Studies and Practices, Quetta; Dr Angela W. Little, Professor and Chair of Education, Institute of Education, University of London; and Dr Manzoor Ahmed, Director of BRAC University, Institute of Educational Development, Bangladesh.

AKU-IED aims to improve the quality of education in less developed countries through capacity building efforts involving research, educational programmes, partnerships, policy initiatives and commitment towards wider social development. Within a relatively short timeframe, AKU-IED has successfully established a set of educational initiatives which form the basis of a coherent programmatic approach to school improvement and broader social development. The programmes are attended by a diverse group of participants representing Afghanistan, Central Asia (Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan), East Africa, South Asia, and Syria.

This conference will further identify new areas of academic and research programmes for AKU-IED and explore avenues for working collaboratively with public and private sector education institutions within and outside Pakistan for enhancing quality of education and promoting culture of research and scholarship.​

value.Title: AKU-IED successfully completes first year of ESRA programmes
value.NewsSummary: The graduation ceremony of the Certificate in Education: Primary Education (Mentoring Focus) for teachers and education department officials of selected districts of Balochistan and Sindh was held at the Multipurpose Hall of AKU-IED on Dec 24, 2004
value.NewsContent:
​The graduation ceremony of the Certificate in Education: Primary Education (Mentoring Focus) for teachers and education department officials of selected districts of Balochistan and Sindh was held at the Multipurpose Hall of AKU-IED on Dec 24, 2004. The ceremony marked the successful completion of AKU-IED's first year of ESRA-sponsored programmes for the two provinces.​

Delivering her speech as chief guest, Dr Iffat Farah, Head of Research and Policy Studies at AKU-IED, congratulated the course participants (CPs) on their graduation. She praised AKU-IED's contribution towards capacity building of teachers, supervisors, learning coordinators, resource persons and senior government officials through the ESRA programmes.

Referring to the CPs, she asked them not to neglect their classes when they go back to their context. "If you break relations with your class, you won't be able to teach others."

She asked the CPs to continue doing research so that they could develop their own action plans.

Despite his busy schedule, Director of AKU-IED, Dr Muhammad Memon, made an appearance. In his speech, he said AKU-IED, with the help of the government and teachers of Balochistan, would continue its struggle for providing quality education to the people.

He said mentoring was a new and innovative approach. He added that his experience showed that primary school teachers were skillful and mindful of their responsibilities, and asked the CPs to understand their profession and refine their teaching skills accordingly. "We need to understand our profession so that we could bring a lasting change in society. Until and unless we don't do that, we won't be able to achieve anything".

Programme Associate of ESRA (Sindh), Iffat Nayyar, spoke about the working of ESRA. She said its purpose was to build the capacity of teachers and institutions. "We are working to create a sustainable structure."​

She hoped that when the CPs go back to their context they would adopt the skills of planning, caring, and reflecting so that they could provide quality education to the children of their areas.

While sharing their reflections of the programme, the CPs said though they came from different backgrounds, they were able to amalgamate without any difficulty. They thanked their facilitators for teaching them new methods and skills. They assured their facilitators that they would adopt the newly-acquired skills and put them into practice once they go to their context.

Earlier in her welcome address, Rana Hussain, Coordinator of ESRA Programmes at AKU-IED, extended her good wishes to the graduates of the programme. She briefed the participants about the planning, implementation and expected outcomes of the programme.

A total of 33 CPs graduated in the Mentoring programme. The ceremony was attended by AKU-IED faculty, staff and students.

value.Title: Special Lecture Series programme Donald McKinnon to speak on commonwealth’s role in shaping the global agenda
value.NewsSummary: His Excellency Right Honourable Donald C. McKinnon, the Secretary-General of the Commonwealth, will be the guest speaker at Aga Khan University (AKU) on Friday, February 17, 2006, where he will deliver a lecture titled ‘Shaping the Global Agenda: The
value.NewsContent:
​His Excellency Right Honourable Donald C. McKinnon, the Secretary-General of the Commonwealth, will be the guest speaker at Aga Khan University (AKU) on Friday, February 17, 2006, where he will deliver a lecture titled ‘Shaping the Global Agenda: The Role of the Commonwealth’.

Rt. Hon. Don McKinnon has had a long and distinguished career in international politics and diplomacy. He became Commonwealth Secretary-General in 1999 after a 21-year career in New Zealand politics. He was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize for his work leading to the signing of a peace agreement in Papua New Guinea in 1997. He has been awarded Honorary Doctorates from Lincoln University, the four Universities of Manchester and the Heriot-Watt University. As Commonwealth Secretary-General, Don McKinnon is credited with modernising the Commonwealth Secretariat's structure and enhancing the Commonwealth’s profile. His achievements also include building strategic partnerships with other international organisations, as well as synergies with civil society, in pursuit of the values and objectives of the Commonwealth. Mr. McKinnon has put young people at the heart of the Commonwealth's work and promoted youth programmes, particularly in relation to HIV/AIDS.

In his lecture at the AKU, Mr McKinnon proposes to explore how the Commonwealth, a global organisation of 53 member-states, straddling every continent, religion, ethnic group and level of economic development, helps to shape the agenda of the international community. The lecture will take place at 7:00 PM at AKU’s Stadium Road campus, and will also include a question-and-answer session.

Mr McKinnon’s lecture is being organised under AKU’s Special Lecture Series (SLS​) programme, which is a part of its policy of encouraging broad-based education whereby eminent personalities are invited to illuminate the University’s constituencies on meaningful and engaging topics of public interest. Past speakers have included H.R.H. Prince Hasan of Jordan; Prof. Stanley Wolpert (author of ‘Jinnah of Pakistan’), Ambassador Dr Maleeha Lodhi and acclaimed artist Gulgee.

value.Title: Nazim urges universities to evaluate city government's trauma injuries plan
value.NewsSummary: City Nazim Mustafa Kamal was the chief guest at a research symposium on trauma and disasters, held at Aga Khan University (AKU) on February 1, 2006.
value.NewsContent:
​City Nazim Mustafa Kamal was the chief guest at a research symposium on trauma and disasters, held at Aga Khan University (AKU) on February 1, 2006. The Nazim urged all local universities to come forward to evaluate the plan being developed for trauma, injuries and disasters by the City Government. He also said that the City Government plans to acquire machines and hardware at the cost of Rs 650 million for Karachi to help in implementing the proposed plan.

A large number of local and foreign experts participated in the symposium titled "Trauma, Injuries and Disasters: Research and Training Imperatives' which was organised under Johns Hopkins-Aga Khan University International Collaborative Trauma and Injury Research Training (ICTIRT) Program.

Dr Ellen MacKenzie of Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health, USA, explained the objectives of the ICTIRT to establish innovative research training programmes between developed and developing country researchers and a sustainable research environment at the collaborating developing country institution. He said that the long term vision included the establishment of a programme or institute for injury and trauma research and training at AKU that can serve Pakistan and other parts of South Asia.  He also pointed out that this was the first annual symposium sponsored by the (ICTIRT) Program.

Health Policy and Systems Specialist, Dr Abdul Ghaffar from Global Forum for Health Research, Geneva said that attention was given to injuries only when there is a catastrophe. He pointed out that  major donors were not willing to commit significant resources to injury prevention and the issue was not an exception to the usual tussle between researchers and policy makers. He also stressed that the poor regulatory and legal systems were affecting research in injury prevention and control.

In his opening remarks, Professor Emeritus AKU, Dr John Bryant, the Symposium Chair, emphasised the importance of research in trauma and injury. He said, "It is extremely important that this issue of trauma and injury be given greater attention. There are people who lose their lives and health for reasons that are preventable. Johns Hopkins and AKU have been partners with the National Institute of Health to develop a programme for training and research in trauma and disaster. This will be very helpful for Pakistan and the whole region."

David Hoyt from the University of California, San Diego Medical Center, Adnan Hyder, and Courtland Robinson of Johns Hopkins University Bloomberg School of Public Health and Huma Qureshi of Pakistan Medical Research Council, Islamabad also addressed the symposium.

This symposium was part of AKU's continued commitment to research and dissemination of information. Activities based on research are strengthened through collaborative linkages with prestigious international institutions with established expertise in particular areas of focus as defined by the University.

value.Title: AKU Special Lecture Series destinies of islamic countries and west interlocked: Dr Maleeha Lodhi
value.NewsSummary: "We live in an age of paradoxes. Globalisation has transformed our life and outlook. It has created a world that is interconnected in ways that are truly amazing. Yet it is a world that is deeply divided. We live in an age of instant information but
value.NewsContent:
​"We live in an age of paradoxes. Globalisation has transformed our life and outlook. It has created a world that is interconnected in ways that are truly amazing. Yet it is a world that is deeply divided. We live in an age of instant information but it is ironic that there is still a knowledge deficit. The gap in understanding and mutual misperceptions between the West and the Muslim world has yet to be meaningfully addressed and bridged. This gap is, in fact, growing."

Dr Maleeha Lodhi, High Commissioner for Pakistan to the UK, delivering a lecture titled ‘Islam and the West: New Perspectives’.
This was stated by Dr Maleeha Lodhi, High Commissioner for Pakistan to the UK, who was the speaker at a Special Lecture Series (SLS) programme organised by Aga Khan University (AKU), Karachi on December 24, 2004. The Special Lecture Series is part of AKU's multidisciplinary and broad-based approach to education which aims to enrich students' understanding of the humanities and social sciences. The general public also benefits from this one-to-one interaction with scholars and other personalities of national and international repute.

In an eloquent discourse titled 'Islam and the West: New Perspectives', Dr Maleeha Lodhi captivated distinguished guests and members of the public as well as faculty, staff and students at a jam-packed AKU Auditorium. Dr Lodhi, who earlier served as Pakistan's Ambassador to the US following an outstanding career in journalism which included editorship of two leading newspapers, stressed that "this is a pivotal or defining moment in world history. Relations between the Islamic world and the West are at a crossroads. If action, as opposed to just words, is not taken, there is a real danger of an iron curtain descending between the Islamic world and the West.

Dr Maleeha Lodhi captivated distinguished guests and members of the public as well as faculty, staff and students with her talk delivered at a Special Lecture Series programme organised by Aga Khan University.

Dr Lodhi warned that "we live in dangerous times because several world civilisations simultaneously feel that they are under siege. Muslims feel they are under siege, and the West too feels it is under siege. The great challenge is how to bridge this gulf; how to build trust and confidence, how to remove mutual misperceptions, how to promote inter-civilisational harmony and be at peace with each other."

Highlighting the challenges ahead, Dr Lodhi emphasised that "the most critical transformation that the Islamic world has to make is from being mere recipients of knowledge and technology to becoming active participants in creating the 'new'. This means unleashing a grand renaissance of intellectual and scientific thought that can become the vehicle for the Muslim world's socio-economic emancipation."

Dr Lodhi pointed out, however, that "these steps cannot be taken in isolation. Reforms in the Muslim world must be accompanied by concrete and meaningful change in the conduct of foreign policy by key western countries." She added that if the policies of some of these countries remain as dogmatic and unilateral - almost mirroring the stance of some extremists in the Muslim world - then those who want reform, renewal and progress will lose out. And attitudes will harden in the Muslim world. In other words, our destinies are interlocked."

Highlighting the need for greater access to western markets, Dr Lodhi pointed out that while many poor countries, including Pakistan, have heeded the West's advice and dismantled trade barriers, the rich western countries have failed to reciprocate.

"I do not believe that there is a clash of values between the West and Islam that is responsible for the gulf we find today. The culprits are policies, political and economic, that urgently need to be re-evaluated, reformed and recast," she concluded.

Earlier in his welcome and introductory address, Mr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha, President of AKU, congratulated Dr Lodhi on the honorary fellowship she received earlier this year from her alma mater, the London School of Economics. Her citation, he said, described her as "a redoubtable woman, who has excelled in three careers so far: academia, journalism and diplomacy." On the diplomatic front, Mr Kassim-Lakha said that Dr Lodhi is "advocating Pakistan's rich heritage and defending its interests at a most difficult time when the image of Islam in the western world needs to be rescued from accusations of inbred association with militancy." Against this backdrop, he added, "we are fortunate that Maleeha Lodhi is flying the true colours of our great nation abroad."

Dr Lodhi's talk was followed by a question-and-answer session that saw active participation from an enthusiastic audience that clearly appreciated the intellectually stimulating event.

value.Title: Worldwide diabetes expected to double in the next 25 years
value.NewsSummary: "Worldwide diabetes is seen in seven to eight per cent of the population and the number is expected to double over the next 25 years," Dr. Abdul Jabbar.
value.NewsContent: ​"Worldwide diabetes is seen in seven to eight per cent of the population and the number is expected to double over the next 25 years," Dr. Abdul Jabbar, Professor and Head Section of Endocrinology and Diabetes, Department of Medicine at Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH), informed the audience while addressing a public health awareness programme held in Dubai.Dr Abdul Jabbar underscored the role of intensive lifestyle interventions such as exercise; maintaining a healthy diet and weight; regular blood sugar and cholesterol monitoring; eye and foot examinations; dental and cardiac care; and refraining from smoking or drinking alcoholic beverages in preventing or delaying the onset of diabetes. He pointed out misunderstandings regarding a 'diabetics' diet,' which are prevalent not only in the general population but also among the health care professionals. He said that patients with diabetes must eat a well balanced diet which will help them control blood sugar as well as help maintain serum cholesterol and lipids levels, thereby minimising the risk of coronary heart disease. "To help achieve the objective of creating awareness among masses, Aga Khan University Hospital has started a monthly diabetes awareness programme", said Dr Abdul Jabbar. He outlined the necessity and importance of a programme like that by telling the audience that diabetes was a common disorder that was growing at an epidemic rate all over the world. The programme, Healthy People 2000, focuses on helping patients to cope with the implications of this disease, incorporates the need for diabetes education and acknowledges the contribution of education in reducing the morbidity and mortality resulting from diabetes.The speaker participated in a question and answer session at the end of the programme.Earlier, welcoming the guests, Dr. Rubab Hasan, Patient Referral Coordinator said that AKUH is a philanthropic non-profit institution committed to deliver quality health care to all segments of society. This University Hospital at present offers 500 beds in all subspecialties of medicine, surgery, pediatrics, obstetrics and gynecology and psychiatry. AKUH, the principle-teaching site of the Aga Khan University (AKU), is part of Aga Khan Development Network, a group of private international development agencies, founded by His Highness the Aga Khan, which works in the developing countries of Asia and Africa.AKUH Representative provides convenience and easy accessibility to the Hospital's high-quality, cost-effective services to patients in the United Arab Emirates.AKUH organises such programmes as part of its outreach programme and societal commitment of creating awareness of early diagnosis and timely treatment. The Hospital has organised over 190 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' programmes in Karachi, Hyderabad and the UAE, benefiting more than 39,000 people. Based on the success of these lectures and in response to the demand for such programmes, this was the eighteenth in the series organised in United Arab Emirates.​
