value.Title: ​AKU provides eighty fellows, residents and interns to serve the nation
value.NewsSummary: ​"AKU is improving standards of postgraduate medical training in Pakistan and some of its graduates are in key positions on the Faculty of the College of Physicians and Surgeons", said Professor Sultan M. Farooqui, President. College of Physicians an
value.NewsContent:
​"AKU is improving standards of postgraduate medical training in Pakistan and some of its graduates are in key positions on the Faculty of the College of Physicians and Surgeons", said Professor Sultan M. Farooqui, President. College of Physicians and Surgeons of Pakistan (CPSP). Professor Sultan was the chief guest at the Graduation Ceremony for fellows, residents and interns organized by the Department of Postgraduate Medical Education (PGME) of TIle Aga Khan University (AKU) on October 23.1999. ​​

The Department of Postgraduate Medical Education has introduced a core curriculum for trainees that stresses not only clinical skills. but also emphasizes instruction in ethics. communication skills and computer literacy. Dr Farhat Moazam, Associate Dean, PGME, emphasized that AKU was committed to producing humane and ethical generalists and specialists for this country. who combine clinical expertise with wisdom and compassion. 

Dr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha. S.I., President, AKU, distributed certificates to 43 residents for completion of training in the 16 disciplines, which are approved by CPSP. In addition, those in General Surgery. Orthopedics, Internal Medicine. Obs/Gyn and Family Medicine are also recognized by the relevant Royal Colleges in tile U'K. 

Dr Camer Vellani. Rector. AKU. awarded certificates to 44 interns. Dr Shahryar Noordin was the recipient of the Best Intern Award for 1999. This was followed by Dr Kashif, who presented the valicditory speech as the representative of the graduating residents. Finally. Professor Farooqui awarded two fellowships in Adult Cardiology and Gastroenterology. 

Since 1986, AKU has graduated 2~2 young men and women from its postgraduate programmes. Among those trained to date. almost 40 percent come from outside Karachi. Following graduation. the majority have continued to work in Pakistan and many are on the AKU faculty having risen to senior ranks in several departments. Even more heartening is the fact that many others are on the staff and faculty of reputable teaching institutions throughout the country. Thus. these residency programmes are providing the nation with an important reserve of skilled specialists. 

This success in training generalists and specialists, oyer a relatively short time. confirms that colleges and universities in the private sector can play a significant role in improving medical postgraduate education and training in Pakistan.

value.Title: ​One in twenty people will have epileptic fit at some point in their life
value.NewsSummary: ​"About one in twenty people will have epileptic fit at some point in their lives", informed Dr Shahid Masud Baig, Consultant Neurologist at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) He was giving a presentation on "Epilepsy" at "Signs. Symptoms and Ca
value.NewsContent:
​​"About one in twenty people will have epileptic fit at some point in their lives", informed Dr Shahid Masud Baig, Consultant Neurologist at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) He was giving a presentation on "Epilepsy" at "Signs. Symptoms and Care”, monthly public health awareness program, held on December 26, 1998. Dr Baig added that epilepsy could strike at any age, however more than 70 percent of the cases occurs in first twenty years of life. A panel of Consultant Neurologists including Dr Farah Minhas, Dr Tehseen Muzaffar and Dr Nadir Ali Syed conducted a question and answer session 

Labeling epilepsy as a major health problem in Pakistan. Dr Baig said it is a very common neurological disorder and can occur at any age and is present in several different forms. The causes for epilepsy vary with age and for more than 66 percent of the cases, there is no known cause for occurrence of this disease. Highlighting the importance of earlv diagnosis for epilepsy, Dr Baig revealed that "if the disorder is recognized at an early stage, then in up to 70 percent of the cases, complete recover is possible with appropriate medication" He stressed that the treatment has to be continued in appropriate dosage under strict supervision of a neurologist. 

Commenting on facts and fiction about the epilepsy, Dr Baig informed that there are absolutely no medical restrictions for epileptic patients to get married and live a normal life.​

value.Title: ​Anemia in children
value.NewsSummary: ​"Anemia or deficiency of hemoglobin is very common in children especially in developing countries. Among the various causes, a poor intake of iron is the commonest reason of this condition and is present in two third of all children.
value.NewsContent:
​"Anemia or deficiency of hemoglobin is very common in children especially in developing countries. Among the various causes, a poor intake of iron is the commonest reason of this condition and is present in two third of all children. The symptoms are a pale look, irritability and loss of appetite. It is also well known that physical and mental development of these children is affected. Thus it is very important to prevent iron deficiency in children. Milk being a poor source of iron, it is important that child after the six months of age should be given pulses, green vegetables, meats and egg in addition to breast milk", informed Dr Ahmed Naqvi, Consultant Paediatrician, Paediatric Haematologist/Oncologist (blood diseases/cancer) and Assistant Professor of Paediatrics, The Aga Khan University Hospital. He was giving a presentation on "Anemia in Children" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care', monthly health awareness program, held on October 23, 1999. 

Dr Naqvi said, ''The other type of anemia commonly seen in Pakistani children is Thalassemia, which results from a genetically determined abnormal hemoglobin. The disease occurs when two genes must be present one from each parent. Thus when both parents are carriers of the abnormal gene (although they do not have severe anemia) there is a 25 percent chance in each pregnancy to have a severely affected baby needing blood transfusion at regular intervals. Intermarriages increase the chance that both parents may carry the gene and thus transmit the disease to their offspring. " 

Dr Naqvi added, ''The treatment for this condition is life long blood transfusion usually at four weekly intervals. This leads to excess of iron in the body, which may affect liver, heart, kidneys, brain, etc. To get rid of this iron these children need daily injections of "Desferrioxamine", which is given under the skin by a pump over a 8 - 12 hour period (during night). The other treatment for this condition is bone marrow transplantation but unfortunately this is not available in Pakistan. Therefore, the best hope for our country is prevention of this disease." 

Dr Naqvi concluded by saying that in communities where Thalassemia is commonly seen, all children and young adults should be screened by doing a simple blood test. If they are carrying the disease then all efforts should be made that such a person should not marry the other carrying the same gene. For couples who have a child with Thalassemia, antenatal diagnosis is available at centres including AKUH. For patients with Thalassemia, it is important to receive regular, screened blood transfusions. In addition they should also receive the iron removing medicine "Desferrioxamine" regularly. These children should also get Hepatitis B vaccination at the earliest possible. The life span of these children with irregular transfusions and no treatment for removing excess iron from their bodies, is usually 10 - 15 years. But with the above measures, i.e. regular blood transfusions and excess iron removal, these children can be expected a normal life of usual longevity."

value.Title: ​AKU nursing programme invited to East Africa
value.NewsSummary: ​"We would like to transplant this excellent institution into Kenya," said the Honourable Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka, Minister for Education and Human Resource Development, Government of Kenya, while addressing a group of fifteen Kenyan nurses and medic
value.NewsContent:
​"We would like to transplant this excellent institution into Kenya," said the Honourable Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka, Minister for Education and Human Resource Development, Government of Kenya, while addressing a group of fifteen Kenyan nurses and medical students currently studying at tile Aga Khan University. 

Honourable Musyoka had arrived in Pakistan on February 15, at tile invitation of the Aga Khan University (AKU) to continue dialogue regarding tile University's proposed programme for Advanced Nursing Studies in East Africa. He was accompanied by senior officials from tile Kenyan health and education ministries including Professor Justin Irina, Secretary, and Commission for Higher Education, Professor Julius Samson Meme, Director of Medical Services, Ministry of Health and Ms. Margaret Kaseje, Regional Health Program Officer, Aga Khan Foundation, Kenya.

Setting up of such a programme had been requested by the East African nursing leadership as well as public and private health officials in order to improve the quality of patient care provided throughout tile region. The Programme would offer continuing education for nurses in practice, research, administration and higher education in several cities of East Africa. In discussions about tile Progranune, Honourable Musyoka said that besides leading to improved nursing practices and healthcare delivery, it reflected the need for greater South to South collaboration.

AKU occupies a pivotal position in tile social development activities of tile Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN). which comprises a group of institutions working to improve living conditions and opporturIities in specific regions of the developing world. The proposed nursing Programme in East Africa would also fulfill AKU's mandate as an international University which seeks to serve multiple constituencies through tile diffusion of its intellectual products. When this progranune is implemented, "We," said Dr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha, President of tile Aga Khan University. "will be the first university in Pakistan to have an overseas campus."

During their week-long stay, tile delegates held meetings with tile Governor of Sindh, Lt. General (Retd.) Moinuddin Haider as well as Federal Ministers of Education and Foreign Affairs and other senior Govenunent officials. Discussions focused on the status of tile proposed Nursing programme in East Africa and of health and education in Pakistan, as well as social development issues of mutual relevance.

On his visit to Aga Khan University School of Nursing (AKUSON), Honourable Musyoka praised tile innovative working and leaming environment of the School and considered it an example for similar institutions throughout tile developing world, Professor Meme, tile Kenyan Health Ministry's Director of Medical Services said with institutions like AKUSON nursing in tile South could enter the new millenium 'with a spring ... not a crawl.'

The AKU Institute for Educational Development focuses on tile professional development of teachers and promoting leadership in education. While visiting AKU-IED, the Minister expressed an interest in tile possible expansion of its activities in East Africa and commended tile Institute's efforts in teacher education and school improvement. The more than two dozen East African course participants described tile attitudinal transformation they had experienced at AKU-IED and how it had enabled tllem to reconceptualize their roles as teachers and teacher educators.

On a visit to Sulranabad, one of Karachi 's squatter settlements (katchi abadis), where AKU participates in various community-based initiatives for education and social uplift, Honourable Musyoka observed, "This was an excellent example of a university's role in promoting the health of the community." 

The Kenyan delegation also travelled to the Northern Areas to familiarize themselves with the activities and projects of AKDN in the fields of health, education and rural development in these under-served, rural parts of Pakistan. During visits to Gilgit, Punyal and Hunza divisions, the delegation met officials of the Government and the AKDN, and noted that these programmes provided good examples of the collaboration between the Government and the NGO sector for the upliftment of the people at the grassroots level.

value.Title: Smoking is the major cause of lung cancer, heart attacks, chronic bronchitis and strokes
value.NewsSummary: ​"Every day, the tobacco industry has to recruit hundreds of people to become smokers to replace the hundreds who die daily as a result of smoking," said Dr Martyn Partridge, Consultant Chest Physician, Whipps Cross Hospital, London. He was speaking
value.NewsContent:
​"Every day, the tobacco industry has to recruit hundreds of people to become smokers to replace the hundreds who die daily as a result of smoking," said Dr Martyn Partridge, Consultant Chest Physician, Whipps Cross Hospital, London. He was speaking at an international seminar on Chest Diseases organised by The Aga Khan University (AKU) in collaboration with the Pakistan Chest Society (Sindh Chapter) from November 2-4.1999 Smoking is just one of the common respiratory problems encountered by a doctor which was discussed at the seminar. Other topics included asthma, tuberculosis and the abuse of antibiotics for treatment of chest diseases. ​

Dr Javed A. Khan, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, AK U, noted that "Smoking IS the single largest cause of death all over the world." In Pakistan, at least 54 percent of men and 20 percent of women regularly use some form of tobacco. Smoking is the major cause of lung cancer, heart attacks, chronic bronchitis and strokes. It also lowers resistance to fight colds and allergies. On average, a smoker shortens his or her life by 5 minutes for every cigarette smoked. Nicotene, the main ingredient of tobacco, is more powerful than heroin as an addictive substance. “But it is never too late to quit smoking," as Professor James Friend, University of Aberdeen, encouragingly said. However, the effects of passive smoking are just as dangerous. During an hour in a smoke filled room, a non-smoker inhales the equivalent of 15 filtered cigarettes 

"Passive smoking of family members significantly increases the risk of children developing asthma and aggravates the condition of those who already have it," said Dr Naseeruddin Mahmood, Assistant Professor, Department of Paediatrics, AKU. He went on to say that 10 percent of Pakistani children are at risk of developing asthma. Although asthma is not curable, with correct management a sufferer can enjoy a healthy and productive life these include getting rid of anything that is likely to attract a lot of dust such as carpets and stuffed toys. Dr Abdul Majeed Memon , Consultant Pulmonologist, AKU, stressed that it was important to guard against the current under diagnosis of asthma and educate asthmatics "in the management of the disease." 

A third common respiratory ailment that received attention was tuberculosis. It is spreading rapidly in Pakistan with over 350,000 active TB patients. An untreated patient can spread the disease to 15 other healthy individuals in a year's time. Dr S. Q. Nizami, Associate Professor and Consultant in Paediatric Infectious Diseases, AKU, highlighted that TB is an "often neglected public health problem with no countrywide data available on the prevalence of this disease in children." 

Dr Arif Sarwari, Consultant in Infectious Diseases, AKU, highlighted the over-usage of antibiotics in the treatment of respiratory diseases in Pakistan. He noted that the "onus Iies on both the patient and physician to be restrained, especially in an environment where regulatory controls are lacking."​

value.Title: ​World renowned cardiologist leads workshop at AKU
value.NewsSummary: ​He is one of the world's leading interventional cardiologists - a recipient of countless international awards and honours including Recognition Awards from the American Heart Association, the Indian National Institute of Heart Diseases and the Pakis
value.NewsContent:
​He is one of the world's leading interventional cardiologists - a recipient of countless international awards and honours including Recognition Awards from the American Heart Association, the Indian National Institute of Heart Diseases and the Pakistan Society of Cardiology. His breadth of experience spans military assignments, academic positions, hospital appointments, and administrative responsibilities. He is currently an Executive Director of the Interventional Cardiology Research Institute in Maryland, a Director of Interventional Cardiology at Washington Adventist Hospital and a Clinical Professor of Cardiology at the George Washington University School of Medicine in Washington D.C. and also serves on the editorial boards of several medical journals.

On February 27, 1999, the Aga Khan University (AKU) hosted a full day cardiology workshop led by the eminent Dr Fayyaz A. Shawl. Held at the AKU Auditorium, the workshop titled, "Update on interventional Cardiology," was part of AKU's Continuing Medical Education programme for physicians, residents and interns. Some hundred eminent cardiologists and cardiac surgeons from the country's medical community were invited to participate in this valuable learning experience and to share the opportunity to upgrade their knowledge and skills in interventional cardiology.

During the workshop, Dr Shawl performed several interventional procedures on selected patients brought to AKU from all over Pakistan. Patients with unique cardiac problems requiring treatment currently not available in the country were able to benefit from Dr Shawl's advanced expertise. Meanwhile, participants viewed the procedures transmitted live from Aga Khan University Hospital's Cardiac Catheterization Laboratory to the AKU Auditorium.

Dr Shawl had been invited by AKU on the initiative of Mr Mumtaz A. Rahim of Brinks Securities with support from other corporate sponsors such as Abbott Laboratories, Toshiba as well as Johnson and Johnson. Arrangements were also made for Dr Shawl to deliver a lecture at the National Institute for Cardiovascular Diseases while he was a guest of AKU.

value.Title: ​Common kidney problems in children and bed wetting
value.NewsSummary: ​"Almost half of our population consists of children less than 18 years. The life span of people has increased from 43 years to 64 years over the last three decades. Similarly death rate and infant mortality have reduced.
value.NewsContent:
​"Almost half of our population consists of children less than 18 years. The life span of people has increased from 43 years to 64 years over the last three decades. Similarly death rate and infant mortality have reduced. Although, we have several adult nephrology units, but there is not a single paediatric nephrology unit in the country", informed Dr Iqtidar Ahmad Khan, Consultant Paediatrician, Paediatric Nephrologist and Associate Professor of Paediatrics, The Aga Khan University Hospital. He was giving a presentation on "Common Kidney Problems in Children and Bed Wetting" at Signs, Symptoms and Care', monthly health awareness program, held on September 25, 1999. ​​

Dr Iqtidar said, "Urinary tract infections are common in infants and children. Some children have underlying congenital anomalies and stone diseases. These infections require early detection, investigations and management to avoid morbidity and mortality in later years. Similarly nephrotic syndrome is a very common disease entity, which presents with remissions and relapses and does not have a specified end point. It affects children 2-6 years old. They leak protein from their kidneys and present with swelling of face, abdomen and whole body. Nephrotic syndrome is much common in our country than in the west.” Dr Iqtidar added that Stone disease is also common in our country. Both kidney and urinary bladder stones cause a lot of suffering in young children. Besides operative treatment, they can now be removed by Extracorporeal Shock Wave Lithotripsy (ESWL). 

Dr Iqtidar said, "Bedwetting (nocturnal enuresis) is another common problem of children. Almost 10 percent of 5 year old and 5 percent of 1 0 year old suffer from this problem. Children usually grow out of this problem. Generally, there is a family history of bedwetting (nocturnal enuresis). These children suffer at the hands of their parents, siblings, friends, etc. They lack self-confidence and self esteem. They can be helped in several ways. A nasal spray (desmopressin) is now licensed for use in nocturnal enuresis." 

Dr Iqtidar concluded by saying that it is about time that we should preserve our meager resources and prevent renal disease from early childhood rather than opening more dialysis and transplant centres. The future demands in giving Paediatric Nephrology a chance, training paediatric nephrologists and opening paediatric nephrology units in all leaching hospitals.​

value.Title: ​Headaches: diagnosis and treatment
value.NewsSummary: "Every year, more of us seek treatment for headache than for any other medical problem. In rare cases, headache can be caused by bleeding, tumor, or infection in the brain, or else by diseases involving teeth, eyes, or sinuses. Flu or any sickness th
value.NewsContent:
​​"Every year, more of us seek treatment for headache than for any other medical problem. In rare cases, headache can be caused by bleeding, tumor, or infection in the brain, or else by diseases involving teeth, eyes, or sinuses. Flu or any sickness that causes fever can also cause headache. Such headache is known as secondary headache because it is due to, or secondary to, other problems, i.e. the headache is only a symptom of some other disorder", informed Dr Nadir Ali Syed, M.D., ABPN, ABEM, Consultant Neurologist and Assistant Professor for Neurology / Medicine. He was giving a presentation on "Headaches: Diagnosis and Treatment" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care', monthly health awareness program, held on August 28, 1999. ​

Dr Nadir said, "The vast majority of people with headaches suffer from what is known as primary headache, including migraine, tension-type headache and cluster headache. For these individuals, the headache itself is the primary problem and not just a symptom of some other disease. Considerable medical evidence suggests that migraine, tension-type and cluster headaches are caused by an electrical and chemical instability of certain key brain centers that regulate blood vessels around the head and the neck, as well as the flow of pain messages into the brain. This instability can be treated by using drugs that stabilize brain chemistry." 

Dr Nadir added that chronic headache is serious because it can interfere with the quality of daily life and reduces human productivity. It is a valid biological disorder, as real as diabetes, arthritis, or heart disease, and deserves the careful attention of the medical profession. There is no reason for people with headaches to suffer in silence. He informed that the first step towards recovery is accurate diagnosis. Since headaches are diagnosed and ultimately treated according to a particular classification, understanding and communicating these symptoms to your doctor can have dramatic results. Diagnosis is usually based upon a careful history and physical examination. Ancillary tests may be necessary in some cases to diagnose underlying conditions. The tests may include blood tests or brain imaging. 

Dr Nadir concluded by saying that fortunately research breakthroughs in the last several years have helped physicians understand much better what actually happens in the body during a headache attack. This knowledge has led to new and highly effective treatments that make control possible for most headache sufferers.

value.Title: Ensures compliance to highest standards of care to patients - Dr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha
value.NewsSummary: ​Six areas of the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) - Nursing Services Division, Clinical Laboratories, Pharmacy, Neurophysiology, Purchase and Bio-Medical Engineering - have met the requirements of the ISO 9002 Quality System.
value.NewsContent:
​Six areas of the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) - Nursing Services Division, Clinical Laboratories, Pharmacy, Neurophysiology, Purchase and Bio-Medical Engineering - have met the requirements of the ISO 9002 Quality System. The two-day audit was carried out in February 1999 by a team of five auditors from AIB Vincotte of Belgium. The auditors were impressed with AKUH's systems in these areas as well as the general level of compliance with all the written policies and procedures. 

At the certificate presentation ceremony, Dr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha, President of AKU, said "It is most important that we deliver quality care to our patients and the ISO process will continue to be useful in ensuring compliance to the highest standards of care that we have set for ourselves". 

"The ISO 9002 journey began in November 1997", said Mr Nadeem Mustafa Khan, Chief Operating Officer of AKUH, "and culminated with the final audit in February 1999. It was all hard work on the part of the staff. We were well-assisted by Mr 1mran Shariff of the Pakistan Institute of Quality Control (PIQC), who provided valuable on-going guidance". 

"Continued focus on providing care and services in accordance with the patient's needs is a must for AKUH", informed Mr John B. Stevens, Director General of the Hospital. He further stressed that it is AKUH's intention to prepare the entire Hospital for an ISO 9002 certification in the year 2000.

value.Title: ​Citibank helps Aga Khan University medical students
value.NewsSummary: ​Citibank has traditionally reinforced its commitment to social welfare by promoting educational programs over the last decade. In keeping with this commitment, Citibank has contributed Rs.1 million to the Aga Khan University’s (AKU) Medical College.
value.NewsContent:
​Citibank has traditionally reinforced its commitment to social welfare by promoting educational programs over the last decade. In keeping with this commitment, Citibank has contributed Rs.1 million to the Aga Khan University’s (AKU) Medical College. This funding will complement AKU’s effort towards covering tuition fees for medical students who are unable to finance their education. Citibank has in recent years assisted various prestigious educational institutions by providing financial assistance as well as teachers who are experienced bankers.

The Aga Khan University Is a component of the Aga Khan Development Network whose mission is social development in developing countries currently, the University provides opportunities for development of skilled manpower in health care and teacher education. The University’s purpose is to develop individuals for competence and leadership in their fields of study and training. The university strives for quality, international standards and relevance in all of its programs.

Though its financial assistance programme, the University ensures that no Pakistan citizen resident in Pakistan, who is otherwise qualified for admission to the medical college or the school of nursing is excluded solely because of inability to pay tuition. Admissions to AKU are on the basis of merit, irrespective of economic status, gender, race, religion or domicile.

During the 1998-1999 academic years, more than one third of the students enrolled were given financial assistance in the form of loans. Scholarships and granting-aid from the University.

value.Title: ​Senator Jamiluddin Aali lauds AKU's role in national integration
value.NewsSummary: ​"The Aga Khan University draws its faculty, staff and students from all the four provinces which is an excellent example of national integration," said Chief Guest Senator Jamiluddin Aali at the Independence Day celebrations at The Aga Khan Universi
value.NewsContent:
​​"The Aga Khan University draws its faculty, staff and students from all the four provinces which is an excellent example of national integration," said Chief Guest Senator Jamiluddin Aali at the Independence Day celebrations at The Aga Khan University (AKU) campus. Commenting on the great natural advantages with which Allah has blessed the nation, Senator Aali said “Seventeen countries of the world have no access to the sea; eleven countries do not have rivers. While eighty-two countries do not produce sugar, rice or wheat and seventy-eight grow no cotton. With its immense resources Pakistan has all the potential to become the great nation Quaid-e-Azam envisioned. " ​

After the impressive flag hoisting ceremony by Dr Shamsh Kassim-Lakha, President of AKU, the Senator and poet delighted the audience with a memorable rendering of the popular patriotic song he has authored - "Jeevay, Jeevay Pakistan." He urged the faculty, staff and their families to treasure Urdu as the language chosen by the Quaid-e-Azam as the national language of Pakistan. Spoken and understood in all four provinces, it is the language that can promote national integration. 

"The people of Pakistan are indebted to the generosity of the Aga Khan for this excellent centre of higher learning," said Senator Jamiluddin Aali. Under the direction and vision of the University's founder and Chancellor the Aga Khan, he said The Aga Khan University is both a repository of advanced knowledge and a training ground for future generations of the country. 

Senator Jamiluddin Aali also highlighted the contributions made by Sir Sultan Mohamed Shah, Aga Khan III, to the Pakistan Movement. He stressed the important role the Aga Khan played in the establishment of the Aligarh Muslim University for the Muslims of India. Building on that tradition, his grandson, His Highness Prince Karim Aga Khan has paved the way for academic excellence by establishing The Aga Khan University in the city of his grandfather's birth.

value.Title: Gastrointestinal bleeding a major cause of death and disease in Pakistan​
value.NewsSummary: "Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a significant cause of disease and death throughout the world and in Pakistan we have an enormous share of this catastrophic problem," said Professor Mohammad Khurshid, Medical Director and Associate Dean Clinical A
value.NewsContent:
​"Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding is a significant cause of disease and death throughout the world and in Pakistan we have an enormous share of this catastrophic problem," said Professor Mohammad Khurshid, Medical Director and Associate Dean Clinical Affairs, Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was speaking at a symposium on "State of the Art Management of Upper GI Bleeding" held on January 1, 2003, at Aga Khan University (AKU).

In his introductory remarks, Professor S.M.Wasim Jafri, Chief of Gastroenterology Section and Chairman, Department of Medicine, AKU, spoke on recent advances in the endoscopic management of GI Bleeding. He elaborated on the various endoscopic modalities available at AKUH to tackle this emergency. "Most GI bleeding problems demanding emergency surgical operations are handled easily by endoscopic skills which involve injection sclerotherapy, esophageal band ligation, ulcer sclerotherapy, argon plasma coagulation, heater probe, hemo clips and other therapeutic interventions. It is therefore critical that doctors are properly trained in endoscopic skills before carrying out interventional procedures," said Professor Jafri. A result of effective endoscopic management of GI bleeding, in those cases where surgical intervention is not mandatory, leads to a patients' hospital stay being shortened as well as fewer surgical complications. 

Dr.Shahab Abid, Assistant Professor, Department of Medicine, AKU, spoke on the initial management of a patient with upper GI bleeding, focusing on important aspects of patients' resuscitation and the availability of blood. Dr. Hasnain Ali Shah, Associate Professor, Department of Medicine, AKU, spoke about the management of variceal bleeding, very common in Pakistan due to the extreme prevalence of chronic liver disease as a result of Hepatitis B and C.

In his lecture on peptic ulcer bleeding, Dr. Saeed Hamid, Associate Professor, Department of Surgery, AKU, highlighted how to manage such an emergency and  discussed its endoscopic management as well as the role of resuscitation. Interventional radiology is most helpful in difficult cases of GI hemorrhage management. Dr. Tanveerul Haq, Assistant Professor, Department of Radiology, AKU, expanded on the role of a radiologist in such cases. Dr. Turab Pishori, Assistant Professor, Department of Surgery, AKU, enlightened the audience on how to manage a case of lower GI bleeding.                                                                                 

The final talk of the symposium was given by Ms. Doulat Hirani, Head Nurse, AKUH, regarding nursing considerations in the management of patients with GI bleeding. She highlighted "The importance of good nursing care in solving numerous problems and avoiding unnecessary complications in GI bleeding cannot be underestimated."

The talks were followed by a question and answer session and the inauguration of a GI Bleeding Unit This Unit will offer state-of-the-art management of gastrointestinal bleeding to patients admitted to AKUH. It will complement the other services currently available at the Hospital to treat gastroenterological problems.​

value.Title: ​Coronary angiography is the gold standard test for determining the extent and severity of coronary artery disease
value.NewsSummary: ​"Coronary angiography was first performed 40 years ago, and remains the gold standard test for diagnosis of coronary artery disease, against which other diagnostic tests arc validated", revealed Dr Asad Pathan. Consultant Clinical and Interventional
value.NewsContent:
​"Coronary angiography was first performed 40 years ago, and remains the gold standard test for diagnosis of coronary artery disease, against which other diagnostic tests arc validated", revealed Dr Asad Pathan. Consultant Clinical and Interventional Cardiologist of the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving a presentation on "Coronary Angiography" at "Signs, Symptoms and Care", a monthly public health awareness program, held on May 8. 1999 at AKUH Dr Path an added, "angiography is currently the only established method for accurately assessing the extent and severity of coronary artery disease", 

Labelling coronary artery, disease as a major cause of illness and deaths in Pakistan, Dr Pathanexplained that this disease leads to the narrowing of the blood vessels of the heart and is a slowly progressing process that may remain clinically unapparent for long periods of time. Coronary disease often becomes clinically evident because of the occurrence of symtoms such as angina or those associated with a heart attack or even sudden death. Dr Pathan stressed on the early detection of the disease and mentioned that coronary angiography is a reliable and safe procedure with a trivial but definable risk. The information obtained from angiography provides diagnostic information and is invaluable in making appropriate decisions about therapeutic interventions such as angioplasty or bypass surgery, which leads to relief of angina and can improve the long term outcome in some patients. 

A panel of Consultant Cardiologists also participated in the panel discussion. This included Dr Khawar Abbass Kazmi, Dr Anwar Ahmed and Dr Momina Mastoor.

value.Title: ​Latest technique for cataract surgery introduced at AKUH
value.NewsSummary: ​Dr Azam Ali, Assistant Professor and Consultant Ophthalmic Surgeon of the Aga Khan University (AKUH) have introduced the state-of-the-art in Cataract surgery at the Hospital. It is the latest procedure in Cataract Surgery in the western world and no
value.NewsContent:
​Dr Azam Ali, Assistant Professor and Consultant Ophthalmic Surgeon of the Aga Khan University (AKUH) have introduced the state-of-the-art in Cataract surgery at the Hospital. It is the latest procedure in Cataract Surgery in the western world and now for the first time it is available in Karachi. 

Dr Azam graduated with honours with the first batch of students of the Aga Khan University in 1988. He spent over five years in the UK learning advanced ophthalmic surgical skills at the world-renowned Moorfields Eye Hospital. 

This procedure involves taking the cataract out by the keyhole approach and the technical name for this procedure is "sutureless, clear cornea, temporal approach, phacoemulsification procedure with a foldable implant". For this particular procedure, a patient does not require any local or general anaesthesia and only eye drops are used. This avoids the risk of giving an injection behind the eye, which at times can lead to complications like haemorrhage.​

value.Title: ​Head injuries major preventable cause of death and disability
value.NewsSummary: "In last 20 years, due to increased number of automobiles on the road, number of road traffic accidents have increased manifolds and will continue to multiply", revealed Dr Naim-Ur- Rehman, Professor and Chief of Neurosurgery of the Aga Khan Universi
value.NewsContent:
​"In last 20 years, due to increased number of automobiles on the road, number of road traffic accidents have increased manifolds and will continue to multiply", revealed Dr Naim-Ur- Rehman, Professor and Chief of Neurosurgery of the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving a presentation on "Head Injuries" at "Signs, Symptoms and Care", a monthly public health awareness program, held on May 29, 1999 at AKUH. Dr Rehman added that, "infant two- third of the people who die as a result of traffic accidents, die from head injuries". 

Labelling head injuries amongst the commonest causes of death and disability in traffic related accidents in Pakistan, Dr Rehman explained that head injuries are no respectors of geography and occur on open highways and far-flung places, which make all the more difficult to provide timely medical attention by a qualified neurosurgeon. Dr Rehman highlighted that timely and efficient care in the initial few hours ofthe injury can significantly reduce the number of fatalities and disability associated with these serious injuries. He further stressed that dissemination of road traffic accidents, fights, falls and bullets which are responsible for death and disability in large number of patients.

A panel of Neurology and Neurosurgery Consultants also participated in the panel discussion, which included Dr Shahid Masud Baig and Dr Ahmed Ali Shah.​

value.Title: ​Combating the process and the diseases of ageing
value.NewsSummary: ​"If we live long enough, all of us will experience deterioration in our bodily functions, of different types and to different degrees," informed Dr Tom Martin, Consultant Obstetrician and Chief of Obstetrics and Gynaecology of the Aga Khan Universit
value.NewsContent:
​"If we live long enough, all of us will experience deterioration in our bodily functions, of different types and to different degrees," informed Dr Tom Martin, Consultant Obstetrician and Chief of Obstetrics and Gynaecology of the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving a presentation on "Combating the Process and the Diseases of Ageing" at "Signs, Symptoms and Care", a monthly public health awareness program, held on June 26, 1999 at AKUH. Dr Martin added that "many of us develop heart diseases, cancer, etc. and the development of diseases associated with ageing can be combated or avoided by modifications of lifestyle and of diet". 

Highlighting the importance of regular exercise and food intake, Dr Martin revealed that by adopting a proactive lifestyle the process of ageing could be retarded. He further informed that around 10 percent-80 percent of women as they would grow older will develop signs and symptoms due to hormone deficiency. These troublesome symptoms occur just before and after menopause and can be avoided with the use of hormones. Dr Martin stressed on the usage of Hormone Replacement Therapy (HRT) in menopausal women to prevent occurrence of serious diseases, such as heart diseases, bone diseases, etc. 

A panel of Consultant Gynaecologists also participated in the panel discussion, which included Dr Rahat Najam Qureshi and Dr Nasreen Chaudhury.

value.Title: ​AKU faculty attends WHO conference in Beirut on primary healthcare
value.NewsSummary: ​As Primary Health Care is a major component of undergraduate medical education at The Aga Khan University (AKU), Dr Parvez Nayani, Senior Instructor, Department of Community Health Sciences, was invited to present the AKU experience at a recent conf
value.NewsContent:
​As Primary Health Care is a major component of undergraduate medical education at The Aga Khan University (AKU), Dr Parvez Nayani, Senior Instructor, Department of Community Health Sciences, was invited to present the AKU experience at a recent conference in Beirut, organized by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the American University of Beirut.

The conference entitled, "Sustaining Primary Health Care in Academic Medicine as Basis to Training Doctors for the 21st Century: How to meet the Challenge," was attended by prominent medical academicians and WHO consultants from Geneva and Eastern Mediterranean Region. The participants analyzed the current situation in Primary Health Care teaching in different academic institutions, and developed approaches for strengthening it in the medical curricula. 

A task group of four participants including Dr Nayani are preparing a detailed report on the conference deliberations. This report, expected within the next six weeks, will then be shared with national governments and medical colleges for implementation of its recommendations. Emphasis on teaching Primary Health Care would ensure that the trained physicians appropriately respond to the needs of their communities, rather than focusing only on tertiary care training.​

value.Title: ​AKUH wins award for its computerized physician order entry system
value.NewsSummary: ​AKUH's award - winning project was its Physician Order Entry (POE) System. Developed by the Pharmacy Department, this computerized system checks drug interaction, dosage and route of administration
value.NewsContent:
​Managerial innovation in healthcare won the Aga University Hospital (AKUH) the prestigious Arthur Andersen I Dr Ed Crosby International runners-up award for 1999. 

AKUH's award - winning project was its Physician Order Entry (POE) System. Developed by the Pharmacy Department, this computerized system checks drug interaction, dosage and route of administration. AKUH physicians now prescribe drugs for patients by directly entering the drug name in the hospital computers and the pharmacist reviews the drug orders on the computer screen before dispensing drugs. This prestigious managerial innovation award is an international recognition for the quality of services provided by AKUH. Mr Abdul Latif Sheikh, Director of AKUH's Pharmacy Services, received the award at an impressive ceremony attended by 400 delegates from all over the world at the International Hospital Federation in Copenhagen, Denmark. 

The International Hospital Federation (IHF) is a key international agency responsible for promoting good practices in hospitals, health services management, training, healthcare policy and planning systems. Arthur Andersen is a global leader in the delivery of professional services and serves as consultants, auditors and financial advisors to the world's leading healthcare delivery organizations. The Award for Managerial Innovation honors select international institutions from the healthcare field that have demonstrated outstanding managerial innovation beyond their primary healthcare activity. A distinguished international selection committee known for their expertise and leadership in the healthcare industry chose this year's finalists.

value.Title: ​AKU confers second advanced diplomas in education
value.NewsSummary: ​The Aga Khan University-Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) conferred its second Advanced Diplomas to teachers and heads from various government and private schools on Saturday, July 31, 1999 at the AKU auditorium. The Chief Guest was Ca
value.NewsContent:
The Aga Khan University-Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) conferred its second Advanced Diplomas to teachers and heads from various government and private schools on Saturday, July 31, 1999 at the AKU auditorium. The Chief Guest was Captain U. A. G. Isani, Chairman, and University Grants Commission of Pakistan. ​

Twenty-seven of the graduates were awarded the Advanced Diploma in School Management (ADISM), while fifteen received the Advanced Diploma in English Language Teaching (ADELT). Thirty percent of the head teachers in the ADISM programme were drawn from government schools and seventy percent from the private sector. Among teachers in the ADELT programme twenty percent came from government schools. 

Graduates of both programmes contribute to total school improvement by working in concert with other educators and AKU-IED graduates at their home schools. 

The Advanced Diploma in School Management (ADISM) is a year-long school-based programme which develops the required attitudes, skills and knowledge and the ability to critically reflect on school management practices, of principals from AKU-IED's co- operating schools. 

The Advanced Diploma in English Language Teaching (ADELT) is a year-long classroom-based programme, designed to enhance content knowledge and to provide subject specialization for professional development of teachers. 

AKU-IED is currently undertaking educational programs in the field of teacher education at Masters, Diploma and Certificate levels. Established in 1993 as the Aga Khan University's first programme after health sciences, AKU-IED has gained recognition as a centre of educational excellence dedicated to the professional development of teachers and overall school improvement in Pakistan and other developing countries.

value.Title: Expert advice on combating antimicrobial resistance in Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: AKU organizes a national symposium on antimicrobial resistance in Pakistan.
value.NewsContent:
Experts have warned that misuse and overuse of antibiotics in humans and animals has resulted in the widespread distribution of resistant organisms in several countries, including Pakistan. That means, antibiotics that were previously able to cure will not work any more. 

They were addressing a national symposium on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) organised by the Aga Khan University. The symposium coincides with the launch of the National Strategic Framework for Antimicrobial Resistance by
A group photo with the speakers at the national symposium on antimicrobial resistance
 the Government of Pakistan last week.

“Antibiotic resistance is as much a problem in Pakistan as in the Western hemisphere,” said Dr Sadia Shakoor, Assistant Professor of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine at AKU.

“We know that infections acquired in the community are becoming resistant because antibiotics are available freely to the population even without prescriptions, leading to overuse. This needs to be checked through physician training to limit prescriptions and legislation to prevent over-the-counter availability of antibiotics.”

Superbugs, resistant to antimicrobials, are estimated to account for 700,000 deaths each year worldwide. A study shows that drug resistant infections will kill an extra 10 million people a year – more than currently die from cancer – by 2050 unless action is taken.

“At the UN General Assembly in September this year, leaders from 193 countries signed a landmark declaration agreeing to combat antimicrobial resistance,” said Dr Rana Hajjeh, Director, Department of Communicable Diseases Prevention and Control, WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean.

“Every signatory has agreed that drug resistant infections must be tackled as a priority. The nations have committed to develop surveillance and regulatory systems on the use and sale of antimicrobial medicines for humans and animals, encourage innovative ways to develop new antibiotics and improve rapid diagnostics, and raise awareness among health professionals and the public on how to prevent drug resistant infections.”

Dr Hajjeh congratulated Pakistan “for developing the first national policy on antimicrobial resistance”.

Dr Rumina Hasan, Professor of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine at AKU highlighted the need for strengthening diagnostic facilities to better diagnose infectious diseases and detect AMR to guide health care providers in selecting appropriate treatment.

AMR develops naturally over time, usually through genetic changes in bacteria. However, misuse and overuse of antimicrobials accelerates this process.

“Most illnesses with fevers, e.g., colds, flu and diarrhea, are caused by viruses, for which antibiotics are not recommended. However, due to over-the-counter availability, antibiotic consumption is found to correlate with these seasonal illnesses implying the misuse of antibiotics,” said Dr Erum Khan, Assistant Professor of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine at AKU.

“Other examples of misuse include use of antibiotics as growth promoters in farming of animals for food – livestock, fish and poultry farming. As for humans, antibiotic usage in animals too should be restricted to manage bacterial infections.

“The rate of discovery of new antibiotics has slowed down drastically and the antibiotic pipeline is running dry. There is an urgent need to conserve and safeguard the antibiotics that we have available.”

Other speakers included Dr Muhammad Salman from National Institute of Health, Dr Ejaz Khan from Shifa International Hospital, Dr Rene Hendriksen from Technical University of Denmark, Dr Ali Ahmed from University of Veterinary and Animal Sciences, and Dr Revathi Gunturu and others from AKU.

The event was organized by AKU’s Department of Pathology and Laboratory Medicine in collaboration with the University’s Department of Continuing Professional Education, Health Security Partners – USA, Medical Microbiology and Infectious Disease Society of Pakistan, and Pakistan Academy of Sciences.​

ISLAMABAD: The jurisdiction of the Federal Board of Intermediate and Secondary Education (FBISE) is going to be expanded in the whole country as the Senate Standing Committee on Federal Education and Professional Training gave a go ahead to the FBISE (Amendment) Act, 2016.

The meeting was presided over by its Chairperson, Senator Ms. Rahila Magsi, which was held on Tuesday at the old PIPS hall in the Parliament Lodges.

The committee considered "FBISE (Amendment) Bill, 2016 introduced by Senator Nuzhat Sadiq in the upper house of the parliament in November 2016.

The 'Federal Board' is an autonomous body working under the Ministry of Federal Education and Professional Training, which is mandated to organise, regulate, develop and control the intermediate and secondary level education while it also conduct examinations in the its affiliated institutions.

Currently, 1350 educational institutions are affiliated with the said board in Islamabad Capital Territory, Cantonments and Garrisons, Federally Administered Northern Areas and Pakistani institutes working abroad, but it is not allowed to affiliate with educational institutions situated in the domain of four provinces; Punjab, Sindh, KP and Balochistan.

value.Title: Pakistan’s newborns face rising risk of non-communicable diseases
value.NewsSummary: Conference on feto-maternal health explores how stress can hurt maternal & newborn health.
value.NewsContent:
​Stress, unhealthy lifestyle habits, and the prevalence of chronic diseases in adults are leaving Pakistan’s newborns more vulnerable to the threat of non-communicable diseases (NCDs), according to speakers at an event at the Aga Khan University on Saturday.

Experts at the International Conference on Stress and Conditioning: Impact on Maternal and Generation Health noted that economic, social and psychological pressures lead to stress and high levels of stress hormones affect the baby in the womb. These chemicals can trigger genetic changes which stall the development trajectory of the brain and heart of a fetus resulting in lifelong effects on the fetus’s learning capability, social functioning and ability to fight disease.

Pakistan has approximately 80 million people who suffer from NCDs or life-style related illnesses such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obesity, chronic lung and kidney disease and mental illnesses. The number of Pakistanis with these diseases is increasing by approximately 10 per cent a year and speakers noted that prospective parents with NCDs are also more likely to pass on their illness to the next generation.

“Our healthcare system is geared towards treating those suffering from NCDs now. But there isn’t enough attention paid to the inter-generational effects of disease. By focusing on early interventions in the period between conception and birth we can reduce the lifelong risk of neurocognitive, metabolic and cardiac disease and ensure that every child achieves their full potential,” said Dr Nuruddin Mohammad, director of maternal and fetal medicine at AKU’s division of women and child health.

During the conference speakers shared how innovations in neurosonographic imaging – advanced ultrasounds of a fetus’s heart and brain – are enabling the early detection of delays in brain and heart development. New technology is also helping identify biomarkers – chemical indicators – that can predict developmental delays that may lead to disease in adulthood.

This makes the first 2,000 days of a child’s life extremely important and investing in healthcare during this period could result in the greatest returns for society in terms of health and wellbeing. Speakers on the day noted that in many cases of NCDs, screening and interventions in adults was significantly less effective as irreversible genetic modifications have already taken place.

Dr Rehan Ali, associate professor in paediatrics at AKU said: “The link between nourishment and lifelong health has been long established. Insights into the developmental origins of health and disease are clearly showing the importance of environmental factors on maternal and fetal health. This research is making a strong case for conducting healthcare initiatives earlier in life to help achieve targets under Sustainable Development Goal 3.”

The one-day conference was preceded by three workshops which enabled the exchange of skills in areas relating to disease management during pregnancy and the sharing of knowledge on ethical issues in obstetrics.

Other speakers at the conference included Dr Stephen Lye, Executive Director, Fraser Mustard Institute for Human Development, Canada; Marleen Temmerman, Chair of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology at the Aga Khan University’s Medical College in Nairobi; and Professor George Chrousos from the Athens University Medical School in Greece.

value.Title: An interview with CIME’s new director
value.NewsSummary: Dr Docherty shares his vision for CIME and his love for spicy food and the outdoors.
value.NewsContent:
​In the early 1990s, Dr Charles Docherty led a team at Glasgow College of Nursing that designed a novel pilot project. The project aimed to use the latest technology to teach nurses how to take care of critically ill patients.​ Charles’s team used one of the first models of a Macintosh computer, a mannequin, video cassette recorders (VCRs) and some of the earliest digitising software to create a six-week-long simulation course based on a patient admitted to the ICU after an accident.

At every stage of treatment, students watched videos about the patient’s condition in which they assessed his health and then decided how to respond in light of their theoretical knowledge and nursing experience. Students logged their responses into a computer programme and instructors were able to give feedback in real-time to students. They also videoed their performance to share with their classmates. Back then this was a novel attempt at integrating new computer and video technology into problem-based learning. Feedback from students about the course was very positive with many saying that they felt confident, rather than nervous, when they began taking care of critically ill patients.


The success of the initiative led to Charles designing a number of other simulation-based courses in Scotland and Jordan and later leading the establishment of a full-scale simulation centre in Bahrain from scratch. ​As the Centre for Innovation in Medical Education (CIME) enters its second year of operations, Charles is keen to bring his expertise in simulation-based learning and his experience of working with people with different sets of skills to improve teaching and learning standards at AKU.​

In this interview, Charles shares his vision for the CIME, some highlights of his time at AKU and his plans for putting innovation at the heart of teaching at the University.

Tell us about your career in nursing and simulation

I initially wanted to be a dentist. But a summer job as a healthcare assistant in an old people’s home in Glasgow gave me a deep appreciation for the importance of nursing. I really enjoyed caring and assisting people with their healthcare needs and in 1976 I started studying at Glasgow Royal Infirmary: a nursing school renowned for being led by one of Florence Nightingale’s pupils, Rebecca Strong. ​
​
I went onto became a charge nurse in intensive care and alongside full-time work I continued my studies to gain a diploma and master's in nursing in the mid-1980s. While working in the hospital I noticed how many nurses were just taught enough theory to inform their clinical practice and I saw how many skills were learnt through trial and error on real patients. 

This made me think about how education can be improved in the discipline and in 1996 I became an instructor in nursing at Glasgow Southern General, the hospital famous for developing the Glasgow Coma Scale (a scoring scale that helps assess a person’s level of consciousness). This is where I became deeply interested in how technology can enhance teaching and learning and my PhD focused on how multimedia can help instructors improve the effectiveness of teaching methods. 

What were your first impressions of the CIME?

I’ve only been here a short time but I’m very impressed by the building, the equipment and videoconferencing facilities. I’m also very pleased that we have the biomedical and information technology expertise to ensure that simulations are supported and that in our ‘Champions’ we have clinical faculty with the advanced skills to manage the training modules. 

CIME has great potential for growth and innovation in how we teach nurses and doctors and I’m looking forward to realising this advantage by working with our schools to embed simulation practices into our curricula.

What projects are underway at the CIME now?

We’ve put together a team of faculty who have been designated as ‘clinical Champions’. They will lead efforts to integrate CIME’s facilities into the curriculum. We’ve already sent some of this group to Boston’s Centre for Medical Simulation, which is jointly run by Harvard and MIT, on a weeklong course on simulation-based instruction. They are back in Karachi now and are working on initiatives to incorporate simulation into our curriculum. 

AKU is also in talks with the UK-based Higher Education Academy to provide a mechanism for teaching fellowships to be accessible for our clinical Champions. Courses we design in-house would certify them as instructors in simulation-based methods and enable us to scale up training of our own faculty.

Staff are also setting up a brainstorming group with students, who are often at the cutting edge of communications and information technology,  so that we understand their expectations of teaching and how we can improve our educational methods and keep them relevant to the coming generations. 

How do you see CIME developing in the future?

The best simulation centres are seamlessly integrated into the curriculum. When you have the right combination of technology, subject matter expertise, technical skills and thoughtful teaching you can really transform the learning process. My focus is currently on linking the subject experience that faculty have with the latest teaching methods being practiced in medical schools around the world. 

The AKU’s programmes have a strong curriculum and simulation-based courses can be developed for each competency required of practicing professionals. Learning objectives can be achieved through using mock scenarios, videos and debriefing sessions that CIME is purpose-built for. By distancing learning from actual practice, patient safety is not compromised and students prosper knowing that if they make mistakes no-one comes to harm. There are a wide range of situations that we can develop for specialty nursing programmes and PGME students. Once established, teaching packages and courses that deliver clinical competence in a standardised way could be accredited so that we can market them to other institutions and thereby raise education standards across the board. 

When it comes to some clinical skills, we have a range of mannequins on which to practice. Some of these have very sophisticated physiological modelling providing instant responses to a whole range of different interventions including pharmacological issues.  But we can also use actors (mock patients) who can demonstrate a range of needs, personality traits and unique demands that cannot be reproduced as yet through artificial means. By practicing in a situation where they aren’t worried about making errors they can truly develop therapeutic communication skills that will benefit them in the real world.

Finally, CIME can make a great contribution in the area of inter-professional learning. Mock surgeries and mock wards require different specialists to work together. Importantly, we can vary conditions to test skills such as leadership, prioritisation, decision making and the application of clinical knowledge under pressure. 

For example in the area of critical care, we have an ideal environment where anaesthesiologists can benefit from mock surgery scenarios in which they have to adjust their plans due to changes in blood pressure brought on by ventilation issues, or hemorrhage, or other adverse events, during surgery. This would require them to work closely with the theatre team to adjust anaesthesia, order blood, blood tests and so on while advising the surgeon on whether to proceed or not. These are situations that will help them feel more confident when they are faced with similar situations in a busy hospital setting.  

When did you first hear about AKU during your time abroad? 

I first heard about AKU when a few colleagues and I were working on a nursing project in Bangladesh in 2006. We were looking for exemplars in nursing in the region and we kept on hearing about AKU’s School of Nursing in Karachi. In Bahrain, I worked with a research assistant who was previously at AKU and he informed me of the humanitarian vision of the institution that I found to be very inspiring.  

That’s work, what about your other interests?

Cycling and gardening are some of my hobbies.  Unusually for a Scot, I have no interest in golf nor football. Another thing that I enjoy is spicy food. My hometown of Glasgow has some wonderful curries, chapattis and tikkas and so far I’ve found that the food in Pakistan to not be spicy enough! I think I should get out more.

How have you found your time at AKU so far?

I’ve only been here for a few weeks but I’m surprised by how green Karachi is. I love the outdoors and the Karachi campus is so beautifully designed and pleasant to walk in. There’s a surprise around every corner with beautiful courtyards and water features. I’ve heard good things about Lahore and the northern areas of Pakistan and I’d love to go there soon too.

I’m delighted to come and work at AKU as I’m aware of the quality of its faculty and how its graduates are spread around the world and are doing great work.

value.Title: English Course for AKU Drivers
value.NewsSummary: 11 AKU drivers have completed a part-time English course.
value.NewsContent:
A group of 11 AKU drivers have completed a part-time English course. The course ran for nine weeks and was designed and delivered by the British Council in Karachi in collaboration ​with ELE_net and HR at AKU.

The content of the co​urse was based on common encounters AKU drivers are likely to experience with passengers in a typical working day. The principal objective was to develop the learners'​ confidence with using English in common work-related contexts. With each module, the drivers learned situational language for these encounters, focusing on vocabulary and functional phrases.​​​

By the end of the course, the drivers reported that they felt far more confident when using English for greeting passengers and engaging in conversations with them. They also felt that they were able to deal better with queries about places to visit in Karachi.

value.Title: GSMC and NTV launch ‘Giving Nature a Voice’
value.NewsSummary: A weekly series on East Africa’s most critical environmental issues
value.NewsContent:
Kenya’s NTV and the Aga Khan University’s Graduate School of Media and Communications have launched a weekly series of original half-hour documentaries Giving Nature a Voice, airing Wednesdays at 10PM from February 1, 2017.

Our goal: to give voice to the truly voiceless – East Africa’s threatened biosphere and the people who call it home. Thanks to the Aga Khan University’s Environmental Reporting Programme, a select group of young African filmmakers were given the opportunity to showcase their compelling, illuminating and impactful environmental films.   

Under the AKU Environmental Challenge, launched last May, we invited filmmakers and broadcast journalists to explore East Africa’s most critical environmental issues.  We asked them to look at efforts to protect the world’s largest population of mega-fauna, its threatened coral reefs and disappearing rainforests.  Winning teams come from Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda and Burundi. Their projects explore a wide range of topics, from deforestation and the threats faced by Mother Africa’s greatest lakes — Victoria, Turkana, Naivasha and Tanganyika  — from the cattle wars that pit pastoralists against each other and wildlife dependent on fragile rangelands, to the struggle by fishermen eking out a living when aquatic resources collapse from overfishing and habit destruction, to the alarming rate at which our imperiled biodiversity is vanishing.

These are stories of immense human drama set amid profound climate and environmental change. Yet they also reflect the new optimism of an emerging environmental consciousness – and activism – in Kenya and elsewhere in East Africa. Filmmakers will profile the effort to teach Kenya’s youngest generations to value and protect their most valuable inheritance and the stunning beauty of our common African home.  Others will give voice not only to nature but the people who live on the edge of the wild, and whose lives are most dependent on its preservation.

All the filmmakers have answered our challenge to produce “smart, ambitious and innovative documentaries that will shape debate, move governments to action and help save our natural heritage.” In January 2017, we announced Round 2 of our Environmental Challenge, offering funding for another set of pioneering reports from the front-lines of our threatened natural world. Our aim: to draw on the unrivalled power of an informed media – to raise awareness, support the new wave of environmental consciousness sweeping Kenya and the region.  Together with like-minded allies and an engaged public, we can change a dangerous trajectory that otherwise would be unstoppable.

value.Title: AKU's golf tournament set to fund additional 100 life-saving paediatric cardiac procedures
value.NewsSummary: AKUH has created a place where congenital heart disease patients can find help and hope
value.NewsContent:
​One hundred members of civil society came together over a game of golf to support the Aga Khan University (AKU)’s efforts in Mending Kids’ Hearts on Sunday.

About 60,000 children – one in every 100 infants born in Pakistan every year – are born with cardiovascular disease resulting in the deaths of many babies without any diagnosis. 

The internationally reported incidence of congenital heart disease (CHD) is 8 to 10 per 1,000 live births. In Pakistan, since most births occur in villages, in remote areas or in ill-equipped basic health units, the true prevalence of CHD at birth is unknown as accurate data is not available. Lack of awareness and inadequate diagnostic and treatment facilities compound the problem as many Pakistani CHD patients do not survive beyond their first few years.

“Pakistan and three other countries India, China and Indonesia contribute to about 50 per cent of children with heart diseases in the world,” said Dr Muneer Amanullah, an associate professor of cardiothoracic surgery and interim associate dean of Postgraduate Medical Education at AKU. “About 15,000 to 20,000 of infants have critical problems and require a surgery or intervention in the first year of life.”

He noted that CHD occurs during the early stages of a mother’s pregnancy, when her baby’s heart is forming, affecting how blood flows through the heart and out to the rest of the body. Some anomalies can be prevented through vaccination, adequate intake of folic acid and iodine through foods or supplementation, and care during pregnancy.

Dr Amanullah addressed these issues to supporters of Mending Kids’ Hearts who had gathered for a fund-raising golf tournament held at the Karachi Golf Club. He said that many of the heart defects such as a small hole in the heart, or missing or poorly formed parts of the heart could be life threatening and contribute to long-term disability. 

He explained that although congenital abnormalities may be the result of one or more factors – genetic (including children born of a consanguineous or close relative marriage), infectious, nutritional or environmental factors – it is often difficult to identify the exact causes.

Dr Amanullah commented that many CHD patients in Pakistan present late, when complications have already developed because of a delay in diagnosis, after a patient’s first few years, adding further to the mortality rate which is already high. If diagnosed and treated in time, children with these conditions can lead a normal life.

“This event wouldn't be possible without our generous community, volunteers, donors and sponsors,” said Mr Hans Kedzierski, CEO, AKUH. “There are only a few hospitals in Pakistan that are able to perform surgeries on these young patients, including infants whose hearts are the size of a strawberry. The Aga Khan University Hospital has created a place where CHD patients can find help and hope.”

Each year, the congenital cardiac programme team at AKUH performs more than 400 paediatric cardiac procedures. It is the only programme in the country to be both accredited by Joint Commission International (JCI) and recognised by the International Quality Improvement Collaborative (IQIC),” added Mr Kedzierski.

“Seventy per cent of CHD patients at AKUH come from families without the financial means to afford the cost of outstanding surgical and medical care,” said Mr Kedzierski. The Hospital’s Patient Welfare Programme has assisted over 2.25 million patient visits with Rs 9.5 billion disbursed since its inception in 1986.

“AKUH is dedicated to the principle that everyone deserves access to quality healthcare, regardless of their income. We are grateful for the support of our partners who are helping us to expand our paediatric cardiac services with an additional 100 CHD corrective surgeries this year,” he said.

AKU President Firoz Rasul noted that “women and child health programmes at AKU are part of the response from the world community to the UN's Sustainable Development Goals. The University has pledged to invest more than US$85 million over the next decade in support of the global strategy that will act as a platform to put women, children and adolescents at the heart of the SDGs”.

“Recently, AKU has also p​artnered with the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation. Under a five-year, US$25 million grant, the Umeed-e-Nau or ‘a new hope’ programme, the University will work with the public sector to boost mother and child health in Pakistan,” he added.
