value.Title: AKU-IED holds graduation ceremony for Advanced Diploma Programmes
value.NewsSummary: Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) held a graduation ceremony for the Class of 2007 in two of its advanced diploma programmes on September 8, 2007 at Aga Khan University (AKU), Karachi.
value.NewsContent:
Aga Khan University Institute for Educational Development (AKU-IED) held a graduation ceremony for the Class of 2007 in two of its advanced diploma programmes on September 8, 2007 at Aga Khan University (AKU), Karachi . The diplomas were awarded to the graduates of ‘Advanced Diploma in Education: Educational Leadership and Management', and ‘ Advanced Diploma in Education: English Language Teaching' by the chief guest Mr Mazharul Haq Siddiqui, Vice-Chancellor, University of Sindh , Jamshoro.

Vice Chancellor Siddiqui said in his address that the work being done by AKU-IED in developing and delivering quality programmes in teacher education, educational leadership, English language teaching, early childhood education and development, and indeed several other areas was commendable. He stressed the importance of public-private partnership in efforts to improve the quality of education in the country. Speaking on the occasion, Dr David Taylor, Acting Provost, AKU, appreciated the support of the Federal and Provincial governments in the implementation of AKU's programmes and initiatives.

Dr Muhammad Memon, Director AKU-IED said that the Institute took the lead to develop programmes in educational leadership for head teachers and principals in response to the needs of the stakeholders. Education systems need to make joint efforts to enhance capacity of teachers, teacher educators and educational managers to develop schools as learning institutions in Pakistan . In order to transform the schools, school heads need to acquire core learning capabilities of fostering aspirations, developing reflective dialogue and understanding the complexity of the system.

AKU-IED's several programmes are field-based and are meant to create a ‘multiplier effect' as the graduates go back to their institutions and impart the benefits of their learning to fellow teachers, teacher administrators, school leaders, and indeed to the students in the classroom. The Advanced Diploma programme in Educational Leadership and Management is designed to facilitate the change process in schools and bring about an improvement in the quality of school management and governance. To date, this programme has graduated 228 teachers and head teachers.

The Advanced Diploma Programme in English Language Teaching addresses the needs of teachers from varied backgrounds, with the aim of enhancing the participants' pedagogical content knowledge with an emphasis on reflective practice and ‘constructivism' for change in teaching practice. The programme takes into account the classroom settings of the teachers in their respective institutions.

The quality of its educational iniatiatives has made AKU a role model for other institutions in the region. When reviewing existing programmes or adding new ones, AKU ensures the attributes of quality, relevance and impact are kept in mind.

value.Title: 27 patients under treatment at Aga Khan University Hospital for viral haemorrhagic fever
value.NewsSummary: At Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH), 27 patients are currently hospitalized with suspect viral haemorrhagic fever; most of them were admitted during the last two weeks.
value.NewsContent:
At Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH), 27 patients are currently hospitalized with suspect viral haemorrhagic fever; most of them were admitted during the last two weeks. This obviously reflects a sudden increase in the number of such cases and is a cause of concern. So far, a total of 528 patients with ages ranging between 6 to 82 years were admitted at AKUH between June 14 to November 8, 2006 with viral haemorrhagic fever. Out of these, eleven patients expired due to severity of disease, while 490 recovered and were discharged. The patients suffered from symptoms ranging from bleeding, diarrhoea, vomiting to abdominal pain.
​
Two hundred and forty seven patients were diagnosed to have Dengue haemorrhagic fever, three patients suffered from Crimean-Congo Haemorrhagic Fever (CCHF), while in the remaining, the special serological tests were either negative or the results are pending. A total of 506 patients were received from Karachi and the remaining patients came from Larkana, Hyderabad, Thatta, Dadu, Saedabad, Nawabshah, Rahim Yar Khan, Gharo, Mirpurkhas, Sujawal, Gilgit, Baluchistan and Saudi Arabia.

Dr Farhat Abbas, Medical Director & Associate Dean, Clinical Affairs, Aga Khan University Hospital

value.Title: Harvard-AKU collaboration brings unique imaging ‘pill’ to Karachi
value.NewsSummary: New optical endomicroscopy device will be used to explore the causes of undernutrition.
value.NewsContent:
Researchers at Aga Khan University have partnered with faculty at the Massachusetts General Hospital, an affiliate of Harvard Medical School, to test a novel pill-shaped imaging device that can offer a low-cost and non-invasive method to understand the causes of malnutrition in children.

This is the first-ever test outside the United States of this optical device which provides high resolution images of the inside of a patient’s gastrointestinal tract. Shaped like a transparent pill, the ingestible device contains a high-resolution infrared system that captures microscopic images of unusual tissue patterns in the stomach and intestine.  

Ongoing research at AKU under the SEEM grant (Study of Environmental Enteropathy and Malnutrition in Pakistan), which is funded by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, is studying if malnourished children have a different set of bacteria in their intestines that limit their growth potential and reduce their immunity to disease. The device will be used to build a visual profile of a malnourished child’s gut that will reveal the microbiological processes that trigger harmful development patterns  

Developed by Professor Gary Tearney from Massachusetts General Hospital’s Wellman Center and department of pathology, the device also offers an alternative to endoscopies: a widely-used technique to detect diseases of the digestive system. Endoscopies involve the insertion of a tube down a patient’s throat which requires sedation or anaesthesia and the presence of trained specialists in a hospital setting.  

Since the pill-shaped device can be swallowed, no sedation nor anaesthesia is required which lowers the cost of the procedure and opens up the possibility of this technology being used in clinics which are more accessible to patients. 

“This novel technology offers a cheaper, non-invasive way to explore the genesis of childhood malnutrition and other gastrointestinal diseases,” said Dr. Asad Ali, associate dean for research and an associate professor in paediatrics and child health at AKU.

“We’re looking forward to further collaborations with Professor Tearney and his team to explore innovative applications of this revolutionary device,” he added. 

Professor Tearney said: “We are very impressed with the competence and can-do attitude of the team at AKU. We are currently exploring a number of technical and procedural solutions that will improve the imaging process and are glad to know that our device can inform research on malnutrition which is such a pressing problem in Pakistan.”

Gary Tearney is a Professor of Pathology at Harvard Medical School and a Mike and Sue Hazard Family MGH Research Scholar. His research interests are focused on the development and clinical validation of non-invasive, high-resolution optical imaging methods for disease diagnosis.

Research under the partnership corresponds with special targets under goal 2 of the global Sustainable Development Goals:  end hunger, achieve food security and improved nutrition, and promote sustainable agriculture. Targets under goal 2.1 call for special efforts to end all forms of malnutrition and stunting in children under the age of five by 2030.
value.BannerCaption: Photo courtesy: Wellman Center for Photomedicine at Massachusetts General Hospital.

value.Title: The role of resilience in promoting mental health
value.NewsSummary: SONAM’S Shireen Shehzad develops a locally relevant scale to promote mental health.
value.NewsContent:
Resilience represents a person’s ability to positively adapt to life’s inevitable ups and downs. In the West, the concept of resilience has been turned into several in-depth assessment scales that help mental health practitioners assess psychological well-being and the attributes that enable a person to adjust to setbacks. 

“People found to have high levels of resilience on these scales tend to think and act in more positive, constructive ways when faced with challenges,” says Shireen Shehzad, an assistant professor at Aga Khan University’s School of Nursing and Midwifery (SONAM).  

“Like a sponge, they’re able to absorb pressure, modify their behaviour and attitude, and bounce back to a state of mental wellbeing. These qualities help protect their mental health from increasingly common conditions such as depression, stress and anxiety which often go unnoticed,” adds Ms Shehzad, 
whose research has led to the development of South Asia’s first validated, local language scale for resilience.

While the use of such resilience scales is common in the West, the absence of tools that reflect South Asia’s frame of reference and mode of expression mean that many aspects of resilience are misunderstood by practitioners in the region. Ms Shehzad and her team of researchers worked to address this gap by collaborating with US-based Dr Gail Wagnild, the creator of one of the world’s most widely accepted measures for resilience, the Wagnild Resilience Scale. 
 
Researchers first produced an Urdu translation of Dr Wagnild’s scale that was reviewed by content experts. This was then translated back to English by two separate individuals and then reviewed by Dr Wagnild to ensure that all the core competencies of resilience had been captured. The scale was then pre-tested on a community of women with similar socio-economic circumstances to the target population.

Community health workers were then trained in the use of the scale which was then applied in two, economically-deprived urban squatter settlements in Karachi’s Shah Faisal Town and Malir. Previous research has already shown a clear link between poverty and a person’s vulnerability to mental health challenges. By testing the scale among married women in some of the poorest communities in Karachi, researchers validated its usefulness in a population at high-risk of negative mental health outcomes. 

They found that the tool helped them explore how they could take charge of their own health and happiness.  Many women said that the questionnaire helped them share mental health issues that they had felt but not expressed before. The local language scale can be used to identity vulnerabilities in people of all ages and social backgrounds in the country thereby enabling mental health professionals to quickly access those most in need of counselling or life-skill building sessions.

“Resilience is not a trait that people are born with or either have or do not have. It involves behaviors, thoughts and actions that can be learned and developed by anyone. Instead of focusing on treating diseases we should look to promote the development of qualities that can safeguard the mental wellbeing of society. By advocating for the widespread application of this tool we hope to promote a more constructive, empowering approach towards mental health,” Ms Shehzad added.

The objectives of the study are in line with global efforts to achieve targets under goal 3 of the Sustainable Development Goals. Goal 3: ensure healthy lives and promote well-being for all at all ages, which calls for special efforts to promote mental health and wellbeing.

Several AKU faculty members were a part of the research team involved in the project: Omrana Pasha, a senior lecturer at the CHS, Professor Rozina Karmaliani from SONAM and the department of community health sciences (CHS), Dr Nargis Asad, an associate professor in the department of psychiatry and Iqbal Azam, an assistant professor at the CHS.

value.Title: Promoting tolerance through literature
value.NewsSummary: A novel research study explores whether literature can be used to counter prejudice.
value.NewsContent:
​A murmur breaks out in a fifth-grade English class in Karachi as the teacher asks 10-year old Wali* to answer a question. But before he can respond, laughter spreads across the room as a classmate comments that Wali won’t know the answer since people from the north are ‘stupid’. 

In his five years of teaching, Munir Lalani, an Institute for Educational Development (IED) alumnus, has noticed many instances in the classroom where students make generalisations about a social group or describe different beliefs as being ‘weird’.   

“Boys and girls are influenced by the behaviour and attitudes of those around them,” says Mr Lalani. “As teachers, we need to challenge prevailing stereotypes about gender, religion and ethnicity so that students learn how to be respectful and tolerant of diversity.” 

Mr Lalani believes that the best teachers have an inspirational effect on their students that motivates them to do their best. This impact extends beyond academics as teachers are also responsible for imparting valuable character-building lessons, he adds. 

For his master’s thesis at the IED, Mr Lalani decided to design a study to test whether literature could be used to introduce students to different points of view thereby promoting tolerance in the classroom. His study saw him choose two classes at an English-speaking school in Karachi; one which would receive a literature-based teaching intervention while a comparison group would be taught concepts tied to pluralism and the dangers of prejudice without the use of literature. 

Before launching his project, he developed a pre and post intervention test to measure prejudice in the areas of gender, religion and ethnicity. Over a period of two months, he worked with IED faculty to validate this assessment method so that Grade 5 and Grade 6 students could relate to the situations mentioned in the test. Students were then introduced to extracts from two-renowned works of non-fiction: The Diary of a Young Girl by Anne Frank; and Hannah Goslar Remembers: A Childhood Friend of Anne Frank. Both works chronicle the lives of two teenagers who endured immense hardship and much prejudice during the Nazi occupation of Amsterdam in World War II. 

Mr Lalani recalls that the students were particularly moved when they read that Anne Frank was forced to switch schools and even stopped from riding a bicycle due to her religion. They were also struck by a scene in which Hannah Goslar meets her childhood friend, Anne Frank, in the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp in northern Germany. 

Besides learning about the emotional journey of the two young women; students took part in activities that made them reflect on the suffering of those facing discrimination. Through the use of role-play, group discussions and assignments focused on the viewpoints of different characters; the project made students consider how they’d react to instances of unfair treatment. 

“Reading personal stories showed the students how prejudice can lead to acts of great cruelty and injustice. They were able to empathise with what Anne and Hannah went through and this helped them question other instances where people were treated differently on the basis of who they were,” he added.   

While both groups benefited from their respective interventions with post-tests showing a reduction in prejudiced attitudes, the group receiving the literature-based intervention reported a more significant reduction in negative attitudes towards other social groups. Mr Lalani noted that the need to respect others and concerns about equality were recurring themes in the presentations at the end of the literature-based activity. He was especially impressed by two students who went on to buy Anne Frank’s diary and another who researched the life of Hannah Goslar on YouTube.

Since his graduation, Mr Lalani has returned to teaching and is grateful for the guidance and supervision he received from IED faculty for his project. 

“Their feedback from review to defence was really helpful as it helped me explore my project from different perspectives. It was wonderful to pursue my passion for pluralism through this study and I’ll always remember how satisfying it was to see students think about what it means to be a tolerant member of society,” he adds. 

*Identities changed to protect privacy.
value.BannerCaption: Munir Lalani stands beside a poster which summarises the process and findings of his research project. Mr Lalani graduated with a Master of Philosophy in Education degree from the IED in 2017.

value.Title: AKU international family medicine conference 'Challenges for the next decade'
value.NewsSummary: The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified unequal access to prevention and care, rising costs of health care, inefficient health care systems, and weak emphasis on generalist training, as major barriers to equitable health care in developing
value.NewsContent:
The World Health Organization (WHO) has identified unequal access to prevention and care, rising costs of health care, inefficient health care systems, and weak emphasis on generalist training, as major barriers to equitable health care in developing countries.

It also acknowledges the family medicine practitioner as a physician most capable of overcoming those barriers.

These will be key issues for debate at the Family Medicine Conference being organised by Aga Khan University (AKU) at its auditorium on February 21-23, 2003. The theme of this conference will be "Family medicine - challenges for the next decade".

There is world-wide recognition that trained family physicians combine knowledge and skills from various medical specialities with knowledge of their patients' holistic dimension to offer accessible, high-quality and cost-effective care. The Department of Family Medicine at AKU is striving to prepare competent, caring, compassionate family physicians, committed to serving individuals and community through a four-year structured training programme approved by the College of Physicians and Surgeons, Pakistan (CPSP) for FCPS and the Royal College of General Practitioners, UK (RCGP, UK) for MRCGP, UK examinations. To celebrate the successful 10 years of completion of this training programme, the department of Family Medicine has organised this international conference in collaboration with World Organization of Family Doctors (WONCA), RCGP, UK, and the College of Family Medicine, Pakistan.

A large number of foreign and Pakistani physicians are participating in this conference and several foreign and national speakers of high repute are addressing the delegates as well as presenting original papers. On the side meetings delegates from developed and developing countries will exchange ideas on promotion and accreditation of the specialty of family medicine with focus on South Asia, Middle East and East Africa. The president and the chief executive of WONCA and Director, International Development Programme, RCGP are also attending this conference. WONCA is the largest organisation of family physicians in the world with 180,000 members across the world from North America to Fareast.

For these reasons, this conference will be the first of its kind in Pakistan, with a large scale international and national participation of the medical community.

value.Title: ​Caring for children with cleft lips and palate
value.NewsSummary: ​Left lip and palate is the most common birth defect of the head and neck area. It is particularly common in Pakistan given the generally poor level of ante-natal care and the high rate of first cousin marriages," said Dr Tahir Shafi Khan, Assistant
value.NewsContent:
​Left lip and palate is the most common birth defect of the head and neck area. It is particularly common in Pakistan given the generally poor level of ante-natal care and the high rate of first cousin marriages," said Dr Tahir Shafi Khan, Assistant Professor and Consultant Plastic Surgeon at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving the presentation on "Team Approach to care for Children with Cleft lip and Palate" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care’ a monthly health awareness programme held on November 25, 2000.
 
Dr Tahir Shafi elaborated,"The condition can cause a severe physical deformity of the face. Due to the deformity there can be problems in feeding, speech, hearing, taste and smell as well as the normal development of the teeth and central part of the face. Moreover a significant number of these children have other birth defects in addition to cleft lip and palate. The presence of a cleft can be devastating for the child and family."
 
Dr Tahir Shafi said,"Comprehensive care of the child and family is usually necessary from birth to adulthood. A variety of health professionals are involved in providing this care in a coordinated sequence to best match the needs of the child at various stage of development. Recognizing this fact, medical centers all over the world, have organized multi-disciplinary cleft palate teams to provide optimum care to these children and their families."
 
Dr Tahir Shafi stressed,"It is the responsibility of the health care providers and the parents to realize that the treatment does not end with one or more operations but that follow up with the cleft palate team is required right up to adulthood. Teams of foreign doctors, comprising mainly of doctors in training, that fly in, operate 'conveyor belt-style' on these children and fly off again do not necessarily provide a service. These doctors practice on unknowing patients to whom they are not responsible or liable. No proper follow up is arranged for complications or ongoing, treatment. The above scenario could be condoned in the past due to the lack of sufficient plastic surgeons in the country."
 
"However, there are now approximately 50 plastic surgeons in the Pakistan Association of Plastic Surgeons and this body has been in existence for 5 years. There are members of this association in each of the major cities of Pakistan and the majority is attempting to apply the team approach to cleft lip and palate care. Given appropriate support and care children with this condition can be restored to a state of normality or near normality and it behoove all of us to strive for that goal,"stated Dr Tahir Shafi.
 
Another speaker, Dr Mehnaz Atiq, Assistant Professor and Consultant Pediatrician cardiologist at AKUH, explained,"Oral clefts (cleft lip and/or palate) are important congenital malformations that can severely compromise growth of infants. The risk factors associated with the poly-factorial disease have been identified to some extent. Important ones include consanguinity (akin), maternal illness, maternal drug intake and family history of congenital (birth) defects." 
 
She further added,"The infants are usually troubled by difficulty in feeding milk, can aspirate milk, develop recurrent ear and lung infection, all this reflects as poor weight gain. There may be associated defects congenital in origins which probably have the same cause as clefts; these have to be looked for, sometimes through special investigations."
 
"Management issues are not easy and proper management in early infancy leads to a good outcome,"said Dr Mehnaz Atiq. 
 
The panel, which consisted of Dr Mubashir Ikram and the speakers, answered questions for the audience at the end of the program.

value.Title: ​First Pakistani scientist receives prestigious Third World Academy of Sciences award in Basic Medical Sciences
value.NewsSummary: Dr Rabia Hussain, Professor and Acting Chair, Department of Microbiology at the Aga Khan University, recently became the first Pakistani to receive the prestigious Third World Academy of Sciences (TWAS) award in Basic Medical Sciences.
value.NewsContent:
Dr Rabia Hussain, Professor and Acting Chair, Department of Microbiology at the Aga Khan University, recently became the first Pakistani to receive the prestigious Third World Academy of Sciences (TWAS) award in Basic Medical Sciences for the year 2000, for her outstanding research contributions in the area of immunity to infectious diseases.
 
TWAS is an autonomous international organisation, founded in 1983 in Trieste, Italy, under the leadership of the late Pakistani Nobel laureate in Physics, Abdus Salam. Representing the best scientific minds in the developing world, it aims to support and promote scientific capacity and excellence for sustainable development in the third world. The TWAS Awards in Basic Sciences are conferred to scientists from developing countries for excellence in scientific research that contributes significantly to the advancement of the basic sciences.
 
The contributions for which Dr Hussain has been cited by TWAS are"Immunology of Infectious Diseases with special reference to classes and subclasses of antibody recognition in filariasis, tuberculosis and leprosy patients." These studies have led to more than 85 publications in journals of international repute.
 
Commenting on this singular acollade, Dr Rabia Hussain said,"The TWAS award has tremendous significance for me as it recognizes work conducted in fly homeland that nurtured me and provided me with the opportunity to develop the necessary skills. I feel very gratified that I can bring honor in some small way to my country. Although, I have been researching for more than 30 years and have received several international awards and honors, I aIways felt that them was nothing unique or special as the research was carried out in the developed world with unlimited resources."
 
Professor Hussain is also a reciepent of the Tamgha-c-Imtiaz from the Government of Pakistan for her pioneering research in the early diagnosis and pathogenesis of leprosy and tuberculosis. These research studies also serve as a role model fo investigations into similar infectious diseases, for scientists in Pakistan and throughout the developing world.
 
Dr Hussain is also a member of international agencies such as the World Health Organization, and is a Fellow of the Royal College of Pathology, UK. She is an elected Council member on the International Society for Infectious Disease. Her earlier career in the USA was equally distinguished, with a fellowship from the National Research Council. This was followed by a senior position in the Laboratory of Parasitic Diseases at the National Institute of Health, Bethesda, where she was internationally recognized for her work on filariasis and schistosomiasis and received the prestigious Berson-Yallow award for the best paper in the development of a radioimmunoassay by the American Society of Nuclear Medicine.

value.Title: ​Viral hemorrhagic fever in Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: Different varieties of viral hemorrhagic fevers are found throughout the world. The one most prevalent to this region is the Congo Crimean virus. Symptoms include high fever and body aches, followed within a few days by bleeding from the nose, mouth.
value.NewsContent:
Different varieties of viral hemorrhagic fevers are found throughout the world. The one most prevalent to this region is the Congo Crimean virus. Symptoms include high fever and body aches, followed within a few days by bleeding from the nose, mouth, ears, lungs or rectum. The virus has been most prevalent in Balochistan. It call be contracted through infected animals and patients' blood and body fluid secretions. There is currently no proven cure for the disease, and most patients die of bleeding complications.
 
A blood sample of a nursing assistant at the Aga Khan University Hospital was recently sent to the Centre of Disease Control, Atlanta, USA. It confirmed on Friday November 3, 2000, that death had occurred due to the virus. The nursing assistant had been caring for a patient from Balochistan who had also died of the virus before it was diagnosed. The Hospital is taking strict precautionary measures needed to ensure immediate detection and containment of those with suspected symptoms, prevention and dissemination of information in the Hospital.
 
Patients, staff and visitors who come in direct contact with such infected patients are appropriately protected, and are safe and are not at risk of acquiring this disease.
 
All hospitals in Karachi are advised to undertake extreme vigilance by immediately isolating those patients showing symptoms of high fever and bleeding. Strict isolation of the patients, the use of gowns, gloves and masks for all health care workers coming in contact with a patient's blood or body fluids is an essential requirement for controlling the spread of the virus.

value.Title: ​Early recognition and appropriate treatment of surgical problems in children is crucial for a successful outcome
value.NewsSummary: "Many of the surgical conditions of childhood are different from those of the adult and are approached from a different view point. Children are not small adults, the working of their body, the way they respond to illness and their disease pattern.
value.NewsContent:
​"Many of the surgical conditions of childhood are different from those of the adult and are approached from a different view point. Children are not small adults, the working of their body, the way they respond to illness and their disease pattern 'is unique and different from that of adults" said Dr Zafar Nazir, Assistant Professor of Pediatric Surgery and Consultant Pediatric Surgeon at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving the presentation on "Surgery in Children" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' a monthly health awareness programme held on October 28. 2000. 
 
Dr Zalar Nazir explained,"When your child needs medical treatment, you want him or her to be seen by a Pediatrician. A doctor who specializes in diseases of children. So if your child needs an operation, you will want to consult a surgeon who is qualified and experienced in operating on children called 'Pediatric Surgeon".
 
Dr Zafar Nazir said,"Pediatric surgeons utilize their expertise in providing care for most of the surgical problems mainly circumcision. Hernia repair, acute appendicitis, obstruction in the intestine, etc. In addition, the) have particular expertise in Neonatal (newborn) surgery prenatal (before birth) diagnosis and counseling, trauma, cancer in children, surgery of kidney and bladder".
 
Dr Zafar azir stressed, “Pediatric surgeons specialize in the surgical care of children. They are surgeons who by training are oriented towards working with children and understanding their special medical and social needs. In addition they work with various specialists to provide best care to their patients. They are able to save whole life times. And have the opportunity to follow their patients through a productive young life into adulthood".
 
 Another speaker Dr M. Arif Mateen Khan, Assistant Professor of Pediatric Surgery and Consultant Pediatric Surgeon at AK U H, elaborated by saying,"the new born period is a time of rapid maturation, adaptation and dependency, which presents a special challenge to the surgeon caring for the new born infants".
 
Dr Arif Mateen emphasized on early recognition and management of common surgical conditions affecting the infant and newborns, through a form of 'continuing surgical education directed at the community, Intestinal obstruction is the most common abdominal emergency in neonates and occurs in about 1/2000 live births.
 
He further outlined the principles of successful management of neonates with suspected obstruction by recognizing the condition early, institute appropriate investigation, assure complete preoperative resuscitation and perform surgical procedure for the underlying condition.
 
The panelists, who included Dr Shabbir Hussain and Dr Muhammad Arshad answered questions for the audience at the end of the program.

value.Title: ​Population growth rate on the decline
value.NewsSummary: A Conference on Pakistan's Population Issues in the 21st Century took place this week in Karachi. It was sponsored jointly by the Population Council and Aga Khan University (AKU).
value.NewsContent:
A Conference on Pakistan's Population Issues in the 21st Century took place this week in Karachi. It was sponsored jointly by the Population Council and Aga Khan University (AKU). The three-day meeting covered a wide range of population issues, such as the 1998 Census, Population and Development, Migration and Urbanization, Reproductive Health, Maternal and Infant Mortality, Fertility and Family Planning and Gender Issues. About 200 participants from all over Pakistan and experts from abroad attended the conference; it was also the occasion of the launching of the Population Association of Pakistan. Dr M.S. Jillani was elected unopposed as the President of the Association. 
 
The chief guest, Dr Shahid Amjad Chaudhry, Deputy Chairman, Planning Commission, said in his inaugural address that"the recent decline in the population growth rate from 3.1 to 2.2 would make the task of creating employment and sending children to school much less difficult." He then focused on the government's policies for the social sectors and showed concern for the increasing poverty in the country. 
 
Dr Carner W. Vellani, Rector, AKU, welcomed the participants, and highlighted that the University recognizes population growth as a key issue and has recently established the Reproductive Health Programme as one of its priority research areas.
  
In his keynote address, Dr Gavin Jones, Convenor, Graduate Programme in Demography, Australian National University, analyzed population growth trends in Pakistan as compared to other Islamic countries. Although Pakistan is finally experiencing a fertility transition, Professor Jones outlined constraints on the speed of this fertility change such as lack of female autonomy and low educational levels. He strongly argued against any religious factor constraining fertility change in Muslim countries generally.
  
Dr Mehtab Karim, Reproductive Health Programme, AKU, summarized the need and purpose of the Conference. Dr Nizamuddin, Director, Asia and Pacific Division, UNFPA, congratulated the organizers for the extensive programme of the Conference, saying that"Now is the time to act, and this Conference provides a very good beginning."
 
The first day's proceedings included a Panel discussion on the results of the 1998 Census, including an interactive session with the audience regarding the reliability and quality of the Census findings. The second day focused on abortions as a Public Health issue in Pakistan. Research findings clearly showed that women with large families are resorting to abortions to avoid unwanted pregnancies, rather t tan using family planning to prevent such births. In his paper on Population and Development, Dr John Wall, Resident Representative of the World Bank, discussed trends and outcomes in the social sector. He said that the"vicious cycle of poverty, poor health and low education" must be turned into a "various cycle" through public sector programmes.
 
On the last day of the conference, in a panel discussion on"Aging as an Emerging Concern", it was emphasised that while aging was not an immediate concern in Pakistan, it would become one in twenty years and it was therefore important to prepare for this eventuality. Dr Franklin White, chairman of Department of Community Health Sciences, AKU, in his concluding remarks highlighting the necessity and immediacy of tackling important population and environmental issues in Pakistan. A consensus was reached that such a conference should be held annually to highlight population related issues in Pakistan.

value.Title: ​International experts to attend AKU symposium on cardiovascular diseases
value.NewsSummary: Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. They are currently responsible for 12 million deaths globally, with over 7 million occurring in developing countries.
value.NewsContent:
Cardiovascular diseases are a leading cause of death and disability worldwide. They are currently responsible for 12 million deaths globally, with over 7 million occurring in developing countries. In Pakistan, the incidence of heart disease is also very steeply on the rise. Research can play a pivotal role in developing effective preventive strategies to combat this alarming trend. For this reason, the Aga Khan University (AKU) has selected cardio-respiratory diseases as the theme for its annual research symposium this year. The Symposium on Cardiovascular and Pulmonary Diseases will be held at AKU on September 25-26, 2000. World-renowned experts in the field of cardio-respiratory medicine from Canada, Sweden and the UK will be participating in the Symposium, which will be followed by a weeklong workshop on Molecular Biology. 
 
Increasing public awareness can be one of the most effective steps in disease control and prevention. As part of it societal commitment, the Aga Khan University in collaboration with Pakistan Cardiac Society, will also be celebrating he first World Heart Day by organising a two-hour public health awareness programme on"Prevention of Heart Diseases," on Sunday, 24th September 2000, at 9:30 a.m. Eminent physicians and cardiologists from all over the country will be participating in this event, which will include presentations on the risk factors of cardiovascular diseases and an open question and answer session.

value.Title: World's first mountain university founded along the Silk Route
value.NewsSummary: Astana, Kazakhstan, 31st August, 2000-President Nursultan Nazarbayev and His Highness the Aga Khan, spiritual leader of the Ismaili Muslims, today concluded the signature of the treaty founding the University of Central Asia.
value.NewsContent:
President Nursultan Nazarbayev and His Highness the Aga Khan, spiritual leader of the Ismaili Muslims, today concluded the signature of the treaty founding the University of Central Asia, the world's first university dedicated exclusively to education and research on mountain regions and societies. Announcing a total endowment of US$15million for the University at its inception, the Aga Khan stated that US$5million of this sum would be allocated for the University's programmes in Kazakhstan. 
 
The signing in Astana follows similar ceremonies in Dushanbe and Bishkek earlier this week at which the Aga Khan signed the Treaty with President Emomali Rahmonov of Tajikistan and President Askar Akaev of the Kyrgyz Republic respectively.
 
Twenty five million people, many of who seek their livelihoods along the Silk Route, on the earth's highest mountain ranges stretching from Western China to the Southern Caucasus, will benefit from the new university.
 
To be situated in countries where the Altai, Tien-Shan, Pamir, Karakorum, and Hindu Kush mountain ranges converge, the University is intended to serve people in the mountainous parts of Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, China, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Iran, and countries in South Asia.
 
The establishment of the university was recommended by an international commission of mountain experts, academicians and regional specialists appointed in 1995 shortly after President Rahmonov and the Aga Khan signed an Agreement to facilitate the work of the Aga Khan Development Network (AKDN) in the region.
 
"Mountain populations experience extremes of poverty and isolation as well as constraints on opportunities and choice,"said the Aga Khan in announcing the launch," but at the same time, they sustain great linguistic, cultural, ethnic and religious pluralism, and show remarkable resilience in the face of extraordinarily harsh circumstances." "By creating intellectual space and resources, "he continued, " this University will help turn the mountains that divide the nations and territories of Central Asia into the links thatunite its peoples and economies in a shared endeavour to improve their future well-being." The regional university will be distinctive in a number of ways. Its charter, academic standards, curricula, faculty and students, academic partnerships and linkages will be international. It will emphasise distance learning, the use of information and computer technologies and create satellite facilities and programmes across the region. Students, faculty and staff will be recruited on merit.
 
The first programmes will be in Continuing Education to upgrade professional skills in the catchment area. English will be the primary medium of instruction in the post-graduate and graduate programmes. The University will not include a faculty of theology. The post-graduate programme will foster research on issues critical to sustainable development (e.g. geology of mountains and mining, hydrology, seismology, mountain ecology, natural resource management, high-altitude agriculture and development economics). An interdisciplinary residential undergraduate programme will cover a wide range of subjects (e.g. forestry, environmental engineering, disaster management, agronomy, civil engineering, mining, energy, computer sciences, economics, business, accounting, sociology, regional languages, anthropology, history, philosophy and ethics).
 
The University will draw on the expertise and experience of the AKDN which has a hundred year-old tradition in operating educational facilities. The Aga Khan University, already created under an international charter in Pakistan in 1984, and its academic programmes in East Africa and Europe, will contribute in a number of ways to the new University. Over the past quarter-century, the AKDN has initiated educational programmes and institutions in the developing and developed worlds in collaboration with Harvard University, the Karolinska Institute.

value.Title: ​Early drug intervention can be helpful in reverting paralysis due to stroke
value.NewsSummary: Stroke is a commonly encountered neurological disorder leading to disability and mortality," revealed by Dr Shahid Masud Baig, Associate Professor of Medicine, Consultant Neurologist and Acting Head of Neurology at the Aga Khan University Hospital.
value.NewsContent:
Stroke is a commonly encountered neurological disorder leading to disability and mortality," revealed by Dr Shahid Masud Baig, Associate Professor of Medicine, Consultant Neurologist and Acting Head of Neurology at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving a presentation on "Stroke" at Signs. Symptoms and Care' monthly health awareness programme held on August 26, 2000.
 
Dr Shahid baig disclosed that"Stoke is a brain disorder that occurs when blood supply to any part of brain is compromised and as a result loss of brain function occurs. Stroke is the third leading cause of death in develop countries In US for example. a stroke affects 4 out of 1,000 people."
 
Dr Shahid baig further added."The incidence of stroke rises dramatically with advancing age and the risk of stroke almost double with each decade after age of 35 years, In Pakistan, the frequency of stroke is about the same, though definite data is not available. Therefore, it is important to know what causes stroke how can we prevent it."
 
A stroke may be caused by reduced blood flow that results in deficient blood supply and death of tissues ill the brain. Causes of ischemic stroke are blood clots that form in the brain, or pieces of other atherosclerotic plaque from vessel or via the clot that travel to the brain from other locations. Brain Hemorrhage can also cause symptoms similar to ischemic stroke, explained Dr Shahid Baig.
 
Dr Shahid Baig emphasized the importance and prevention of risk factors for stroke and said,"optimal control of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, cigarette smoking, diabetes, and heart diseases could significant reduce the onset of stroke."
 
"Early admission and treatment in the hospital may prevent from progression or reversal of paralysis due to stroke Dr Shahid Baig."He further elaborated on commonly encountered signs and symptoms due tu stroke. Dr Shahid Baig concluded by explaining the pivotal role of rehabilitation of patients with stroke and the efficacy of new medications in the prevention of stroke. Some new drugs could even revert the paralysis due to stroke provided the patient is given medicine within three hours of onset of symptoms.
 
At the end of the program the panelists. which included Dr Nadir Ali Syed, Dr Mohammad Wasay and Dr Saad Shafqat explanation to the queries of the audience.

value.Title: ​AKU Conference on Postgraduate Medical Education
value.NewsSummary: ​The Department of Postgraduate Medical Education (PGME) of the Aga Khan University (AKU), organized a conference on "Healthcare: Keeping Pace with New Challenges." The conference covered several areas of importance to both young physicians and those
value.NewsContent:
The Department of Postgraduate Medical Education (PGME) of the Aga Khan University (AKU), organized a conference on "Healthcare: Keeping Pace with New Challenges." The conference covered several areas of importance to both young physicians and those involved in their training. It included a series of lectures by national and international speakers and workshops for residents in patient consultation skills and data analysis.
 
Professor Roger A. L. Sutton, Dean, Faculty of Health Sciences, AKU, welcomed the guests and highlighted the necessity for developing strong postgraduate programs to impact the health needs of Pakistan. AKU has graduated 241 clinical generalists and specialists from its 24 postgraduate programs since 1991, many of whom are now working at AKU and as faculty and staff at other teaching institutions in the country.
 
Professor Farhat Moazam, Associate Dean of PGME at AKU, noted in her presentation that educators must recognize the imbalance that exists between the service and educational components of most training programs in the country. She said that"postgraduate programs, by labeling their residents as 'trainees' tend to primarily focus on acquisition of technical skills. As a result, the equally important attributes that must be inculcated in physicians, such as ethical behavior, a compassionate approach, professionalism and communication skills, are often ignored." Recognizing this deficiency, AKU has introduced a mandatory core curriculum for residents, which addresses these aspects of resident education.
 
The first session of the conference dealt with the experiences of other specialized centers of excellence in Pakistan, involved in providing care to the ill in specific areas. This included a presentation by Professor Adibul Hasan Rizvi, Director, Sindh Institute of Urology and Transplantation (SlUT), about the struggles and achievements of SlUT. Dr Yusuf Kamal Mirza, CEO of the Shaukat Khanum Memorial Cancer Hospital, also gave an outline of the inception and mission of that institution. Dr Ashfaq Ali Khan, Director Training, Marie Adelaide Leprosy Center, spoke about the successful fight against leprosy in Pakistan, and AKU's role in helping them achieve this goal.
 
The plenary session devoted to postgraduate medical education began with an overview of the problems and challenges of postgraduate training in Pakistan, presented by Professor Naeem A. Jafarey, Vice Chancellor of Ziauddin Medical University. He was followed by Professor Rosslynne Freeman from the University of London, who elaborated on the changing culture of postgraduate medical education and how it must serve as a force for change. The trend is for educators to move from an authoritarian mode of teaching to one that is facilitatory and interactive. Professor Renee Fox from the University of Pennsylvania spoke on bioethics as a component of medical education, and the difficulties inherent in applying a western, secular model of ethics in societies where codes of ethic are family centered and based on religious values.
 
Dr Qasim Mehdi, Director General, Biomedical and Genetic Engineering Division, Dr A. Q. Khan Research Laboratory, focused on the discovery in his laboratory of novel genes in inherited eye diseases, and the international reputation that young Pakistani researchers have acquired in this field. He believed that with the will, right support and resources, researchers in this country could be second to none in the world. Professor Sarwar Zuberi, Scientist Emeritus, Pakistan Medical Research Council (PMRC) and Dean for Research at Ziauddin Medical University, then enumerated the hurdles that the PMRC continues to face in promoting medical research.

value.Title: ​Osteoporosis - The Silent Bone Killer
value.NewsSummary: ​"Osteoporosis is thinning and weakening of bones and affects all of us as we age involving both men and women," revealed Dr Mirza Rehman Beg, Associate Professor and Consultant Orthopedic Surgeon at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH).
value.NewsContent:
​"Osteoporosis is thinning and weakening of bones and affects all of us as we age involving both men and women," revealed Dr Mirza Rehman Beg, Associate Professor and Consultant Orthopedic Surgeon at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH). He was giving a presentation on "Osteoporosis - The Silent Bone Killer" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care' monthly health awareness programme held on May 13, 2000.
 
Dr Beg informed that it is a universal problem,"In 1990, 1.6 million fractures occurred in United Stated and Europe requiring surgery. Figures in Pakistan should be comparable or perhaps more because of lack of awareness in our population and poor nutritional status especially in our urban population. Although this condition is preventable and treatable yet it goes unrecognized and untreated due to lack of awareness in the public and in many general physicians."
 
Dr Beg further added that,"as we grow older our bones lose their density and become weaker but certain factors can accelerate this process to the extent that some bones like hip and wrist fracture require operation. Simple movements such as coughing, sneezing, weight lifting, etc. can lead to vertebral (backbone) fracture. The accelerating factors for osteoporosis are mainly dietary deficiency of calcium, vitamin and minerals. 

Menopause in women, which drops the estrogen hormone level, these women require hormone replacement therapy in-addition to calcium, vitamin and minerals. Lack of exercises especially in urban population will accelerate osteoporosis. Smoking and alcohol usage also accelerates osteoporosis."
 
Dr Beg concluded by saying that,"Osteoporosis is preventable by diet and exercise, HRT in women who have had menopause and early' recognition and treatment."

value.Title: ​First ever Vena Caval Filter placement in Pakistan at AKUH
value.NewsSummary: The Interventional Radiologist at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) took the lead by placing the first ever Vena Caval Filter, which is a highly specialized procedure for the first time in Pakistan.
value.NewsContent:
The Interventional Radiologist at the Aga Khan University Hospital (AKUH) took the lead by placing the first ever Vena Caval Filter, which is a highly specialized procedure for the first time in Pakistan. AKUH is one of the leading hospitals providing opportunities for higher training, developing skills and creating environment for such sophisticated procedures.

Patients who have surgeries or long term bed confinement are prone to develop clotting in their leg veins. These clots can move into circulation and get impacted in the lung's major vessels. If a clot is large, it can cause sudden death. These clots when lodged into the lung vessels are removed by a major surgery.
 
A more sophisticated procedure for prevention of clots from reaching the lungs is to place a filter into a major vein, which connects the leg veins to the lungs and prevents any life- threatening pulmonary embolism. The procedure was done in the Radiology Department by a interventional radiologist under local anesthesia. The procedure takes 15 minutes to 1 hour without any risk to the patient.

value.Title: Capacity building for qualitative research in Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: ​The Social Policy Development Centre (SPDC) in collaboration with The Aga Khan University's Institute [or Educational Development (AKU-IED) is organizing an 'intensive workshop on participatory research methods.
value.NewsContent:
​The Social Policy Development Centre (SPDC) in collaboration with The Aga Khan University's Institute [or Educational Development (AKU-IED) is organizing an 'intensive workshop on participatory research methods titled "Qualitative Research: Life Beyond Numbers.” Dr Hafiz Pasha, the Managing Director, SPDC, made the opening remarks following a welcome address by Dr Robert Baker, Director, AKU-lED. The workshop is being conducted at AKU-IED in Karimabad, Karachi, by Colin Stewart, a consultant on social policy from Ottawa, Canada. The workshop started on December 9, 1999, and will continue till May next year. 
 
Dr Hafiz Pasha said that qualitative research in Pakistan was still underdeveloped because working with people and getting to communities was not emphasised. He urged the participants familiar with quantitative techniques to create a balance by integrating qualitative research methodologies in their work.
 
Dr Baker complemented SPDC on the quality and contribution of their work in Pakistan and South Asia as a whole. He hoped that participants would benefit from the interaction in the workshop and from the others at AKU-IED.
 
Colin Stewart, the workshop facilitator, is interested in blending both approaches for research. He said that innovations in qualitative research, of which participatory research is a part, are not coming from the West or North but from developing country experiences in Africa, Asia and generally from the South.
 
The first part of the workshop is being held from December 9 to 24, 1999. This will be followed by fieldwork and a final integration workshop during April-May 2000 to compile detailed research reports. Participants are from SPDC, AKU-IED and its collaborating institutions.
 
Established in 1993 as the University's first programme in addition to those in the health sciences, AKU-IED has gained recognition as a centre of educational excellence dedicated to the professional development of teachers and overall school improvement in Pakistan and other developing countries. AKU-IED is also committed to leading reform in education through innovation, practice, policy development and outreach.

value.Title: ​Hepatits A to E and liver cancer
value.NewsSummary: "Diagnosis of acute viral Hepatitis is established by blood tests and are presented in two modes, i.e. Jaundice and Non-Jaundice. Out of five serologically distinguishable types - Hepatitis B,C and 0 may culminates in chronic types",informed Dr Wasim
value.NewsContent:
"Diagnosis of acute viral Hepatitis is established by blood tests and are presented in two modes, i.e. Jaundice and Non-Jaundice. Out of five serologically distinguishable types - Hepatitis B, C and 0 may culminates in chronic types", informed Dr Wasim Jafri, Consultant Gastroentrologist and Associate Professor of Medicine, The Aga Khan University Hospital, Karachi. He was giving a presentation on "Hepatitis A to E and Liver Cancer" at 'Signs, Symptoms and Care', monthly health awareness program, held on December 18, 1999. 
 
Dr Jafri added,"In the past 20 to 30 years, Hepatitis C produce chronically in more than 70 percent- 90 percent of the cases and chronic liver disease (Cirrhosis) develops in 20 percent-30 percent of patients. Bad hygiene, infected water and food transmit types A and E whereas types B, C, and 0 are mainly through blood, blood products and sexual contacts. The source of infection is unknown in one third of Hepatitis B and one half of Hepatitis C." 
 
Dr Jafri concluded by saying that Hepatitis Band C could result in chronic Liver disease and Liver Cancer. Active and passive prophylaxis is available for Hepatitis A and B only."

value.Title: Dr Nafis Sadik to address Reproductive Health- Seminar at AKU
value.NewsSummary: Pakistan has one of the highest fertility rates in Asia which has led to a spiralling population growth rate. To address this, the Government of Pakistan has adopted a reproductive health package emanating from the recommendations of the Internationa
value.NewsContent:
​Pakistan has one of the highest fertility rates in Asia which has led to a spiralling population growth rate. To address this, the Government of Pakistan has adopted a reproductive health package emanating from the recommendations of the International Conference on Population & Development held in Cairo in 1994.
 
The highlights of Pakistan's Reproductive Health Package will be presented at a seminar on"Pakistan's Reproductive Health Agenda" on December 21, 1999 at the Aga Khan University (AKU). Dr Nafis Sadik, Executive Director, UNFPA, will be chief guest and keynote speaker at the seminar, which will include national experts and will be open to participant comments and discussion. Attendance at the seminar is free of cost and is open to all academics and professionals working in the fields of population and health. Further information can be obtained from AKU's Community Health Sciences Department.

value.Title: ​Thirty six thousand patients annually treated at AKUH's emergency
value.NewsSummary: The Aga Khan University Hospital's Section of Emergency Medicine handles 36,000 patients annually out of which 20 percent are paediatric patients and 15 percent come with cardiac problems. Section of Emergency Medicine provides care.
value.NewsContent:
The Aga Khan University Hospital's Section of Emergency Medicine handles 36,000 patients annually out of which 20 percent are paediatric patients and 15 percent come with cardiac problems. Section of Emergency Medicine provides care to all types of Surgical, Medical, Obstetrical/ Gynecological, Paediatric, Psychiatric and Orthopaedic emergencies. About 60 percent of the totals are medical emergencies, similar to other emergency departments around the world. 
 
The Head of the Section, Dr Rifat Rehmani, the only physician in Pakistan who has a Fellowship in Accident and Emergency from Royal College of Surgeons of Edinburgh, said that cardiac emergencies are the most common Dr Rehmani explained that the five warning signs of heart attack are prolonged pressure or squeezing pain in the center of chest or abdomen; pain spreading to or from the shoulder, neck or jaw; sweating; nausea and vomiting, and shortness of breath."Ignoring the symptoms is like playing with dynamite", added Dr Rehmani. He advised that if someone is experiencing any of these warning signs, then they should not wait but must immediately seek medical help as the first few hours after a heart attack are critical and with timely treatment many lives could be saved. 
 
AKUH's Section of Emergency Medicine provides evaluation and treatment to patients 24- hours a day as well as 7 days a week. In addition, it provides"Triage", prioritization of patients according to medical acuity. Once a patient reaches the Emergency, he/she is greeted by a "Triage" nurse. The patients are not treated on first come first serve basis, but on their medical conditions. The Hospital has started a service for patients with minor illnesses or injuries - these patients receive prompt, efficient and high quality treatment through a "Fast Track", where they are seen and discharged within 60 minutes. This service is staffed by emergency physicians, residency-trained paediatric doctors, who have more than 10 years of experience, and specially trained and experienced nurses in Emergency Medicine are available at all times.​

value.Title: ​AKU hosts international workshop on malnutrition in South Asia malnutrition results in Eeonomic loss worldwide - US$ 8.7 billion due to reducesed labour productivity
value.NewsSummary: The Aga Khan University (AKU) will hold a two-day workshop on "Maternal and Foetal Malnutrition and Human Development in South Asia" on October 28 and 29, 1999. This will be followed by a seminar on ''Women and Nutrition in South Asia"
value.NewsContent:
​The Aga Khan University (AKU) will hold a two-day workshop on "Maternal and Foetal Malnutrition and Human Development in South Asia" on October 28 and 29, 1999. This will be followed by a seminar on ''Women and Nutrition in South Asia: Issues and Strategies for Change" on October 30. Numerous issues such as maternal nutrition, low birth weight and reproductive health will be discussed by eminent speakers and experts from Pakistan and abroad. Malnutrition during childhood and adult life reduces school performance, labour productivity and general economic growth with long term effects of reduced intellectual capacity and the risk of chronic diseases. Economic losses worldwide from reduced labour productivity alone are US$ 8.7 billion. Clearly, it is an issue that deserves urgent attention in the South Asian context. 
 
Over 500 million people world-wide, do not get enough food to lead healthy and productive lives. The majorities of these are poor and live in South Asia and Africa. In addition, each year about 24 million children are born underweight, largely due to malnutrition in women during pregnancy and in early life. About 5 million infants are unable to cope with this malnutrition and low birth weight and die before they reach their fifth birthday. Furthermore, half of the 170 million malnourished preschool children are found in just three countries, Bangladesh, India and Pakistan.
 
A crucial determinant of a newborn's survival and healthy start in life is the mother's health and nutritional status. In Pakistan, 20-40 percent of women are underweight and 40-50 percent suffer from anaemia. As a result, 25-30 percent of Pakistani infants are born with low birth weights (less than 2.5 kilograms). These statistics have remained static for several decades. Not only are these women and children more prone to infections and early death, but also grow up as malnourished children, adolescents and adults, who are unable to realize their full physical and intellectual potential.
 
South Asia has the worst malnutrition levels in the world, contributing to a vicious cycle of poor growth from generation to generation. Malnourished mothers are more likely to have low birth weight babies who if female, will be predisposed to produce weak infants. This cycle is very evident in patriarchal South Asian societies, where cultural biases towards boys often means that the girl child is less well cared for, being fed last and getting the least to eat. The mortality rate for girls and women is therefore much higher than for men in South Asia. For every 100 men there are only 94 women who survive. According to these figures, 74 million women who should be alive in South Asia today are missing.
 
The international workshop and seminar hosted by AKU will seek to develop a framework for maternal and child care and nutritional interventions to bring about change in the short and long term in South Asia.

value.Title: ​AKU graduates over eighty fellows, residents and interns
value.NewsSummary: The annual graduation ceremony for Fellows, Residents and Interns of The Aga Khan University's (AKU) Postgraduate Medical Education Programme will be held on Saturday, October 23, 1999. The President, College of Physicians and Surgeons, Pakistan.
value.NewsContent:
​The annual graduation ceremony for Fellows, Residents and Interns of The Aga Khan University's (AKU) Postgraduate Medical Education Programme will be held on Saturday, October 23, 1999. The President, College of Physicians and Surgeons, Pakistan, Professor M. Sultan Farooqui, will be the chief guest. 
 
This year, 44 interns will be receiving certificates and 43 residents will be awarded certificates for sub-specialty training in several clinical disciplines. These include Adult Cardiology, Anesthesia, Community Medicine, Diagnostic Radiology, Family Medicine, General Surgery, Internal Medicine, Neurology, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Orthopedic Surgery, Pathology and Pediatrics.
 
AKU offers clinical training after M.B.B.S. in 22 specialties, which are recognized by the College of Physicians and Surgeons, Pakistan. In addition, programmes in General Surgery, Obstetrics and Gynecology, Orthopedics, Internal Medicine, Pediatrics and Family Medicine are also recognized by the concerned Royal Colleges in the UK.
 
Since 1990, 418 interns and 201 residents have graduated from AKU's postgraduate programmes. Approximately 70 percent of these physicians and specialists trained at AKU are currently working in Pakistan. Fifty-seven graduates are now on the full time faculty of the University and others are teaching in highly recognized medical institutions throughout the country.

value.Title: ​Tuberculosis and hepatitis are leading killer diseases in Pakistan
value.NewsSummary: At the annual National Symposium hosted by The Aga Khan University (AKU) on September 20-22, medical scientists and experts highlighted Tuberculosis and Hepatitis as the two major life threatening diseases prevalent in Pakistan.
value.NewsContent:
At the annual National Symposium hosted by The Aga Khan University (AKU) on September 20-22, medical scientists and experts highlighted Tuberculosis and Hepatitis as the two major life threatening diseases prevalent in Pakistan. 
 
Internationally renowned experts in Infectious Diseases contributed to this conference. Guest speakers at the inaugural session of this two-day symposium included Dr Douglas Young, Professor and Chair of Microbiology at the Imperial College School of Medicine, London, UK, and Dr Andrew Lever, Professor of Virology and Infectious Diseases, Cambridge University, UK. Dr Young is a world renowned expert in molecular biology and genomics of mycobacteria (organisms that cause TB and leprosy). He was a WHO consultant for these diseases for almost a decade. He described the genomic structure of the TB bacillus and its possible application to epidemiology and diagnosis while Dr Andrew Lever presented exciting developments pertaining to gene therapy and discussed the potential of this type of treatment in persistent viral infections especially in the context of HIV and AIDS.
 
The Plenary session was followed by a review by Dr Indira Nath, INSA Professor at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences in New Delhi She is a world-recognized scientist in the field of lmmunology of leprosy. She delivered a talk on cytokine responses and their significance in protection in mycobacterial diseases. Several original research papers were also presented by Dr Rabia Hussain's group at The Aga Khan University on Immunology of tuberculosis and leprosy. Dr Bushra Jamil and Dr Javed Khan discussed the problems of multidrug treatment and compliance of doctors in following recommended treatment for TB. This was followed by a session on epidemiology of infectious diseases chaired by Dr Franklin White, Professor and Chair of Community Health Sciences (CHS) Department of AKU. The other AKU invited speakers in this session were Dr Zeba Rasmussen of CHS from Gilgit and Dr Saeed Hamid of the Department of Medicine
 
The second day of the annual National Symposium proceedings covered major infectious killers such as meningitis, diarrhoea and malaria. In the scientific sessions on Bacteriology, Dr Raymond Smego of the University of Witwatersrand, South Africa, spoke on"The role of Antimicrobials in Fever" while Dr Zulfiqar Ahmed Bhutta, AKU, discussed the current trends in the "Epidemiology of Typhoid". At the scientific sessions on Viral and Parasitic Infections, Dr Andrew Lever of the University of Cambridge and Dr Viqar Zaman of AKU's Department of Microbiology gave interesting and informative presentations respectively on "Viral Latency" and "Plasmodium Morphology including Ultrastructure”. 
 
Concurrently there was a hands on Workshop on the Molecular Biology of lnfectious Diseases at which distinguished scientists from Saudi Arabia, Iran, India, UK and USA interacted with researchers from Pakistan. The Aga Khan University's National Symposium was well attended with over 200 participants of national and international standing. Additionally, over 70 abstracts were received from all over the country.​

value.Title: ​AKU to host infectious diseases symposium
value.NewsSummary: The Aga Khan University (AKU) will hold a two-day Symposium on Infectious Diseases on September 20 and September 21, 1999, which will be followed by a Molecular Biology Workshop on infectious disease from September 22-26.
value.NewsContent:
​The Aga Khan University (AKU) will hold a two-day Symposium on Infectious Diseases on September 20 and September 21, 1999, which will be followed by a Molecular Biology Workshop on infectious disease from September 22-26. The major focus of the symposium will be infectious diseases of national relevance, such as tuberculosis, hepatitis, malaria and typhoid. In 1990, the worldwide estimates of deaths over the age of five resulting from these diseases were: 1.9 million for tuberculosis, 0.3 million for malaria and 2 million for other tropical diseases. Pakistan is among the top ten countries for deaths from these diseases. Tuberculosis was among the two major causes of deaths in women in 1990. These figures have risen dramatically in the last decade. 
 
The prevention and treatment of infectious diseases, therefore represent one of the greatest challenges of national health care in Pakistan. This forum is being organized to bring together international and national experts and researchers in key areas of infectious disease of national relevance. The main objective of the symposium is to stimulate further research in order to reduce mortality and morbidity from these diseases.
 
Scholars of international repute have been invited to give the keynote plenary talks. Dr Douglas Young of the Department of Microbiology, Imperial College School of Medicine, University of London, will speak on"Mycobacterial genomics and its applications to diagnosis and epidemiology," while Dr Andrew Lever of Cambridge University will discuss the "Gene therapy of persistent viral infections." Other speakers will discuss epidemiology, molecular biology, pathogenesis and management of infectious diseases. 
 
There will be oral and poster presentations in sessions devoted to mycobacterial, bacterial, viral and parasitic diseases. A general session will cover aspects of medicine and health other than infectious disease. In addition to AKU faculty, participants will include faculty and researchers from national medical colleges and universities, representatives of the College of Physicians and Surgeons of Pakistan, general practitioners, and all those health professionals who have an interest in infectious disease and health related issues.

value.Title: ​AKU organizes seminar on asthma
value.NewsSummary: "A seminar titled ""Update on Asthma"" was organized by the Aga Khan University (AKU) on December 6, to support ""World Asthma Day"" on December 11, 1998. The seminar was attended by physicians, medical students and other healthcare professionals fro
value.NewsContent:
"A seminar titled ""Update on Asthma"" was organized by the Aga Khan University (AKU) on December 6, to support ""World Asthma Day"" on December 11, 1998. The seminar was attended by physicians, medical students and other healthcare professionals from across the country.

Asthma is a serious global health problem with current estimates suggesting that over 150 million people in the world suffer from the disease. The number of children and adults with asthma has risen steadily during the 20th century and has almost doubled in the past 20 years. In Pakistan, almost 10 percent of children are effected by asthma. Lack of awareness concerning the causes and management of the disease and inadequate attention given to this life- threatening condition make it one of today's most crucial health problems.
 
AKU faculty participated in the seminar to discuss and promote awareness about various asthma-related issues. Presentations laid special emphasis on the diagnostic and management problems faced by community physicians from both ambulatory care and hospital practice perspectives.

Dr Yousuf Kamal Mirza, Medical Director and Associate Dean of Clinical Affairs, in his welcome address emphasized the need for further research and training in asthma management. Providing a global perspective, Dr Javaid AKhan, Associate Professor of Medicine, outlined some of the steps that can be taken to control the rising incidence of asthma worldwide. Misconceptions relating to asthma in Pakistan were highlighted by Dr Majeed Mernon, Consultant Chest physician, who particularly discouraged the mythological association of the condition with various foods Dr Hasan Arshad, a Visiting Consultant Physician from Southampton General Hospital, UK, underscored the role of allergen avoidance in preventing asthma.

Professor of Paediatrics, Dr Ghaffar Billoo articulated the need to educate parents and relatives of asthmatic children in how to cope with the condition as this was one of the most important and often neglected aspects of its treatment.

He also pointed to the fact that asthma remains under-diagnosed and under-treated mainly because of social stigmas and the subsequent need to dispel the fears and myths associated with the disease. While reviewing both the immediate and long-term management of childhood asthma, Dr Naseeruddin Mehmood urged the use of inhalation therapy for children. Other AKU faculty including Dr Fayyaz Hussain, Dr Zulfiqar A Bhutta, Dr Raana Haqqee and Dr Riaz Qureshi also made presentations on various asthma-related topics. The participants also had the opportunity to ask questions and actively interact with the experts in two panel discussions."​

value.Title: ​Inauguration of new maternal childhealth centre in Nara Desert
value.NewsSummary: Dr Hadi Bux Jatoi, Director General Health of Sindh, inaugurated the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Centre, established by Aga Khan University (AKU) in conjunction with the local community, in Nara Taluka of district Khairpur.
value.NewsContent:
Dr Hadi Bux Jatoi, Director General Health of Sindh, inaugurated the Maternal and Child Health (MCH) Centre, established by Aga Khan University (AKU) in conjunction with the local community, in Nara Taluka of district Khairpur. The Centre aims to benefit the community of this remote and underdeveloped area and was funded by a multinational, Lasmo Oil Pakistan Limited, which is operating in the same area. The MCH Centre establisment is one of the initiatives of the Lasmo funded Rural Community Development Project run by AKU's Department of Community Health Sciences. The project seeks to establish a primary health care network with the Centre as its focal point of village based activities 
 
On what is considered a"diamond" approach, the local community, the Red Crescent Society, Khairpur, and AKU will collectively manage tile Centre. To ensure sustainability, AKU's technical input and Lasmo funding will gradually decrease over a five-year period, as the local community with the help of Red Crescent Society, develops its own capacity to manage the project. A Memorandum of Agreement was signed between all the concerned parties, and was presided over by Dr Roger Sutton, Dean of Faculty of Health Sciences, and AKU. The MCH Centre also has the collaboration of Department of Health, Sindh, which is making it a reporting centre for its female staff and health workers. At a time when there is increasing demand for innovation with Private-NGO-Public Partnership, tile MCH centre can be regarded as a pioneer effort. 
 
The inauguration ceremony of MCH Centre took place in a colorful manner in Nara amidst overwhelming participation from the local community and was well attended by the Commissioner, Sukkur, he Deputy Commissioner, Khairpur and active members of Red Crescent, local doctors and AKU faculty members.

value.Title: ​Cricket match inaugurates first phase of AKU sports centre
value.NewsSummary: ​To mark the commissioning of the first phase of the Aga Khan University (AKU) Sports Centre, a cricket match was held on December 13, 1998, between the Rector's XI, a team of faculty and students and the President's XI, consisting of staff and volun
value.NewsContent:
​"​To mark the commissioning of the first phase of the Aga Khan University (AKU) Sports Centre, a cricket match was held on December 13, 1998, between the Rector's XI, a team of faculty and students and the President's XI, consisting of staff and volunteers. The Chief Guest was Mr Zaheer Abbas, former Captain of the Pakistan cricket team.

AKU Sport Centre's Phase 1 facilities were completed on schedule, and include the cricket and football fields, tennis and volleyball courts and a jogging track. The Centre is expected to be fully operational in the year 2000, when it will offer various indoor, outdoor and water sports. Highlights of the Sports Centre include an air-conditioned gymnasium, Olympic length swimming pool, tennis and squash courts, weight training and aerobics rooms. One unique feature of the Centre will be its Patient Rehabilitation Programme. Designed to aid and facilitate the recovery of patients suffering from heart attacks, strokes, traffic accident disabilities and sports' injuries. It will be the first service of its kind in Pakistan.

Demonstrating a spirit of volunteer ism and giving, over 50,000 young people from 30 countries participated in the grassroots fund-raising campaign for the Rs.276 million Centre. A significant proportion of the contributions came from donors within Pakistan who rose more than Rs.36.8 million from the total fund-raising target of Rs.138 million. The balance of Rs.138 million was generously matched by His Highness the Aga Khan.

Designed in strict accordance with the highest international standards, the AKU Sports Centre's activities will complement academic programmes by enhancing the learning process and fostering a healthier environment. Although the Sports Centre will primarily be used by the University's students, faculty and staff, it will also serve as a venue for intercollegiate, national and international sports events. AKU Sports Centre will also provide much-needed facilities for women, who form the majority of the student body and the professional staff, and currently have little opportunity for sports and fitness activities.

The Sports Centre is a reflection of AKU’s continuous commitment to excellence and broad outlook and will serve as a replicable model for other such facilities across the country."​
