value.Title: Interfaith Unity at AKU Nakawa Campus Dedication
value.NewsSummary: Diverse leaders gather at AKU's new Nakawa Campus, fostering unity and shared vision
value.NewsContent:
​

The Aga Khan University (AKU) in Uganda recently held a significant outreach event at its new Nakawa Campus, ahead of its official launch later in the year. Religious leaders from different faiths came together to tour the new campus and learn more about AKU's impact in the country and the region. The leaders included Sheikh Muhammad Ali Wasswa, Second Deputy Mufti of Uganda and Imam at Makerere University Business School, Nakawa; Reverend Emmanuel Kalagala, Archdeacon of the Church of the Resurrection Bugolobi; and Mr Mukesh Shukra from the Hindu community. Also present were diplomats, University staff, alumni, development partners, and local stakeholders. 

This new campus represents a substantial step forward in AKU's long-term vision for Uganda and the broader East African region. AKU President Dr Sulaiman Shahabuddin emphasized that the Nakawa campus is a crucial element in fulfilling the overarching mission initiated by the Founding Chancellor His Highness the Aga Khan IV: to ensure Ugandans have access to quality education and healthcare within their own country. This enduring vision is now being championed by the Chancellor His Highness the Aga Khan V and Pro-Chancellor Princess Zahra Aga Khan.

The new Nakawa campus is poised to significantly advance contextually relevant education, deliver world-class healthcare, and drive impactful research. It directly aligns with AKU's global vision and mission, as well as Uganda's national development agenda. 

Dr Shahabuddin emphasised the immense potential the new campus brings, highlighting its role in cultivating skilled professionals who will contribute directly to Uganda's growth and beyond. "We can build beautiful structures and invest in cutting-edge technologies, but the real value of a university lies in its alumni," he stated, commending the alumni for their contributions in academics, research, and community service.

Nakibobeka Moureen, BSc Nursing, Class of 2024 expressed her enthusiasm for the new facilities: "This campus speaks to me. It represents a wave of opportunities for students to grow academically and in research. With its world-class infrastructure and modern equipment, I believe it will shape Uganda's next generation of skilled professionals."

Similarly, Anthony Magemeso, an alumnus and student preceptor, described the campus opening as a “magnificent start" that brings renewed energy to the University's mission.

Later this year, AKU will welcome the first cohort of the new four-year Bachelor of Nursing Science – Direct Entry programme. At full capacity, the campus will be home to 100 faculty and staff and 700 students – 164 of whom will be living full-time on campus in the new student housing building.

A highly anticipated addition to the campus is the upcoming Aga Khan University Hospital, which promises to revolutionize healthcare delivery in Uganda. This cutting-edge facility will not only serve as a premier training ground for AKU students but will also substantially boost the country's healthcare capacity. Once operational, the Aga Khan University Hospital will provide international-quality care in nearly two dozen specialties – from cardiology to oncology, from neurology to obstetrics and gynaecology. It will also form a vital node in the Aga Khan Development Network's health system in East Africa, which already serves more than 1.8 million patients each year.

The University Leadership extended its gratitude to President Yoweri Kaguta Museveni and the Government of Uganda for fostering an enabling environment for its growth. Appreciation was also extended to the Uganda and global communities, donors, volunteers, and the alumni network for their continued support.

value.Title: BMI staff gain hands-on skills in brain health research
value.NewsSummary: Practical training workshop on neuroimaging, wearable sensors and AI tools
value.NewsContent:
​Brain and neurological conditions are becoming more common across Africa, yet research in this area is still limited. To help address this gap, the Brain and Mind Institute (BMI) at Aga Khan University held a practical training workshop on July 2 and 3, 2025, in Nairobi. The focus was on strengthening research skills in neuroimaging, wearable technology, and artificial intelligence.

The one-and-a-half-day workshop brought together staff from BMI, Haematology-Oncology, Clinical Research Unit (CRU), and the Radiology and Imaging Department. It provided participants with hands-on training to support current and future brain health research at the university. 

Dr. Karen Blackmon, Consultant Neuropsychologist at BMI and lead facilitator, said the training was a step toward building stronger local expertise. “We are addressing a data gap that has kept Africa underrepresented in global brain science. Workshops like this are essential for building scientific equity and ensuring our research reflects the lived experiences of all populations,” she said.

The sessions combined short lectures, live demonstrations and practical exercises. Participants learned how to use MRI scan software to study brain structure. They also explored how wearable sensors and mobile-based assessments can help researchers gather real-time data on people’s health, mood, and behavior in their everyday environments.

Dr. Thomas Thesen, a cognitive neuroscientist and co-lead facilitator, emphasized the importance of local researchers having the confidence and skills to use these tools. “We want researchers here to be able to guide how these technologies are used in African contexts. The level of interest and engagement during the sessions was very encouraging, ” he said.

Wearable sensors, in particular, offer new ways to collect health data outside of hospitals and labs. They can help researchers reach people in remote or underserved areas and understand how everyday experiences affect brain health over time.

Dr. Benard Alaka, a postdoctoral fellow at BMI who led the session on wearables, explained how these tools are opening new possibilities.

“They allow us to meet people where they are. We can run studies in real-world settings and collect insights that are more accurate and relevant to the communities we serve.”

For many participants, the workshop provided a rare opportunity to move from theory to practice.

“It is one thing to learn about neuroimaging in class,” said Dr. Litha Musili, a research associate at BMI. “It is another to actually clean the data, run the analysis and understand what the results mean. This experience gave me the skills and confidence to support our research in a more meaningful way.”

The training reflects BMI’s commitment to growing local research capacity in neuroscience and mental health. As noncommunicable diseases continue to rise across the continent, investments in people and practical skills are essential. Through this and other initiatives, BMI is helping build a stronger foundation for African-led brain health research that can support well-being across the lifespan.

value.Title: Experts call for increased taxation to curb rising alcohol and cannabis misuse
value.NewsSummary: Researchers propose WHO treaty to protect brain health
value.NewsContent:
​Press Release

Nairobi, Kenya – June 25, 2025 – A global team of researchers is proposing the introduction of a global minimum tax rate of 70% on alcohol and cannabis products and a ban on their advertising and sponsorship to regulate their rising misuse. 

Led by the Aga Khan University's Brain and Mind Institute and the Global Brain Health Institute, the researchers also want the introduction of a “harm-to-others” tax on cannabis to reflect the broader social and health impacts of cannabis.

The proposals are contained in a proposed international treaty to regulate the rising misuse of alcohol and cannabis, echoing the success of the World Health Organization’s (WHO) Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (FCTC).

Published in Nature Medicine, the commentary highlights alarming increases in alcohol and cannabis consumption worldwide, particularly among young people, and the resulting surge in brain-related health issues, including cognitive decline and dementia.
 
“We are seeing a silent epidemic,” said Cyprian Mostert, lead author and Brain Health Economist at the Aga Khan University’s Brain and Mind Institute. “Alcohol and cannabis are now the most widely used psychoactive substances after tobacco, and their impact on brain health is being dangerously underestimated, especially in low- and middle-income countries where public health infrastructure is already strained.”

The proposed WHO-led treaty would also include Support prevention, treatment and research programs, especially in underserved regions like Africa.
According to the article:
• Global alcohol consumption is projected to rise by 25% by 2030.
• Cannabis use is soaring, with daily users exceeding 200 million globally.
• Excessive use of either substance, especially in combination, accelerates brain aging and increases the risk of dementia.

The authors argue that the WHO should urgently convene member states to draft the global treaty, modelled on the FCTC, which contributed to a 25% global reduction in tobacco smoking since its adoption in 2003. "Taxation is not just about revenue, it is one of the most powerful levers we have to reduce harmful consumption,” said Professor Zul Merali, Director of the AKU’s Brain and Mind Institute. 
“We now have strong evidence that progressive taxes directly reduce alcohol-related brain disorders.”

The researchers also emphasize the importance of aligning global policies on cannabis as more countries move toward legalization. Without a harmonized approach, the world risks repeating the mistakes made with tobacco and alcohol regulation decades ago.
About the Authors

The article is co-authored by experts from the Aga Khan University’s Brain and Mind Institute, Global Brain Health Institute, Wake Forest University and Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, with affiliations across Kenya, Ireland, Chile and the USA.

value.Title: Director Message - July 2025
value.NewsSubTitle: BMI team continues to lead in brain and mental health research
value.NewsSummary: From Rome to Karachi, Kilifi to Nairobi, the work of the Institute continues to expand in reach and relevance.
value.NewsContent:
Last month I stood in St. Peter's Square, watching white smoke rise over the Vatican. A new pope had just been chosen. But I was there for another reason; to attend The Memory: A Symposium Addressing the Opportunities and Challenges of an Aging Global Population, the first of its kind hosted by the Vatican in collaboration with the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP). It was an extraordinary gathering that brought together scientists, policymakers and faith leaders to reimagine aging. I had the honour of speaking about brain health across the life course and the need for culturally grounded strategies, especially in low- and middle-income countries where aging is accelerating fastest and systems remain underprepared.

That global urgency is mirrored in our work here at the Brain and Mind Institute. This November, we will host our second International Conference, this time in Karachi, Pakistan, from November 3–5. With the theme Building Thriving Communities: Promoting Brain and Mental Health in the Global South, this convening will bring together researchers, practitioners and community leaders from across the world to explore how brain and mental health can become the foundation for more resilient, equitable societies.

In research, our teams continue to lead. Our recent publication in ScienceDirect explores how climate shocks are affecting women's mental health in rural Kilifi, Kenya, linking environmental instability to depression and suicidal ideation. And in Nature Medicine, our researchers have put forward a bold global policy proposal: introducing a 70% minimum tax on alcohol and cannabis products, coupled with a ban on advertising and sponsorship. We believe such action is essential to reversing the rise in substance misuse, especially among vulnerable populations.

This past month, we also joined forces with the Shamiri Institute to host a hybrid forum on Adverse Childhood Experiences (ACEs) among adolescents in Kenya. The findings were deeply concerning. 1 in 5 young people has experienced four or more ACEs, significantly increasing their risk of depression, anxiety and bullying. The forum emphasized the urgent need for trauma-informed school-based mental health interventions, and the value of youth voices in shaping policy.

And finally, in June, we proudly concluded the second cohort of the African College of Neuropsychopharmacology (AfCNP) School, a space where the next generation of mental health scientists and practitioners are taking shape, led by African priorities, evidence and ambition.

From Rome to Karachi, Kilifi to Nairobi, the work of the Institute continues to expand in reach and relevance. Thank you for walking this journey with us, as partners, colleagues and champions of brain and mental health in the Global South.

Zul Merali,
Founding Director, Brain and Mind Institute​​​

value.Title: Maryanne’s Turning Point in Advocacy
value.NewsSummary: Transforming Disability Advocacy Through Strategic Media Engagement
value.NewsContent:
​

Maryanne Emomeri a dedicated professional deeply committed to media relations and advocacy for the disability community, discovered a pivotal opportunity in the Media Relations Training Programme at GSMC. She initially saw it as a chance to hone her skills and amplify the voices of people with disabilities. What she didn't anticipate, however, was the profound transformation it would bring to her understanding of media engagement.

Prior to the training, Maryanne's perception of media relations largely revolved around pushing narratives and securing coverage. Yet, as she delved into the comprehensive curriculum, she uncovered a more nuanced truth: effective media engagement transcends mere visibility; it's about cultivating authentic relationships. "I learned that media relations isn’t just about getting coverage; it’s about creating meaningful connections with the right people," she shared.

A significant revelation for Maryanne was recognizing that media professionals are not simply gatekeepers, but individuals with their own interests and priorities. This shift in perspective led her to approach them not as a means to an end, but as partners in storytelling. "Understanding that media professionals have their own interests and needs helped me craft better, more impactful messages," she explained. This realization fundamentally reshaped her interactions with journalists, enabling her to frame stories in ways that genuinely resonated with their perspectives.

Opinion writing emerged as another particularly valuable skill for Maryanne. Always keen to articulate the experiences and challenges faced by the disability community with greater impact, the training provided her with the essential tools to do so. "I’ve already started writing opinion pieces, and I feel more confident in getting my message across effectively," she stated. The course also equipped her with insights into tailoring media messages, strategically timing press interactions, and identifying the ideal journalists for specific stories.

The program's facilitators played a crucial role in Maryanne's learning journey. Their instruction was not merely theoretical but grounded in extensive real-world industry experience. The culminating capstone project, which mandated the practical application of acquired knowledge, solidified her understanding and instilled the confidence needed to implement these skills in her professional endeavors.

Reflecting on the experience, Maryanne views the training as a definitive turning point in her media relations trajectory. She now approaches media engagement with a newfound sense of strategy and purpose. For other professionals contemplating the program, her advice is concise: "Be open-minded. This course goes beyond the basics and makes you see that there’s so much more to learn if you choose to."

For Maryanne, this wasn't just another training; it was an eye-opening journey that has irrevocably altered her approach to communication and advocacy for a cause she deeply champions.

value.Title: Empowering mental health integration through implementation science
value.NewsSummary: Insights from Nida Zahid, global mental health fellow (Harvard–AKU)
value.NewsContent:
As the fourth researcher selected for the prestigious Harvard–AKU Global Mental Health Fellowship, Dr. Nida Zahid is taking on a critical challenge, integrating mental health into cancer care in low-resource settings. The fellowship, a joint initiative of Harvard Medical School and AKU's Brain and Mind Institute, supports post-doctoral leaders advancing mental health implementation science in South & Central Asia and East Africa.

We spoke with Nida about what drives her work, why brain tumor patients in Pakistan need more than just biomedical treatment, and how this fellowship is helping her turn research into real-world impact.

1. What drew you to mental health research, and how will this fellowship amplify your impact?

My fascination with mental health began early, witnessing a gap between biomedical treatment and psychological support, especially for cancer patients in low-resource settings. Despite their emotional and cognitive burdens, mental health often gets sidelined.

As I built a decade-length career spanning medicine, epidemiology and neuro-oncology, I dedicated myself to understanding how resilience and neurocognitive health affect long-term wellbeing among cancer survivors. This global mental health fellowship offers a powerful stage to collaborate with global leaders and deepen implementation research. It will help me scale culturally relevant interventions, mentor emerging scholars, and shape psychosocial policies in LMICs.

2. Can you outline your research focus under this fellowship?

My efforts will center on implementing a culturally tailored psychological intervention for patients with brain tumors in Pakistan. While survival rates improve, the neurocognitive and psycho-social aftermath, worsened by stigma, financial hardship and weak mental health systems, goes largely unaddressed.

Using implementation science, I will map context-specific barriers and build strategies with patients, clinicians, caregivers and policymakers. Ultimately, the aim is to generate practical, evidence-based insights that can inform policy and practice not only in Pakistan but also in other low- and middle-income countries facing similar challenges in integrating mental health into cancer care.

3. How will the fellowship support your evolution as a global mental health leader?

I have led multidisciplinary teams and mentored researchers, but translating evidence into system-wide practice remains a challenge. This fellowship will hone my leadership in implementation science, system integration and policy advocacy, working alongside Harvard and AKU experts.

With mentorship and collaboration, I will refine strategies to institutionalize evidence-based interventions, linking mental health with larger health and development systems. Ultimately, this builds toward my goal of leading cross-sectoral projects that bring tangible, life-changing improvements.

4. What unique perspectives or experiences do you bring to this fellowship?

I bring a multidisciplinary lens shaped by over a decade of work across research, clinical care and academic leadership. With a background in medicine, a Master's in Epidemiology and Biostatistics, and a PhD, I have focused on mental health and neurocognitive outcomes among cancer patients in low-resource settings. This experience has grounded me in the realities of health systems where stigma, resource constraints and limited mental health infrastructure are everyday challenges.

Beyond research, I have held leadership roles at the departmental and institutional level, giving me insight into how to build systems that balance scientific rigor with community relevance. I am particularly committed to equity and capacity building and have mentored junior researchers and clinicians in mental health. These experiences have shown me that technical knowledge must be paired with cultural humility, community engagement and systems thinking. I look forward to bringing that perspective into this fellowship and continuing to grow as a collaborative leader in global mental health.

5. What advice would you offer to early-career researchers, especially women in science?

Your voice matters. Leadership is shaped by purpose, not position. Fields like mental health and implementation science thrive on curiosity, empath, and interdisciplinary insight.

Having balanced parenthood and a demanding doctorate while rising in my field, I have learned that lived experiences, working in under-resourced settings and mentoring others, are strengths. They shape contextually rich, patient-centered solutions.

So, find mentors, build leadership skills, learn broadly and remain anchored in your why. Impact isn't just in research, even more in making that evidence reach the people who need it most.

value.Title: SFU Students Explore Tanzanian Climate Solutions
value.NewsSummary: Field school at AKU-ACER fostered drone tech use for soil analysis, research collaboration
value.NewsContent:
​

Nine students from Simon Fraser University's (SFU) Mechatronics Systems Engineering Laboratory visited AKU's Arusha Climate and Environmental Research Centre (AKU-ACER) for the CAPESTONE field school. Led by Professor Woo Soo Kim, they underwent a two-week immersive experience from April 28 to May 9, 2025 at the site. A postdoctoral fellow and five researchers from the Nelson Mandela African Institution of Science and Technology (NM-AIST) joined them as well.

The programme showcased the innovative use of drone technology to assess vital soil nutrients across AKU-ACER's living laboratory, which includes coffee, flower, and avocado plantations. This initiative fostered a vibrant exchange of knowledge, culture, and technical expertise.

 “When I reflect on the trip, I have immense gratitude for the cultural exchange," said Azzam Haq, a student at SFU. “One day we're on a safari, and the next day we're jumping with the Maasai… And then the next day, we're out in the fields in the avocado trees, flying our drones. So, I just think it's kind of beautiful how we were able to do so much in so little time and meet so many people, across three different universities… immense gratitude."

Professor Woo Soo Kim, expressed his satisfaction with the field school saying, “Our second mechatronics engineering field trip was completed and it's successful. During these two weeks... we had two workshops and then the student's demonstration and a very tight interaction with the local farmers and local researchers and friends."

He stressed the significance of seeing climate issues firsthand, adding, “It's not just about the knowledge, but... how we can try different technologies from the mechatronic engineering to tackle those issues and challenges."

SFU PhD student Pranjal Biswas noted key contrasts in farming practices, observing, “The cultural approach to agriculture in Tanzania has a huge emphasis on involving the community... This differs a lot from Western agriculture practices... Coming here was really important to see how the technology... might end up being used differently in Tanzania."

 “I remember standing in the field watching a farmer explain how difficult it is to know what their soil really needs... It made me realize how deeply personal agriculture is," said Timothy John Suarez, an SFU student. “It's not just about crops or data, it's about people's livelihoods... This experience has changed how I see my role not just as someone who's building solutions, but as someone who's building with and for others."

NM-AIST PhD student Liston Kiwoli praised AKU-ACER's facilities, saying, “I've learnt that for successful research, we need either an environment where we can collect samples or... get data and then go back to the laboratory and analyze them to get results."

Ramadhani Sinde, NM-AIST Senior Lecturer, emphasized future collaboration, remarking, “It was great experience… we exchanged a lot... I see there is room of collaboration… I'm hoping to continue with this collaboration."

SFU MSc student Hasti Mohammadi reflected, “Seeing parts of the world you never thought you'd see makes you realize how pointless some of your worries are—and how the world is so much bigger than you."

Professor Emmanuel Sulle, Director at AKU-ACER underlined the partnership's importance, highlighting its role in enabling young engineers to “connect technical work with social and cultural contexts, and integrate science with its real-world users."

The 2025 CAPESTONE Field School stands as evidence of how international collaboration can drive innovation, foster cultural understanding, and deepen appreciation for the real-world impact of a living laboratory.

value.Title: Dr Bhutta Wins Virchow Prize 2025 for Global Health
value.NewsSummary: AKU's Dr Zulfiqar Bhutta honoured for pioneering maternal, child health equity
value.NewsContent:
​

Dr Zulfiqar A. Bhutta, Founding Director of the Institute for Global Health and Development at the Aga Khan University (AKU), has been bestowed with the esteemed Virchow Prize 2025. This major international award recognizes his pioneering, lifelong leadership in advancing maternal, newborn, and child health equity through community-centred, evidence-based research. Dr Bhutta shares this year's prize with co-laureate Professor Quarraisha Abdool Karim from South Africa.

The Virchow Prize, awarded by the Virchow Foundation, celebrates outstanding achievements in global health aligned with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) towards "Health for All, " and is one of the highest awards in global health. The prize underscores the critical importance of addressing health disparities and fostering structural change.

The independent Virchow Prize Committee highlighted Dr Bhutta's exceptionally impressive and outstanding contributions since his earliest academic beginnings. His decades of transformative policy influence have redefined the global health architecture by focusing on those marginalized and historically excluded from mainstream health systems and scientific discourse.

"Dr Bhutta's work has been instrumental in shaping global health guidelines and influencing and influencing national policies for maternal, child health and nutrition in low- and middle-income countries," stated the Virchow Prize Committee in their rationale. "As the Founding Director of the Institute for Global Health and Development at Aga Khan University and Co-Director of the SickKids Centre for Global Child Health, Dr Bhutta has championed community-based primary care models, large-scale randomised trials, and implementation research within vulnerable communities and fragile settings."

His research has consistently demonstrated the effectiveness of locally embedded interventions, empowering community health workers and nutrition programmes targeting the critical first 1,000 days of life. With over 1,400 scientific publications and active advisory roles in organizations like WHO, UNICEF, and the Partnership for Maternal, Newborn and Child Health (PMNCH), Dr Bhutta's contributions exemplify scientific excellence that translates into life-saving policies and equitable health systems. His work has significantly advanced strategies to reduce maternal and child mortality in South-Central Asia, sub-Saharan Africa, and diverse humanitarian settings.

Dr Bhutta said, “This award is a recognition of the ongoing contribution by numerous collaborators, students and trainees who have worked tirelessly to address some of the world's most challenging problems affecting its women and children; to them I owe a tremendous debt of gratitude for being part of this ongoing journey!"

The recognition of Dr Bhutta with the Virchow Prize is a monumental achievement for Aga Khan University and a source of immense pride for Pakistan. It underscores AKU's commitment to impactful, globally relevant research and its role in addressing critical health challenges in the developing world. For Pakistan, this award signifies global recognition of its intellectual leadership and contributions to public health, inspiring a new generation of scientists and policymakers to pursue health equity.

“As President of Aga Khan University, it is a personal privilege to congratulate Dr Bhutta on receiving the Virchow Prize 2025 – an honour both profound and richly deserved," said Dr Sulaiman Shahabuddin, AKU President. “It is a moment of great pride for both me and the University to have him as part of our community. His lifelong dedication to improving maternal, newborn, and child health in underserved communities speaks directly to the heart of our mission. This recognition not only celebrates his remarkable impact but also reaffirms AKU's commitment to advancing global health equity and driving meaningful, lasting change."

Dr Bhutta's distinguished career has been marked by numerous accolades, including the John Dirks Canada Gairdner Global Health Award (2022), Roux Prize (2021), International Paediatric Association's Lifetime Achievement Award (2025), and some of the highest national honours of Pakistan (President of Pakistan Pride of Performance 2017 and Sitara-e-Imtiaz 2023) as well as the Order of Canada (2024).

value.Title: Irene Abalo Otto's Unyielding Journey in Journalism
value.NewsSummary: Irene's journey is one of resilience and transformation amidst life challenges
value.NewsContent:
​

Irene Abalo Otto’s journey into the Master of Arts in Digital Journalism (MADJ) programme at the Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC) wasn’t just a step in her career; it was a pivotal moment. Having deepened her passion for digital storytelling during the Nation Media Lab Programme, she was ready to elevate her skills and pursue journalism at a higher level.

As a seasoned journalist and sub-editor at Nation Media Group in Uganda, Irene was no stranger to challenges. But nothing could have prepared her for the one she faced just days before classes began: a brutal assault on February 17, 2021, left her with severe injuries to her lower left leg. "My injuries were the result of a beating using batons,” she explains. “I’ve since undergone two surgeries to help regenerate the damaged tissues around my ankle."

Despite the chronic pain and physical limitations that followed, Irene's commitment to learning remained unshaken. "I had to sit in class with my leg elevated on a pillow,” she recalls. “But the hospital, classmates, and faculty were all so understanding."

What truly sets Irene’s GSMC experience apart is not just her incredible personal resilience, but the extraordinary support she found within the GSMC community. From fellow students to faculty, Irene discovered a sense of belonging that empowered her through immense physical and emotional hurdles. "The university never made me feel like a burden. I was slow, but I was part of the team," she affirms. Even travel, with its unhelpful airport experiences, couldn’t dim her spirit. "I didn’t give up. I asked the doctors to teach me how to manage the pain, with or without medication. I embraced every chance to leave the house and be with people."

Balancing pain management, research, and coursework, Irene not only completed her master’s in digital journalism but, remarkably, also graduated in the same year with another master’s in international relations and diplomacy. With quiet pride, she shares, "I was doing research for one while studying for the other. I graduated with two master’s degrees in one year." Throughout this demanding period, her dedication to growth and contribution remained steadfast. While her injury prevents her from reporting from the field, this experience ignited a significant and inspiring career shift: Irene now dedicates her efforts to training the next generation of journalists across Uganda.

"I realized I could teach. I could train others on mobile journalism, gender reporting in elections, investigations, and health reporting," Irene explains. Her passion for journalism was rekindled within the classroom, where GSMC’s emphasis on mentorship, gender equality, and practical storytelling profoundly shaped her. "I came back with knowledge I couldn’t apply fully but I wasn’t going to let it sit idle. I’m now empowering others to tell impactful stories." This spirit of altruism earned her GSMC’s Community Service Award, a recognition she found both unexpected and deeply affirming. "You never know who’s watching. That award felt like the final topping on the cake."

Irene’s message to aspiring journalists is clear and compelling: "Keep standing out for journalism. Keep training people to tell stories that change lives. In this age of social media noise, we need impactful, ethical journalism more than ever."

​​

value.Title: Tanzania Delegation Visits AKU to Strengthen Partnership
value.NewsSummary: Official visit underscores shared commitment to advance health, education in Tanzania
value.NewsContent:
​

Aga Khan University (AKU) recently hosted a high-level delegation from the Ministry of Health, Tanzania, led by Dr Grace Magembe, Chief Medical Officer. The visit to AKU's Pakistan campus underscored a shared commitment to advancing health and education in Tanzania through strategic collaboration. 

Dr Magembe met with AKU leadership, including President Sulaiman Shahabuddin and Regional CEO of Aga Khan Health Services, East Africa, Zeenat Sulaiman. Discussions focused on strengthening health systems, expanding specialized training, and leveraging technology to enhance healthcare access across Tanzania.

“With Tanzania, AKDN has a rich history that goes way back, almost 100 years," said Dr Sulaiman Shahabuddin, President of AKU. “Looking ahead, AKU and AKDN are exploring opportunities to further contribute to the country's social, cultural, and economic development."

Dr Magembe emphasized the Tanzanian government's vision for healthcare, stating, "Health is a human right – and technology can help us reach the most people." She also appreciated the long-standing contribution of the AKDN to the social and economic development of Tanzania.

The Tanzanian delegation included Dr Saitore Laizer, Director of Human Resource Development (Training and Development); Ms Esther Elisamia Msechu, Senior ICT Officer; and Mr Simon Ernest, Personal Assistant to the CMO. Representatives from AKU Tanzania's Medical College, Professor Paschal Ruggajo, Associate Dean, and Dr. Samina Somji, Director of Postgraduate Medical Education, as well as Mr Sisawo Konteh, CEO of Aga Khan Health Services, Dar es Salaam, were also part of the discussions.

During the visit, the two sides agreed to collaborate in the following areas:

  • Health and Education as Key Priorities: Strengthening health-related education and training at both university and middle-cadre professional levels to build Tanzania's health workforce.
  • Focus on Primary Health Care: With approximately 70% of the Tanzanian population residing in rural areas and relying on primary healthcare, there's a strong need to equip graduates with skills to effectively serve these communities.
  • Health System Strengthening and Technology Integration: Integration of technology into health systems, including telemedicine and e-learning, to expand access to services and improve training capacity.
  • Specialized Training and Capacity Building: There is a strong demand for support in specialized and super-specialized healthcare training to build capacity in advanced care. 

Both sides expressed eagerness to work closely to translate these plans into reality.

value.Title: Dr Sanaa Alimia wins AIPS Book Prize for Refugee Cities
value.NewsSummary: The AIPS Award recognises groundbreaking research on Afghan refugees in Pakistan
value.NewsContent:
​

Dr Sanaa Alimia, Assistant Professor at AKU's Institute for the Study of Muslim Civilisations (AKU-ISMC), has been awarded the prestigious 2025 Annual Book Prize by the American Institute of Pakistan Studies (AIPS) for her book Refugee Cities: How Afghans Changed Urban Pakistan, published by the University of Pennsylvania Press.

Drawing on years of fieldwork in cities such as Karachi and Peshawar, Refugee Cities documents how Afghan refugees have shaped urban life in Pakistan - not only through labour and economic contributions, but by building communities, engaging in activism, and resisting marginalisation. The book weaves together political anthropology, migration studies, and urban history to reveal the lives of those who often remain invisible in policy and media discourse.

The AIPS Book Prize Committee praised the book for its “ethnographic insight" and its ability to show “how refugee communities are neither passive nor peripheral."

Reflecting on the award, Dr Alimia said, "This recognition is deeply humbling. My hope is that the book invites us to rethink labels like 'refugee' and reflect on how we uphold justice, rights, and inclusion for all. We must stop viewing people through the labels of 'refugees' versus 'citizens'. That lens is dehumanising – and it hides the real structures driving displacement."

At AKU-ISMC, Dr Alimia's work exemplifies the Centre's mission to produce socially relevant scholarship rooted in Muslim contexts and committed to amplifying marginalised voices. Her research speaks to wider debates on migration, citizenship, and pluralism in South and Central Asia and beyond.

value.Title: GSMC Student Appointed New Communications Staff at AKU Uganda
value.NewsSummary: Proscovia Nabatte aims to bridge her coursework with her new role on staff
value.NewsContent:
​

Proscovia Nabatte has always believed in the power of storytelling. Now, she's living one of her own, navigating a unique chapter as both a Master's student at Aga Khan University's Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC) and the newly appointed Communications and Marketing Specialist for AKU in Uganda.

“It's a mix of emotions," Proscovia says with a smile. “Being both a student and now a staff member at Aga Khan University feels surreal. It's a role that demands a lot; balancing academics with professional responsibilities, especially in such a pivotal communications role for the Uganda campus and Nakawa Specialty Centre."

Currently pursuing a Master of Arts in Strategic Communications, Proscovia describes her new position as more than a job. It's an opportunity to live out her coursework in real time.

“This experience is already expanding my career perspective, and it's exactly the kind of professional development I've always hoped for," she says. “Even in these first few days, I've realized that working at AKU demands deep knowledge and a constant growth mindset, nationally, regionally, and internationally."

Her passion for the programme at GSMC is clear. “Back in 2019, I was looking for a postgraduate programme that would fit the realities of being a communications professional. Most of what I found leaned too heavily on theory," she recalls. “This course is different. It's grounded in the real world. Practical case studies, strategic thinking, and storytelling I can immediately apply in my work."

That immediacy is part of what makes Proscovia's journey so striking. Her role requires her to lead communications and marketing initiatives for both AKU's academics and health services in Uganda – while balancing her own coursework.

“When I first visited the new campus at Nakawa, two words came to mind: impact and quality," she says. “It's not just the architecture; it's what the presence of AKU here means. For many years, Ugandans had to travel to Nairobi for specialized healthcare or postgraduate studies. Now, that level of excellence is right here at home."

And she's wasting no time putting theory into action. “One of the strongest tools I'm bringing into this role is storytelling," she says. “We've moved beyond direct marketing. Today, storytelling is the most effective form of engagement. I plan to integrate public relations, advocacy, strategic marketing, and communications into a single, purpose-driven model."

It's rare to find someone whose professional and academic lives align so closely. For AKU in Uganda, Proscovia Nabatte represents a promising bridge between vision and execution, theory and practice, and the future of communications in East Africa.

value.Title: Free Medical Camp Serves Nakawa Community at AKU Open Day
value.NewsSummary: AKU and Hospital provide health checks, connect with future students at new Nakawa campus
value.NewsContent:
​

Over 250 residents of Nakawa Division received free health services during a medical camp organized by the Aga Khan University (AKU), in partnership with the Aga Khan University Hospital. Held on July 11, 2025, at the University's newly constructed Nakawa campus, the initiative was part of an Open Day designed to connect with the community and future students.

The medical camp was a key highlight of the Open Day, an event that offered prospective students, parents, and community members a unique opportunity to explore AKU's academic offerings. Visitors learned about various programmes, including the newly introduced Bachelor of Nursing Science-Direct Entry programme, gained insights into admission requirements, and experienced the vibrant student life at AKU.

Dr Joseph Mwizerwa, Associate Vice Provost at Aga Khan University, emphasized the events significance. “This Open Day is a chance for prospective students, parents, and the general public to understand what Aga Khan University offers from rigorous academics to a vibrant student community and innovative research. It has been purposefully staged here to give our stakeholders, partners, and the wider community a firsthand experience of the newly completed Nakawa campus ahead of its grand opening." He added.

Beyond academic exposure, the free medical camp provided comprehensive health screenings and consultations. Services included blood pressure and blood sugar testing, BMI assessments, dental and eye check-ups, and health education and counselling.

“Most of the cases we examined today were non-communicable diseases, including diabetes and high blood pressure. We also treated peptic ulcers. The results indicate a growing burden of lifestyle-related conditions in our communities," noted Diana Namubiru Ssewanyana, Director of Aga Khan University Hospital, Uganda.

Residents warmly welcomed the initiative, with many receiving both treatment and free medication. Susan Namakula, a local resident, expressed her gratitude: “This is a great gesture. For such a reputable university and hospital to open their doors to the community shows a commitment to being good neighbours. We have been examined, advised, and now we better understand how to manage our health."

Paul Mugambe, Mayor of Nakawa Division, lauded AKU and the hospital for bringing critical services closer to the people and for inspiring educational ambition among the youth. He urged the University and hospital leadership to make the medical camp an annual event, highlighting the positive impact on the community.

During the Open Day, visitors also toured the state-of-the-art Nakawa campus, including modern hostel facilities and the Nakawa Clinic. This immersive experience further reinforced AKU's mission of academic excellence and its commitment to community-centred service.

value.Title: Julius Odeke’s Story of Transformation
value.NewsSummary: Julius credits GSMC with significantly sharpening his skills and broadening his worldview
value.NewsContent:
​

When Julius Odeke decided to pursue a Master of Arts in Digital Journalism (MADJ) at the Aga Khan University Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC), it was more than an academic decision; it was a profound turning point. 

Hailing from a region deeply affected by conflict, Julius was drawn to GSMC’s stellar reputation, inclusive environment, and the promise of financial aid.. "The opportunity to engage with renowned faculty and a diverse student body, along with the potential for career growth, made GSMC a clear choice," he shares.

His journey at GSMC was filled with memorable moments, especially the unexpected impact of a student award. "It didn’t seem like a big award at the time," he recalls, "but it ended up changing everything." A generous donor in the UK, touched by Julius’ story, offered to cover his outstanding tuition. This act of kindness reinforced his belief in the power of recognition and community. He also speaks fondly of the inspiration and mentorship he received from faculty like Professor Peter Kimani and Mr Joseph Warungu, whose guidance was instrumental in his professional growth.

Like many working professionals returning to school, Julius faced his share of challenges, including needing to retake two courses. Yet, with discipline and determination, he overcame these hurdles. "As a journalist, I’m used to deadlines," he explains. "I also don’t go out much, so I made time for study and work." His ability to effectively balance his responsibilities was key to his academic success.

Today, Julius credits GSMC with significantly sharpening his skills and broadening his worldview. His time at AKU fostered a greater appreciation for cultural diversity and enhanced his journalistic practice, particularly in investigative writing and photojournalism. "In 2023, I was ranked among the best photographers in Uganda by the Uganda Photography Press Association," he proudly notes, attributing this recognition to the practical training he received at GSMC.

Looking ahead, Julius dreams of earning a PhD and eventually returning to GSMC as faculty. "I’ve already recommended several students to the university," he says, "because it offers hands-on, real-world journalism training." 

For him, GSMC is more than just an institution; it is a launching pad. As he aptly puts it: "The GSMC is a world-class academic institution that strives for excellence — and it shows in the success of its alumni."


​

value.Title: AKU Achieves Full AAALAC International Accreditation
value.NewsSummary: Global body accredits AKU’s animal care and use program
value.NewsContent:
​The Aga Khan University Medical College has been granted full accreditation by AAALAC International, an internationally respected recognition that highlights AKU’s commitment to the highest standards of animal care and ethical research practices.

The accreditation follows an extensive review process that began in 2021, including multiple rounds of evaluation followed by program improvements addressing the findings. The AAALAC International Council recently confirmed that all previous review findings have been addressed in accordance with global benchmarks commended the University for its thoughtful improvements and approved its accreditation with AAALAC International.

“AAALAC International is the only accreditation agency of its kind that evaluates animal research programs around the world,” said Dr Tashfeen, Head of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee. “It’s not just a title; it’s a global mark of credibility. Even the World Health Organization and National Institutes of Health, U.S. look for this accreditation when considering research partnerships.”

For AKU, the journey toward accreditation began long before the review process. “When I was appointed to lead the animal program at the University in 2012, a process for review and approval of animal care and use was in-place and an animal facility was functional, but these were not fully aligned with the current best international standards,” shared Dr Tashfeen. “Over the years, we worked hard to bring operational practices in line with our institutional mission and global expectations. Today, the quality of our animal care and use program truly reflects AKU’s vision.”

When asked how the University ensures animals are treated with care and respect, he emphasized a culture of ethical responsibility. “We provide detailed guidelines to everyone involved, scientists, veterinarians, and staff, ensuring that all handling of animals is humane and adheres to strict safety protocols. We always explore alternatives before involving animals in research.” Students and faculty in biomedical and life sciences also benefit from this structured, ethical approach. “The health and safety of our researchers, particularly students, is a priority,” said Dr Tashfeen. “Protocols are in place to protect them from allergies and harmful animal exposure. Students also gain hands-on learning opportunities in a way that prepares them for real-world biomedical research, without compromising on ethics.”

Now fully accredited for its mouse and rat research facility, the University’s responsibilities continue. “AAALAC International has defined conditions that we must continue to fulfill, and we are committed to ongoing improvement,” he noted. “We regularly hold workshops and lectures, collaborating with other educational institutions from across Pakistan. We’re also in conversation with the government, because currently, there are no national laws on the ethical use of animals in research, and that needs to change.”

In a heartfelt message to students and young researchers, Dr Tashfeen said, “Whenever you are dealing with animals, remember they can feel pain and distress. It’s our moral duty to minimize their suffering. Always consider alternatives first, and if animals must be used, do so with the utmost care and respect.”


This achievement would not have been possible without the visionary leadership and relentless support by the Institutional Official for the Animal Programme Dr. Syed Ather Enam, and Director Laboratories Dr. Azhar Hussain, and the tireless dedication of members of the Ethics Committee for Animal Care and Use, Institutional Biosafety Committee, lab management, technical and admin staff, and numerous colleagues in Design, Project Management, Facilities Management, Family Medicine, Security, Purchase and other departments behind the scenes. Dr Tashfeen expressed his special gratitude to former Dean Dr. Adil Haider, Vice Provosts Dr. Fauziah Rabbani and Dr. Anjum Halai, Provost Dr. Carl Amrhein, Dean Research and Graduate Studies Dr. Elnasir Lalani, and Associate Dean Research Dr. Anwar Ali Siddiqui.

value.Title: Birds of a Feather: From Livestock Hills to Bana Grass Field
value.NewsSummary: A reflective blog article by Banafsha, a student at AKU's Faculty of Arts and Sciences
value.NewsContent:
​

“Birds of a feather flock together", is a famous song by Billie Eilish. Since I landed in Tanzania, East Africa, I have carried this thought in my mind through its different landscapes and experiences. It resonates deeply with me now in a way I have never felt before. ​​

I am Banafsha, and my friends call me Bana. I grew up in a small village located in the northern region of Pakistan, where livestock, especially goats and sheep, form the hub of daily life. Our livelihood was modest; we raised livestock for survival, not for profit. Yet even at a tiny scale, I witnessed firsthand how unsustainable these practices could be. Animals graze freely on the hills, stripping vegetation to the roots. Each year, around ten trees are cut to supplement their feed, not because the leaves are very nutritious, but because they are the only option. Honestly, a gust of wind could have blown them away, not just the leaves, but the animals as well. In addition to it, a single bout of rain often turned into sudden flash floods due to the bare slopes left behind.

Years later, I pursued environmental studies in my university, AKU, hoping that science would show me a new side to livestock farming, perhaps a more sustainable and balanced one. But the deeper I dug, the more I began to realize that even the earliest stages of livestock rearing are fraught with ecological challenges. It starts with something as simple as what animals eat and how that food is sourced.

In my own household, I saw how difficult it was to maintain a healthy balance. Our goats and sheep grazed freely on the surrounding hills until the land was bare. When natural fodder ran short, we turned to cutting tree branches. This wasn't a large-scale operation, but even at this small scale, the stress on the land was visible.

This internal debate followed me across borders, all the way from Pakistan to Tanzania, where I began a new chapter at the Aga Khan University's Arusha Climate and Environmental Research Center (AKU, ACER). On my very first day, as I roamed around, something caught my eye: a tall, lush plant unlike anything I had before. It was vibrant, alive, almost too green to be real. To my surprise, I soon learned its name is Bana grass.

It was as though the land itself was calling out to me, not just through its beauty, but through a kind of poetic symmetry. Bana meets Bana. 

Quite curiously, I began researching the plant. What I found greatly surprising me.  According to a study conducted by the College of Tropical Agriculture and Human Resources, University of Hawai'i at Manoa, green Bana grass isn't just tall and beautiful, it is also a high-yielding tropical forage that provides essential nutrients like calcium, phosphorus, and protein. What impressed me the most was its natural features, which make it sustainable for the people and the environment. This grass grows back quickly after cutting, tolerates dry conditions, and requires minimal fertilizer. Communities use it in a cut-and-carry system, where farmers harvest the grass and bring it to livestock, instead of letting animals roam freely, because its size is quite big, making it very easy to harvest.

This simple change makes a big difference. Overgrazing leads to the erosion of the land, but Bana grass helps reverse that. Its deep roots hold the soil together and retain water, helping in restoring degraded land, which is one of the major issues in Pakistan and in Tanzania as well. I used to see livestock farming and sustainability as contradictory with each other. But there I realized that they can go hand in hand, not because of big industrial changes, but through small, thoughtful innovations.

This realization remained me for a while, and as a curious young environmentalist, eager to find meaningful solutions, I finally had the opportunity to speak with Didier Van Bignoot, a global advisor in agriculture, food security, and climate resilience at AKF who works in partnership with ACER.

He shared something with me that added a new layer of insight. ACER isn't just growing Bana Grass; they are actively distributing it to local communities to promote wider adoption. But it's not a handout. For every plant given, farmers are encouraged to multiply and give 10 plants back to ACER in the future. It is a very ideal model that encourages ownership, sustainability, long-term impacts, and most importantly, responsibility.

For the first time, I saw a way forward. Not by abandoning livestock altogether, but by rethinking how we feed and manage them. Encountering thriving green grass in an area so far from where I grew up made me realize that solutions don't always have to be complex. What began as a roam through the fields turned into a moment of revelation. I came with confusion, shaped by the erosion of my land and the weight of the unfriendly practices, but I left with hope, left with a hope for farming that values both people and the earth.

To me, Bana grass is more than just a plant. It is a sign of regeneration, resilience, and most importantly, responsibility. It reminds us that sustainability is not about abandoning what we know but about building it. Sometimes, the answers we seek are already rooted in the land, waiting for us to stop, listen, and nurture them.

And maybe, just maybe, birds of a feather flock together for a reason. Sometimes, they even find each other halfway across the world, in the form of a tall, lush, hopeful blade of grass. ​

value.Title: What Does It Mean to Be A Climate Advocate?
value.NewsSummary: FAS Student Didar Ali reflects on the true meaning of a climate activist
value.NewsContent:
​

I wasn't holding a placard the first time I realized I had to do something about the climate crisis. I wasn't on a panel or in a protest. I was standing near a stream in my village that had had fed our valley for years. In the last decade, the stream had been causing devastation with increased flooding year after year.

In my hometown in the high mountains of Gilgit-Baltistan - a region home to over 7,000 glaciers, the largest number outside the Arctic and Antarctic and often called the "Third Pole" - spoke about how the seasons no longer made sense. How water arrived too late or disappeared too early. At first, I didn't know what to do with all  that worry. I just knew it wasn't enough to stay quiet.

Most people think a climate advocate or activist is someone always speaking at global summits, leading movements, or being featured in the media. But the truth is, most climate activists are doing work that goes unseen. They're organizing school workshops, clean-up drives, debate national policies, protesting, translating climate knowledge into local languages, working with communities, cleaning rivers, or just starting conversations that matter.

The climate crisis is enormous. But not every response has to be. What matters is that we show up with care, honesty, and consistency. That's what I've learned over the past few years, not from a textbook, but through lived experience. I've worked with youth-led climate organizations, joined climate camps in Chitral and Balochistan, interned at research centers in Central Asia and now in East Africa, and worked closely with young people back home in Gilgit-Baltistan.

My first step wasn't fancy. I joined a local clean-up campaign. Picking up trash might seem minor when glaciers are melting and floods are destroying homes, but it was my way in. From there, I started reading more, writing about what I learned, joining student-led climate groups, and slowly finding people who cared about the same things.

That's the thing - climate activism doesn't begin with a viral campaign. It begins with small actions, taken seriously. It starts in classrooms, WhatsApp groups, local parks, and yes, in quiet worry by a stream. If you want to begin, begin where you are. Pick up a book. Join a club. Volunteer for a small event. You don't need to have all the answers. You just need to care enough to ask the right questions.

For a year, I worked in Chitral teaching youth about environmental conservation. Later, I joined one of Pakistan's leading climate organizations, the Climate Forward Pakistan (CFP), where I had the chance to grow further and learn from people across the country.

One of the most powerful moments in my journey was at a youth-led climate camp in coastal Balochistan. I met young people from different regions and backgrounds. Some were facing drought, others rising seas. Some had never been asked what they thought about climate change but all of them had stories.


That's when it clicked for me. Activism isn't just about fighting for the planet. It's about people. It's about justice. Climate change is not just an environmental issue, it's about inequality, displacement, food, water, health, and dignity. So, if you want to become a climate activist, start by finding people. Sit with elders. Listen to farmers. Work with students. Talk to girls who want to make their voices heard. Movements grow through connection, not competition.

During my internships, I worked on climate research projects, tracking fossil fuel developments, reviewing policy documents, and mapping climate trends. But I quickly realized something. Research on its own isn't enough. If people can't access or understand the knowledge, it doesn't help them.

That's why I believe our job as activists isn't to act like we know everything. It's to listen. The people we often consider "illiterate" are sometimes the ones who carry the deepest Indigenous Knowledge. They've been protecting the Earth long before we had terms like climate resilience. One thing we can do is translate key climate ideas into local languages, turn reports into simple visuals, and create spaces for open discussion. We don't need more complicated data. We need clearer ways to share what we already know and what else we need to know more.

Let's be real. Climate activists often get criticised. “You're just doing this for recognition," people say. “You want to go to conferences and win awards." I've heard it. Maybe you have too.

But for many of us, the work is deeply personal. It's unpaid, often unrecognized, and done on the side of everything else in life. We do it because we care. Because we're scared. Because we see what's happening to our people and our lands and we refuse to stay silent.

There's also a deeper reason why this work matters. British Philosopher & Ethicist Elizabeth Cripps writes about the no-harm principle which states that each of us has a moral duty not to cause serious harm to others, including future generations. When it comes to climate change, personal lifestyle changes aren't enough. The problem is too big, too systemic. The only way to prevent harm is through collective action. That means organizing, resisting, building, and yes, activism.

You don't have to lead a movement to be part of one. You just have to join in.

So, what does it mean to be a climate activist?

It means picking up the plastic bottle and the microphone. It means reading quietly and speaking loudly. It means showing up, again and again, whether or not anyone is watching.

You don't need to be perfect. You just need to be present. Climate activism isn't a title you earn it's a way of showing up in the world.

I never imagined that a stream would be my turning point. But it was. And now, I carry that moment with me everywhere I go.

Maybe your turning point hasn't come yet. Or maybe it already has, and you just haven't named it.

Either way, if you care enough to do something you're already part of this.

And the Earth needs every single one of us.

value.Title: AKU-ACER July 2025 Highlights
value.NewsSummary: Month highlights include internship programme and research collaboration
value.NewsContent:
​

July 2025 marked a significant milestone for AKU-ACER as it welcomed its first-ever undergraduate interns, Didar Ali and Banafsha Saeed, from AKU's Karachi Campus. This pioneering programme underscores AKU-ACER's commitment to nurturing future research leaders and strengthening connections across the University's global network.

Didar and Banafsha, students from the Faculty of Arts and Sciences, were inspired to join AKU-ACER after attending lectures by Miriam Kugele, who highlighted her collaborations with the Centre. During their internship, they actively contributed to ongoing research projects, pursued their individual academic interests, and immersed themselves in local communities. A highlight for both was a visit to a Maasai village, accompanied by a Maasai elder and lecturer. This unique experience offered invaluable insights into indigenous knowledge systems, deeply enriching their understanding of community-led initiatives.

Banafsha reflected on how the internship deepened her appreciation for locally grounded research's power to transcend academia, fostering resilience and strengthening community ties. Didar was particularly moved by his conversation with Alais Morindat, a respected Maasai elder, who adeptly bridges scientific and traditional knowledge for the benefit of his community. The interns have already published three blogs based on their experiences and will continue to contribute to AKU-ACER's research projects from Karachi – you can read them here.

Beyond the internship programme, AKU-ACER continues to expand its collaborative efforts. Professor Emmanuel Sulle, Director, AKU-ACER, successfully defended the third phase of "Future Rural Africa," an interdisciplinary research collaboration with the Universities of Cologne and Bonn, with funding decisions expected in November 2025.

The AKU-ACER team is also actively preparing for two major upcoming conferences. They are co-hosting the 5 University Consortium Conference (5UCC) from September 30 to October 2, 2025, in Morogoro, Tanzania. Themed “Beyond Survival: Building Inclusive and Climate-Resilient Societies," this conference promises to be a vital platform for discussion. Additionally, AKU-ACER, in partnership with the Tanzania Wildlife Research Institute (TAWIRI), will co-host a symposium on “Ecological Innovation for Urban Futures" as part of the 15th TAWIRI International Scientific Conference in December 2025.

value.Title: AKU Maintains Momentum in Global Research Awards
value.NewsSummary: AKU’s Adnan Altaf joins 2025 Future of the Field honourees
value.NewsContent:
For the second consecutive year, the Aga Khan University (AKU) has been recognised by the Society of Research Administrators International (SRAI), underscoring the University's growing influence and excellence in research support and leadership. Adnan Altaf, Senior Manager at AKU's Research Office in Pakistan, has been named a 2025 honouree in SRAI's prestigious Future of the Field programme.

Selected from a competitive pool of global nominees, Adnan is recognised among the next generation of leaders shaping the future of research administration. SRAI is the world's leading network of research management professionals, with members across more than 40 countries. Through education, professional development, and knowledge-sharing, it advances research excellence across institutions and regions.

Its Future of the Field initiative honours early- to mid-career professionals who demonstrate innovation, leadership, and impact—both institutionally and globally. AKU received the same distinction in 2024 when Melaine D'Cruze of the Research Office was selected, making this back-to-back recognition a significant milestone for the University.

“In a field as dynamic as research administration, the need for visionary, adaptable leaders has never been greater," said Dara C. Little, President of SRAI. “The recipients of Future of the Field are not only navigating complexity—they are driving the profession forward."

Adnan's entry into research administration was grounded in financial management and shaped through years of experience on international health and education projects. At AKU, he has played a key role in professionalising research support services, strengthening compliance systems, and leading capacity-building initiatives across the institution.

Reflecting on the award, Adnan shared, “I remain committed to advancing research administration as both a profession and a catalyst for equitable global impact. This recognition is also a testament to the incredible work of colleagues across our research ecosystem who make complex, meaningful research possible every day."

In addition to this honour, Adnan received the 2025 SRAI John Robinson Travel Scholarship, awarded to a select few whose applications demonstrate exceptional promise and merit.

Commenting on the recognition, Dr Salim Virani, Vice Provost of Research and Professor of Medicine at AKU, said, “Global engagement through SRAI enhances AKU's ability to serve research communities with excellence and integrity. Adnan's recognition not only reflects his  leadership but also strengthens our capacity to integrate global best practices and deliver research that drives meaningful change. That two of our professionals have received this honour in consecutive years is a powerful testament to our institutional momentum."

The 2025 Future of the Field honourees also include professionals from the University of California, University of Zimbabwe, Kenyatta Hospital, Virginia Commonwealth University School of the Arts in Qatar, and Vital Pakistan Trust.

value.Title: The Library as a Green Hub for a Sustainable Future
value.NewsSummary: New study shows academic libraries are transforming into climate action centres
value.NewsContent:
​Academic libraries in East Africa are emerging as dynamic agents of sustainability. They're not just about books and research anymore; these institutions are blending their traditional roles with innovative, climate-conscious practices. A recent publication by Dr Arnold Mwanzu, Associate Professor and Associate University Librarian, East Africa at AKU, and researcher Joseph Mwangi, offers new insights into how these libraries are contributing to the global Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), particularly through the lens of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD).

Drawing on research from over 170 institutions across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, and Ghana, the study explores how academic libraries are adapting their spaces, policies, and programmes to support environmental stewardship. It highlights that libraries are not just repositories of knowledge; they are becoming proactive, community-focused hubs where climate literacy and sustainable values are nurtured.

This research, published in a global academic volume, explores the UNESCO framework of ESD which encourages learners and institutions to actively work towards achieving the SDGs. For Dr Mwanzu, the work is consciously personal. “I'm passionate about green libraries," he shared. “While there's a lot of research from Europe and North America, there's almost nothing from sub-Sahara Africa. We wanted to change that."

Some impressive examples include Kenya's United States International University-Africa (USIU-A), where large windows and zoned lighting in the library significantly cut down on electricity use. Catholic University, another Kenyan institution, conserves municipal water by using harvested rainwater to maintain its gardens. Both institutions track their energy consumption and integrate green values into campus life.

“These libraries are not just passive buildings," Dr Mwanzu explained. “They are actively reducing their carbon footprints and educating students on sustainable living. USIU was even shortlisted for the IFLA Green Library Award in 2017, a major moment for African libraries on the global stage."

In Uganda, Makerere University stood out for its community outreach,​ organising tree planting drives and public awareness campaigns. Rwanda's University of Global Health Equity links environmental sustainability with public health, while the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania leads the way in educating users on climate literacy.

Despite these strides, progress is uneven. One of the key challenges, according to Dr Mwanzu, is not funding, but perception.

“There's a widespread view that climate change is someone else's responsibility, especially because Africa contributes relatively little to global emissions. But that mindset is a barrier," he said. “Libraries are in a unique position to build eco-consciousness and shift those narratives."

Indeed, the role of academic libraries is evolving rapidly. No longer just storehouses of books, they are becoming vibrant civic spaces that offer workshops, exhibitions, and curated resources on climate action. Many are now embracing “green information literacy", a shift from traditional research skills to those that empower students to critically evaluate environmental data, policy, and misinformation.

This last point is crucial. In an era of rising anti-intellectualism and misinformation, particularly around climate science, libraries are trusted institutions that can provide accurate, unbiased knowledge. “Libraries are knowledge guardians," Dr Mwanzu said. “But they're also becoming knowledge activists. And for that, they need recognition and support."

His call to action is clear: empower libraries as strategic partners in development, not just through infrastructure, but through collaboration, research investment, and policy support.

“Every small action counts," he said. “And when libraries lead, communities follow."

value.Title: “Don’t think too long, just start” says GSMC Alumna
value.NewsSummary: Scarlet Chemarum, a Communications Manager, sets her eyes on Media Business Leadership
value.NewsContent:
​

For Scarlet Chemarum, a master's degree wasn't just another line on a resume. Having completed her undergraduate studies in Uganda, she had a clear mission: to become a key player in Kenya's dynamic media and communications industry. She knew she needed more than a degree; that's why she chose the Aga Khan University's Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC) to pursue a Master of Arts in Digital Journalism. Its stellar reputation and pragmatic, real-world approach were exactly what she needed to bridge her past experience with her future ambitions.

Scarlet's time at GSMC was nothing short of transformative. She found every aspect of the programme – from the dedicated faculty and their engaging teaching methods to life-changing opportunities like international internships – to be meticulously designed and deeply purposeful.

Yet this journey was not without its inherent challenges. She was a young mother, juggling demanding coursework with the responsibilities of family life, all while navigating financial pressures. The path was challenging but she found immense strength in the programme's flexible structure and the unwavering support of her faculty. She fondly refers to them as her "God-sent," recalling those late nights spent balancing the needs of a newborn with stringent thesis deadlines.

The impact of GSMC reached far beyond the classroom. It was through the School's robust peer network that Scarlet landed her first major opportunity post-graduation. This experience powerfully showed her that the programme's community is one of its most valuable assets.  

Today, Scarlet is a thriving Brand and Communications Manager at Bamburi Cement Plc. Her ambitions don't stop there; she's set her sights on a directorship and, eventually, starting her own consultancy. "There are so many paths I can take with the skills I now have. GSMC gave me the mindset and tools to dream bigger," she shares, embodying the ambitious spirit the institution champions.

Scarlet's perspective on the media industry also evolved. While some saw the rise of digital media as a threat, she saw it as an opportunity. Fortified with the advanced digital tools and strategic foresight she gained at GSMC, she isn't just navigating the changing landscape – she's leading in it. "We looked at the digital takeover as a threat, but now, we're thriving thanks to the skills we gained at GSMC," she says, highlighting the programme's proactive mindset.

For anyone considering the journey she took, Scarlet's advice is simple and clear: “Don't think too long, just start. It's worth it." For her, GSMC didn't just fulfil a professional need; it ignited a lifelong passion for continuous learning. It gave her the confidence to embrace whatever future challenges may arise.

When asked to summarize her experience, Scarlet's response is full of enthusiasm: “If I could sum it up in one sentence? Let's do it again!"

​

value.Title: Anne’s Journey in Shaping the Future of Children’s Media
value.NewsSummary: GSMC alumna Anne Junny Sato builds a future of children’s edutainment in Africa
value.NewsContent:
​

When Anne Junny Sato enrolled in the Executive Masters in Media Leadership and Innovation (EMMLI) programme at the Graduate School of Media and Communications (GSMC), she was already navigating the demanding responsibilities of a senior leadership role at Akili Network. But she recognized a need to deepen her leadership skills and strengthen her ability to guide a mission-driven media organization.

“I wanted to better myself as a leader," Anne explains. “GSMC's world-class, holistic approach to media education offered exactly that."

One of the most transformative aspects of the programme, she says, was the collaborative learning environment. “Engaging with other media leaders from across East Africa was incredibly enriching." The relationships she built during the programme extended beyond the classroom. “We still touch base and lift each other up in our respective roles. That support has been invaluable."

Balancing the demands of the programme with her professional and family life was no small feat. The academic load, particularly the research component, was intense. But Anne took it in stride. “Sacrifice, commitment, and passion kept me going," she reflects. “Beyond the theory, I discovered practical, innovative solutions to real-world challenges in the media industry."

Today, Anne leads with greater clarity, purpose, and confidence. She credits the programme with sharpening her strategic thinking and strengthening her decision-making through the use of data and evidence. “I now approach problems with a mindset focused on impact. From audience growth to revenue strategies, I see tangible results in our work."

Looking ahead, Anne envisions herself as a pioneer in the children's edutainment space and as a mentor to the next generation of media professionals. She remains committed to advancing high-quality, educational content for young audiences across Africa.

“GSMC transformed me," she says. “It gave me the mindset, networks, and tools to lead boldly in a rapidly evolving media landscape."

To those considering the EMMLI programme, Anne has clear advice. “You're not just signing up for a degree. You're stepping into a transformative journey that will challenge, inspire, and empower you."​
